answers.accuracy_reason: Man as the image of the image (Christ being the image of God) is an old patristic idea. Burton's following English does explain it rather than translate it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Summum genus is correctly defined as the most general class in the scholastic (Porphyrian) scheme.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is indeed the title of a tract that Burton cites.
answers.usefulness_reason: Only labels the phrase as a title and says nothing about the work or its author.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Caepit' is an early-modern spelling of 'coepit', and 'delirare' does mean to rave or dote.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote does go on to cite Boissardus, book 1. 'De praestig.' points to his work on magical illusions (De divinatione et magicis praestigiis).

answers.accuracy_reason: Innatae is an adjective going with 'causes', and Burton does gloss the three Latin terms as 'inward, innate, and inbred'.

answers.accuracy_reason: A popina was a cookshop or low eating-house, and the phrase is scornful.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the sense of popina and the tone of the phrase, but does not locate it in Seneca.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote sits at 'slaves' in the main text, and Burton's English takes up only 'mancipia'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The citation does refer to Egnatius (Giovanni Battista Egnazio), who wrote on and annotated the lives of the emperors. The main text names him.

answers.accuracy_reason: Understanding 'drink' as the object fits Pliny NH 14. But the claim that the sentence goes on in item 1.2.2.2-f96 cannot be confirmed; the continuation 'ut magna pars…' follows straight on in the text, and the numbering gap looks odd.

answers.accuracy_reason: Philippians 3:19 reads 'quorum Deus venter est' in the Vulgate; this is clearly the allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: In humoral medicine 'crude' means unconcocted, or undigested.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses a technical term, but the main text already says 'raw, and as yet undigested'.

answers.accuracy_reason: De officiis 3.1 reads 'numquam se minus otiosum esse quam cum otiosus, nec minus solum quam cum solus esset'. That is indirect speech with the leisure clause first, as the note says.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tellus is the Roman personified Earth goddess.
answers.usefulness_reason: The gloss is correct but slight. It misses that in Hyginus Tellus also claims the right to name the creature.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 412 reads 'Qui studet optatam cursu contingere metam'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It notes a small verbal variant and does not name the work. This is close to a textual working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: The saying is proverbial. Its classical source is Sallust, Jugurtha 8.1 ('Romae omnia venalia esse') and 35.10, which the note does not mention, though nothing it says is false.
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats what Burton says and misses the Sallust source a reader would want.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'iisdem pro arbitrio abutentes' has no equivalent of 'make them say what they propose'. The phrase is Burton's addition.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'indigna quae vel recipiantur in triviis' does end the preceding clause, and haras/aras is a deliberate wordplay.

answers.accuracy_reason: The continuation 'putidi dicterium de clero usurpare' is quoted correctly, and the gloss is reasonable.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.85 reads 'hoc est quod palles? cur quis non prandeat hoc est?', and it mocks the pale, fasting philosopher.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Alciato's emblem on poverty holding back talent, 'Ut me pluma levat' is line 2 and 'Ingenio poteram' is line 3. Burton reverses them and leaves out the rest of the emblem.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the emblem, describes its image and says how Burton cuts and reorders it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The guess about the sense is hedged with 'perhaps', and Burton does credit 'Austin'. However, Augustine's analogy is about many small sins, so the 'vermin in the body' reading is a speculative guess.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's English does expand 'publica hilaritas' into 'all good fellowship, peace, mirth, and plenty'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Leonardo Loredan was Doge from 1501 to 1521, so he held office during the War of the League of Cambrai. Bembo records the herald's address to him in the Senate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Doge and explains whose words these are, which the reader needs.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'corum' makes no sense in Latin, and 'eorum' fits both the sense and the translation.
answers.usefulness_reason: This is a textual or misprint note, a translator's working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Per consensum' (sympathy, consent of parts) is a standard term of Galenic medicine, and here it is applied to body and soul.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical medical term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gellius 13.11 gives Varro's Menippean satire the title 'Nescis quid vesper serus vehat', and Georgics 1.461 has 'quid vesper serus vehat'. The other claims are also correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the proverb's source and shows how Burton changes the wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 7–8 reads 'velut aegri somnia, vanae / fingentur species'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The variant is correct, but it does not even name the poem, so it is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.3.11–12, says of Tigellius 'habebat saepe ducentos, saepe decem servos' as an example of his inconsistency.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies 'the Poet' and the figure meant, and it explains the point of the allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Latin is grammatically loose, and the main text does say 'of what complexion the part is, of black or red'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It notes a minor difference between the sidenote and Burton's paraphrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are rare Tertullianic words, and Burton's main text has 'imbonities, insuavities'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains Burton's odd English words, but only slightly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is the last line of Martial 10.47, not Horace.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's misattribution and gives the true source.

answers.accuracy_reason: διαιτητική is the art of regimen, or dietetics.
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats the translation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Kepler wrote the Somnium (published 1634) and the Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo (1610), his reply to Galileo.
answers.usefulness_reason: It expands Burton's cryptic abbreviations into the two works and gives their context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Naulum is the Greek-derived word for a passage fee, the coin paid to Charon for the ferry.
answers.usefulness_reason: A correct gloss, but Burton's own 'no fees to be paid' and his mention of Charon already make the sense clear.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's Latin does run on into 'stili tantum & ingenii causa'. Cunaeus's disclaimer echoes Lucian, True History 1.4, where Lucian says he will write of things that neither are nor could be.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage is from Seneca, Natural Questions 7.25 (on comets), which has 'tam rarum mundi spectaculum' and no 'fortasse'. Burton's 'cap. 35' does not match that numbering.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton changes and shortens it, adding 'perhaps' and turning Seneca's point toward God's providence.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Without book' did mean 'by heart, from memory' in early modern English.
answers.usefulness_reason: A small but helpful gloss on an old English phrase; the translation already says 'by heart'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton means Roger Bacon's Epistola de secretis operibus artis et naturae. The machines Burton lists (a chariot moving without animals, flying devices) come from that letter.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the actual work Burton cites and its full title.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's English on either side of the Latin does give its sense.
answers.usefulness_reason: It only repeats what the translation and Burton's own English already say.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source (Velleius 2.107: an old German visits Tiberius on the Elbe) is right. But 'dies' can be feminine in Latin, so it is too strong to say 'ullam' does not agree with 'diem'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out that Burton misremembers the source, putting Caesar and the Rhine in place of Tiberius and the Elbe.

answers.accuracy_reason: Valescus de Taranta was a Montpellier physician who was active around 1380–1420; his Philonium dates from 1418.
answers.usefulness_reason: A brief identification of the author; useful, but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: The grammar it describes is right: the phrase means he went even though he himself shrank from it.
answers.usefulness_reason: This is a grammar note for the translator, not for the reader.

answers.accuracy_reason: The saying is Publilius Syrus's, and it usually reads 'Comes facundus in via pro vehiculo est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of the proverb and points out Burton's change of 'facundus' to 'jucundus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.763–5 compares Mezentius to Orion and reads 'quam magnus Orion' and 'scindens'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the original context of the simile and shows how Burton adapts it to his giants.

answers.accuracy_reason: The completion it gives matches Burton's own text.
answers.usefulness_reason: It only repeats the Latin and English that come straight after the passage.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Philippics 2.65, quotes 'male parta male dilabuntur' as the words of an unnamed poet, probably Naevius, so it is a line of verse.
answers.usefulness_reason: Placing the jingle in Cicero is worth knowing, but the note gives no locus and is very brief.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.168 is quoted correctly. The note hedges its suggestion about where the Seneca sidenote belongs ('probably').
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Juvenal echo about Alexander and helps the reader place the sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a proverbial saying. It is related to the old monastic saying that a monk out of his cell is like a fish out of water.
answers.usefulness_reason: Correct, but the note gives no origin or context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's English does add 'to live at home' to Pliny's sentence (NH 16.1.4).
answers.usefulness_reason: Pointing out how Burton bends the phrase is useful, but the note does not name Pliny as the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.646: Anchises refuses to leave burning Troy.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgilian source and the speaker, which gives the phrase its force here.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a well-known proverb.
answers.usefulness_reason: A single word that tells most readers nothing new.

answers.accuracy_reason: Giulio Cesare Barricelli wrote a book called Hortus genialis (1620), and Burton cites it in the ablative.
answers.usefulness_reason: Naming the author and the book helps, but the part about the ablative is a grammar note.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Compescunt' does mean 'check' or 'restrain', and 'presently' meant 'immediately' in early modern English.
answers.usefulness_reason: The gloss on 'presently' prevents a misreading, but the rest is about word choice.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 11.16.9–10 is cited correctly, and the standard text does read 'leget'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Leone Ebreo's Dialoghi do discuss intellectual or rational love. I cannot confirm that he uses the exact term 'amor cognitionis', which may come from a Latin version, so the claim is stated too firmly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The reading is offered with hedges ('may mean', 'seems likely'), and the note claims nothing it cannot support.

answers.accuracy_reason: The definition of 'parentare' is correct.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sentence does continue in 'veraciter amicus esse hominis…', and Burton's English gloss covers the whole of it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note's reading is plausible: the clause continues the series of 'alius' examples after the Aelian statue story, and 'ne qua pars probro vacet' leads into the next sentence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.204: Aeneas says 'horresco referens' as he tells how the serpents came over the sea for Laocoön.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch's Amatorius is set around Ismenodora's carrying off of the youth Bacchon, which matches Burton's sidenote 'In amatorio'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's couplet does leave out the trembling and the 'breath of seething desire'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aristotle states the mirror-clouding belief in De insomniis 459b, while Burton cites the Problems.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the belief and corrects the locus Burton gives.

answers.accuracy_reason: The text does read 'thorosaque brachia', split across two passages.
answers.usefulness_reason: A note on how the passage is split.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Met. 1.527–8, Daphne fleeing Apollo.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plotinus, Enneads 3.5.3, derives erōs from horasis (sight).

answers.accuracy_reason: Heroides 12, Medea to Jason, recalling the moment she first saw him.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gelasimus is the hungry parasite in Plautus' Stichus, and the name comes from Greek gelasimos, 'laughable'; the reading of 'de monte aureo' as a mock title is a fair interpretation.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a proverbial tag, and Burton introduces it with 'as they say'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The violas/violentius/violas/violenta wordplay is correctly described, and Burton's English (Violets, violent, violate) does keep it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase does continue the sentence attributed to Haedus ('Summo studio parentur epulae (saith Haedus)').
answers.usefulness_reason: It only repeats what the text already shows.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton gives this as the subject of Astyanassa's writing, citing Suidas, and concubitus does mean sexual intercourse.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are Phaedra's words in Seneca's Phaedra (103–104). Pallas presides over weaving, and pensa is the allotted wool.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are a Latin version of an Anacreontic ode (the 'I would be your mirror' poem).

answers.accuracy_reason: 'John come kiss me now' was a well-known English tune and song of the period.

answers.accuracy_reason: It rightly ties the note, with suitable hedging, to the Latin rendering of Mimnermus fr. 1 (originally Greek).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the bare sidenote, but only slightly.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Memorabilia 1.3.13, Socrates advises Critobulus to stay away for a year (Xenophon himself is told to flee). Xenophon wrote in Greek.
answers.usefulness_reason: Useful but slight; the sidenote already gives the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Calcagnini's dialogue, Galatea does complain of Triton's fickleness, and the main text paraphrases it loosely.

answers.accuracy_reason: It accurately describes how the passage is marked off and identifies Platina's dialogue on love.
answers.usefulness_reason: This is mostly a working note about where the passage is marked.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase does close Burton's list of authorities.

answers.accuracy_reason: The gloss of exuviae is right, and the reading of 'exuviae noctis' is properly hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It helps with an obscure phrase but doesn't identify the source (Leech, 'Leochaeus').

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Vita jugata' does mean married, yoked life, and the quotation does break off at 'Me juvat, &c.'
answers.usefulness_reason: Explaining 'jugata' helps a little, but the remark that the quotation breaks off only repeats the '&c.'

answers.accuracy_reason: Valerius Maximus (7.2 ext. 1) reports that Socrates, asked whether a man should marry, answered that he would repent whichever he did.
answers.usefulness_reason: It links Burton's line to the classical story behind his sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are the opening lines of Terence's Adelphoe: Micio calls his slave Storax and worries about Aeschinus, his adopted son.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and situation but not the play or Terence, which is what the reader most needs.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is a play on sounds (lacerat/lacertum/Largi), and 'lacertus' is the upper arm.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase does finish Erasmus's clause, which begins 'Melius sic errare, quam zelotypiae curis'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines scan as a hexameter followed by a pentameter, so they are an elegiac couplet, and the main text gives the gist as 'such a mother, such a daughter'.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Aliud agere' is a standard Latin idiom for attending to something other than what one should.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the idiom briefly, and the translation already conveys most of it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton does render 'ob metum publicae potestatis' loosely as 'for fear of Laws'.
answers.usefulness_reason: A working note comparing Burton's English with the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Socinians did make right reason the norm for interpreting Scripture.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names the Socinians, so the note adds only a little context.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Discourses II.2 Machiavelli argues that Christianity has made men weak, and the note is right to hedge on where the Latin comes from (Burton likely used the Latin translation of the Discourses).
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, explains how the Latin relates to it, and adds a useful shade of meaning.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase does continue Burton's quotation from Josephus that begins 'exertos praebentes jugulos'.
answers.usefulness_reason: A working note on how the passage joins up, and it doesn't give the Josephus passage.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Nero 38, tells how someone quoted 'When I am dead, let earth be mingled with fire' and Nero answered 'No, while I live'; the original is in Greek.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of the anecdote and explains how Burton's Latin relates to the Greek.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Ovid, Amores 3.9.35–36, the elegy on Tibullus, and the standard text does read 'Cum rapiunt'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the exact poem and points out Burton's variant.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote points to Chrysostom's homily on Ephesians, and the description of the passage fits.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker but adds little beyond what the context already shows.

answers.accuracy_reason: It correctly completes Justin's sentence (book 20) as Burton quotes it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It only joins up and retranslates the sentence that is already in the text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Contraventio is a late or medieval Latin word. Acting against one's scruples was the casuists' standard remedy, and the note hedges this properly.
answers.usefulness_reason: The casuistry context is useful, but the punctuation remark is a translator's working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: The reading follows Agrippa's 'lapides loquimur' image of hard sayings as stones that could knock out a reader's brains.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the image but does not give Agrippa's source passage or how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the closing sentence of the Phaedo, and there Phaedo addresses Echecrates.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and corrects Burton's 'Eucrates'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Quintilian, Institutio 2.12, does attack frenzied declaimers, and the remark about the garbled syntax is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context and helps with the construction, but adds little else.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.3.50–51, reads 'hic dextrorsum abit … partibus' without 'omnes', just as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton changes it, though it gives no exact line reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: The meanings given for privus and privatus are correct.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, In Catilinam 1.30, has 'tam adultam rei publicae pestem', and the identification is hedged properly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The quotation is Juvenal 10.188, and Seneca, Letter 10.5, does read 'hominem'. 'The rest' is a little loose, since the opening 'O Jupiter contingat…' clause is not Seneca's.

answers.accuracy_reason: The infinitive is indeed reported speech.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a grammar note for the translator.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton does give the Latin as an alternative to 'supervisors', and praefecti aerarii were indeed Roman officers of the public treasury (the aerarium Saturni).

answers.accuracy_reason: Theognis 230 does read χρήματά τοι θνητοῖς γίγνεται ἀφροσύνη, and Burton's τοῖς is a variant or corruption; his Latin rendering does follow in the same sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note is right. Burton's 'pro and con' is the English phrase taken from Latin 'pro et contra', meaning for and against.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.274 reads 'quantum mutatus ab illo / Hectore, qui redit exuvias indutus Achilli'. The note correctly describes the run-on and Burton's new application of the words.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at Isaiah 28:19 has '(tantummodo) sola vexatio intellectum dabit auditui'. The tag is a proverbial shortening of it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Letters 7.26, on how illness makes men virtuous, is addressed to Maximus. The Latin tag is Burton's summary, not a quotation.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Magnum miraculum est homo' comes from Asclepius 6, which Pico quotes at the start of his Oration. Burton's text does credit Plato.
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces the real source of a famous Renaissance tag that Burton attributes elsewhere.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the legend told in the Golden Legend and elsewhere, Peter leaves his daughter Petronilla sick of a fever because 'sic expedit ei'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an allusion a reader would not otherwise understand.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.4.9–11 reads '…et cui / gratia, fama, valetudo contingat abunde'. Burton's 'forma' is a variant reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at 1 Corinthians 10:12 has 'qui se existimat stare, videat ne cadat'. Deuteronomy 8:11 is the source of the English caveat.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tristia 5.7.45–46 describes the Getae and Sarmatians around Tomis, where Ovid lived in exile.
answers.usefulness_reason: The exile context is helpful, but the sidenote already gives the source and the note is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Coma vigil was described in this way in early modern medicine, and vigilia meant morbid sleeplessness.

answers.accuracy_reason: The scholastic sense is right, and the remark about how Burton's sentence is built is a fair reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Phaedra 177–179 does read 'quae memoras scio / vera esse, nutrix; sed furor cogit sequi / peiora', and the note describes Burton's changes correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 5.21–22: Palinurus says this of the storm that turns the fleet towards Sicily; Burton's English does carry the sentence on.

answers.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 7.19–20 opens 'sed trahit invitam nova vis'; Medea speaks there, torn between love of Jason and duty to her father.

answers.accuracy_reason: Amores 2.4.5 is correct; the poem is Ovid confessing his own faults.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Peccant' was an English medical term for a faulty or morbid humour, from Latin peccans; Burton does gloss it 'or diseased'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Latin serum means whey, and physicians used the word for the watery part of the blood.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cambium did mean 'exchange' in later Latin, and medical writers listed it with ros and gluten among the secondary humours that restore the radical moisture.

answers.accuracy_reason: A 'similar part' is a homoeomerous tissue; vis cutifica is the faculty that forms skin; Burton's main text gives only the covering function.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the technical term 'similar part' and how the sidenote relates to the main text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pia mater is correctly described; the name is a medieval Latin rendering of an Arabic term ('umm raqīqa', thin/tender mother).

answers.accuracy_reason: Treatises De anima such as Melanchthon's did include anatomy, and the sidenote 'De anima.' does appear in the following section.

answers.accuracy_reason: The name duodenum comes from duodeni, after its length of twelve finger-breadths (Greek dodekadaktylon); Burton's 'twelve inches' echoes this.

answers.accuracy_reason: The mesentery attaches the intestines; 'midriff' properly means the diaphragm, so Burton's gloss is loose.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase is a standard scholastic tag about the heart. It rests on Aristotle's view (De generatione animalium II) that the heart is formed first and fails last.

answers.accuracy_reason: Mirach (Arabic marāqq) was the Arabists' term for the epigastric region or abdominal wall. Mirachial melancholy is the same thing as hypochondriacal melancholy.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aspera arteria is the old name for the trachea, called 'rough' from its cartilage rings. Ancient anatomy treated arteries as air vessels.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obsolete anatomical term and the reasoning behind it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The dura mater is the tough outer meninx. The Latin 'mater' terms come from medieval translations of the Arabic umm ('mother') names for the membranes.
answers.usefulness_reason: The origin of the odd name 'mother' is context a reader would not have.

answers.accuracy_reason: Entelechy as actuality is right, and Burton does gloss it with 'perfectio & actus primus' and then gives the English.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aristotle, De anima II.3 (414b), compares the nested faculties of soul to the triangle contained in the quadrilateral.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the point of the geometric analogy Burton cites.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid X.467–9 continues 'sed famam extendere factis, hoc virtutis opus', and Burton does break off before it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The axiom matches 'excellens sensibile corrumpit sensum', which derives from Aristotle's De anima on excessive sensibles. The remark about Burton's English preceding the axiom is accurate.

answers.accuracy_reason: The etymology is correct. Aristotle lists epichairekakia among the passions in Nicomachean Ethics II (1107a, 1108b), and Burton's English does add grief at others' prosperity.

answers.accuracy_reason: Position (keisthai, situs) is one of Aristotle's ten categories, which the schools called predicaments.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains Burton's technical phrase 'predicament of Situs'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tradux means a vine-layer, and 'ex traduce' is the standard formula for traducianism.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives both the image behind the word and the doctrine it names.

answers.accuracy_reason: Goclenius published his collection Psychologia (Ψυχολογία, hoc est de hominis perfectione…) at Marburg in 1590.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the book behind Burton's abbreviated reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's 'lib. 10 de rep.' is the myth of Er (Republic 614b–621d), where souls draw lots and choose their next lives.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Lucretius, De rerum natura 3.445–446; Burton's 'lib. 1' is a misreference.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the correct scholastic sense of the term, and Burton's next words ('Dotage, or Anguish of the mind') do name the genus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Appetitus caninus or fames canina is the standard old medical name for morbid, ravenous hunger, i.e. bulimia.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aetius's Tetrabiblos is divided into four tetrabibloi of four sermones each, and Tetrab. 2 serm. 2 cap. 9 is on melancholy.

answers.accuracy_reason: Mirach (from Arabic marāqq) means the abdominal wall or lower belly in medieval Latin medicine, so mirachialis melancholy is the abdominal (hypochondriacal) kind.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains an obscure Arabic-Latin technical term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.65 reads 'et quid opus Cratero magnos promittere montis?'; Craterus was a well-known physician, also named by Horace and Cicero.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'ad classica' is right (De III cons. Honorii 98). But the lines speak to Honorius ('cui… cui'), praising him as heaven's favourite, so the note's 'fighting on Theodosius's side' is only loosely right (the battle, at the Frigidus, was Theodosius's).

answers.accuracy_reason: Theodoret (HE 3.20/25) does report Julian's 'Vicisti, Galilaee', and the words are rightly called legendary.

answers.accuracy_reason: Psalm 90(91):6 in the Vulgate has 'daemonio meridiano', the noonday demon, and the gloss matches Burton's 'noonday'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Damianus à Goes is Damião de Góis, the Portuguese humanist who wrote on the northern peoples (e.g. the Lapps). The identification is right.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pica is the morbid craving for unfit foods, classically linked with pregnancy, and it matches the 'longing' in the main text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Adurere/adust refers to the overheating of humours thought to produce melancholy. That is correct humoral theory.

answers.accuracy_reason: The anti-beer verses, including 'Stygiae monstrum conforme paludi', are by Henry of Avranches, and the note describes Burton's attribution correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'De subtiliss. dieta' is Galen's De victu attenuante (the thinning diet), and the gibe is read correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Per accidens as opposed to per se is the correct scholastic distinction.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Annals 16.18, uses 'erudito luxu' of Petronius, the elegantiae arbiter.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a Tacitean allusion a reader would likely miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ecclesiasticus 37:34 in the Vulgate does read 'propter crapulam multi obierunt'. The note fairly calls the saying proverbial.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.140–144 describes a man who eats a whole boar alone and then takes an undigested peacock into the bath. Sudden death and dying without a will follow, so the note is right.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 1.250–251 describes the antipodes, and the line reads 'illic sera rubens accendit lumina Vesper'. Burton's 'Illis' is indeed his change.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Verr. 2.5.26 says Verres was seldom seen 'non modo extra tectum, sed ne extra lectum quidem'. That is the source of the jingle.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.738–739 reads 'ille impiger hausit / spumantem pateram', said of Bitias at Dido's feast. There is no 'vino' in Virgil's text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Santorio's De statica medicina (Venice, 1614) taught regimen by weighing the body and what goes in and out of it. The identification is plausible and properly hedged ('almost certainly').
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a book title that a reader would likely take as a generic phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Philippians 3:19 in the Vulgate reads 'quorum deus venter est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the biblical allusion behind Burton's tag.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 2.272 does read 'adeo in teneris consuescere multum est'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In early modern medicine a cautery was used to open an 'issue', a sore kept open on purpose so that humours could drain. Here it has dried up. The note matches 'issue' in the main text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.36 reads 'inversum contristat Aquarius annum'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 6.70.15 reads 'non est vivere, sed valere vita est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a source Burton does not name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 3.995–7 is the political Sisyphus passage, ending 'semper victus tristisque recedit'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Euripides, IA c. 450, Agamemnon complains that kings are slaves to the crowd. The note's doubt about Homer is properly hedged.

answers.accuracy_reason: Nabal means 'fool', and 1 Sam. 25:25 plays on the name ('Nabal is his name, and folly is with him').

answers.accuracy_reason: The two senses of genius and the idiom 'genium defraudare' (Terence, Phormio 44; Plautus) are correctly given.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aeneid 6.417–22 the Sibyl throws Cerberus an offa drugged with honey and medicated grain, and the note presents this only as an allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.28–29 has 'sponsi Penelopae nebulones Alcinoique / in cute curanda plus aequo operata iuventus', describing idle consumers, and the note gives Burton's use of it correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.20.18 reads 'balba senectus', so Burton's 'alba' is indeed a variant.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 5.125–7 has 'duceris… ponere foris… temptaveris', in the second person, and Burton recasts this in the third person.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tithonus, given immortality without youth, became a cicada, and Latona turned the Lycian peasants into frogs (Ovid, Met. 6).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains both mythological allusions, which a reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is a well-known medieval proverbial distich. Galen stands for medicine, Justinian for law, and genus/species (terms of logic) for philosophy and the arts.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 83 does have the line 'et qui sollicitat nuptas, ad praemia peccat' before 'sola pruinosis…', and the standard reading is 'castra', not 'rostra'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Persius 3.85 the centurion uses these words to mock the philosophers' pale, hungry study, and the text reads 'hoc est quod palles?'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 9.73.7 reads 'At me litterulas stulti docuere parentes', so Burton's 'Quid' does make it a question.

answers.accuracy_reason: The quotation is Horace, Satires 1.1.66–67, and the note's paraphrase is correct.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is Horace, Epistles 1.1.65–66 ('rem facias, rem, / si possis, recte, si non, quocumque modo rem'), and the paraphrase is accurate.

answers.accuracy_reason: Fasti 1.357–358 reads 'rode, caper, vitem; tamen hinc, cum stabis ad aram…', and the vine-gnawing goat is sacrificed for it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Q. Servilius Caepio plundered the sacred gold of Tolosa in 106 BC, and his ruin made the phrase proverbial.

answers.accuracy_reason: The usual form ends 'nescit regnare', and the note rightly hedges the attribution (Louis XI, Frederick I, Sigismund and others are named).

answers.accuracy_reason: In Pharsalia 10.185–186 Caesar speaks to Acoreus and says 'vacavi', so the sidenote's 'lib. 8' is indeed wrong.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker, gives Burton's change of person and corrects his reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 3.80 reads 'rex Anius, rex idem hominum Phoebique sacerdos', which describes the king of Delos.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source correctly, but very briefly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The unguentum armarium was the weapon-salve, applied to the weapon and supposed to heal by sympathy. This was the subject of the Goclenius and Libavius dispute.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical and historical term that a modern reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Paracelsus does describe imagination as a star or astrum working within a man, and Burton names Paracelsus just before.
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces an unusual phrase to its Paracelsian source and explains what it means.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Georgics 2.272 reads 'adeo in teneris consuescere multum est', not 'adeo a teneris assuescere multum est'. The note puts Burton's wording into Virgil's mouth. The other claims (the misprint, Ovid, Met. 7.20–21, and the main text rendering only the first sentence) are right.

answers.accuracy_reason: Chrysostom's treatise 'Quod nemo laeditur nisi a seipso' does exist, and this is its title.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the patristic source of the tag.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aphorisms 6.23 says only that lasting fear and despondency are melancholic. The circular causation is not in it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The gloss of atribilarius is right. The identification with James Hepburn, who died insane in Danish captivity, is properly hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical word and suggests who the man is.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Augustus 78 does read 'neque in tenebris vigilavit umquam nisi assidente aliquo', and Burton has rearranged it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows how Burton reworks the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Fidus Achates' is Virgil's standing epithet in the Aeneid and became proverbial.
answers.usefulness_reason: Many readers already know the allusion, but the note is a brief help.

answers.accuracy_reason: Paolo Giovio wrote the Elogia, short lives of famous men.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source but says nothing more about it.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.1.61, the phrase describes the good man with a clear conscience, and Burton applies it to the shameless.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton reverses the sense of his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is Horace, Epistles 1.2.58–59, which begins with 'invidia'. Burton's sidenote reads only 'Hor.'
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the locus and the word Burton leaves out, which is the subject of the passage.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate Psalm 72:3 reads 'quia zelavi super iniquos', so Burton's Latin is not the Vulgate wording.
answers.usefulness_reason: The main text already cites Psalm 73, so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.775–776, his portrait of Invidia.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source of an uncited quotation, though it gives no exact locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.780–2, reads 'intabescitque videndo / successus hominum carpitque et carpitur una / suppliciumque suum est'. So Burton's dash does leave out 'carpitque et carpitur una'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It restores the striking phrase Burton cut and shows how he trims his source, where his sidenote gives only 'Ovid.'

answers.accuracy_reason: Sallust, Catiline 10.1, reads 'Carthago aemula imperi Romani ab stirpe interiit'. The two changes the note describes are real.
answers.usefulness_reason: This is an accurate comparison with the source, but it records only small verbal changes that matter little to a reader.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal, Satires 3.182–3, reads 'hic vivimus ambitiosa / paupertate omnes'. Burton does replace 'vivimus' with 'laboramus'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the unmarked source and shows how Burton changes the verb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.4 refers to Aeneas being tossed on land and sea because of Juno's wrath. Burton applies it to the ruin of Troy.
answers.usefulness_reason: The point about how Burton shifts the line is fair but small, and the note doesn't give the locus (Aeneid 1.4).

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.8, is about the Iliad (the 'fabula' about Paris and the Greeks), which 'stultorum regum et populorum continet aestus'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader what 'it' refers to in Horace, which the bare quotation hides.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Amatoria 3.503–4 does read 'nigrescunt sanguine venae' and 'Gorgoneo saevius igne micant'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus where Burton's sidenote says only 'Ovid.' and notes how his text differs.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.367 is spoken by Dido to Aeneas, accusing him of having been suckled by Hyrcanian tigresses.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the speaker and the context of the allusion and links them to Burton's argument about nurses' milk.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Fabius' is indeed Quintilian, who speaks of dry, severe teachers ('aridi magistri') in Institutio Oratoria book 2. The sense given for 'dry' is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifying 'Fabius' as Quintilian helps a reader who would not otherwise know who is meant.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal, Satires 7.187–8, reads 'res nulla minoris / constabit patri quam filius', and it is said in the context of fathers grudging money for their sons' teachers.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and the context, which shows the line means 'costs less' rather than 'is worth less'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Camerarius, Centuria II, emblem 77, is plausibly the ape emblem, but I cannot confirm that its motto reads 'perdit amando' or that Burton cut that motto short.
answers.usefulness_reason: Linking the emblem to 'Aesop's Ape' and the ape that kills its young by hugging them explains the allusion well.

answers.accuracy_reason: Sophocles' Ajax was traditionally titled 'Mastigophoros' (the Whip-bearer). In the play the maddened Ajax slaughters and flogs captured livestock that he takes for the Greek leaders.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a learned joke that a reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Confessions 1.14.23 contrasts 'liberam curiositatem' with 'meticulosam necessitatem'. Burton's 'cap. 4' doesn't match that numbering; he probably meant chapter 14.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the right locus, corrects Burton's reference, and supplies the contrast that gives the phrase its point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Alciato's emblem 'In subitum terrorem' has Pan/Faunus asking who blows his horns, and the link to 'panic' is right. The double sense of 'cornua' is a fair reading of the joke.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the emblem's link to 'panic fears' in the main text and the point of the pun.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.883 is Anchises speaking of Marcellus, Octavia's son and Augustus' nephew. Donatus' Life of Virgil says Octavia fainted, not Livia.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the allusion and points out that Burton has the wrong woman faint.

answers.accuracy_reason: Eclogue 7.26 reads 'invidia rumpantur ut ilia Codro', and Burton does reuse it for laughter.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton bends it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aristotle's eutrapelia is the mean between boorishness (agroikia) and buffoonery (bomolochia), which matches Burton's rusticity and scurrility.
answers.usefulness_reason: The Aristotelian background explains the frame of Burton's definition.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.12 reads 'sum petulanti splene cachinno'. The spleen was traditionally held to be the seat of laughter (Pliny and others).
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source line and the physiology behind the phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 5.2 reads 'ut bona summa putes aliena vivere quadra', and 'quadra' is a square piece of bread.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus, explains a term and shows Burton reframing the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Devizes was commonly called 'the Vies' locally.
answers.usefulness_reason: It clears up a small sidenote, which is helpful but minor.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca Ep. 4.5 reads 'inter mortis metum et vitae tormenta... vivere nolunt, mori nesciunt'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds an unacknowledged echo, which Burton's own English ('betwixt fear of death, and torments of life') also follows.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 2.458 reads 'O fortunatos nimium, sua si bona norint, agricolas'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the famous allusion and its context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace Sat. 1.3.127–28 mocks the Chrysippean claim that the wise man is a cobbler though he never made a shoe.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Stoic paradox that Burton's 'how doth he prove it?' plays on.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 83 reads 'sola pruinosis horret facundia pannis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already names Petronius, and the omitted 'sola' is a minor textual point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Porcius Licinus' verses in Suetonius' Vita Terenti read 'abit Graeciam in terram ultimam'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an unattributed quotation and its source.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Gnatho's speech at Eunuchus 2.2, 'video sentum squalidum aegrum, pannis annisque obsitum' comes several lines before 'hic ego illum contempsi prae me', so Burton does join separate lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Genium defraudare' (Terence, Phormio 44, 'suom defrudans genium') is the idiom for stinting oneself, and the note explains it correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch (Demosthenes 20) and Cicero (De Divinatione 2.118) report Demosthenes' gibe that the Pythia 'philippizes'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an allusion a reader would not otherwise understand.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.353, on Narcissus, reads 'multae cupiere puellae'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and Burton's change of a word.

answers.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Satyricon 137.9: 'Quisquis habet nummos, secura navigat aura… uxorem ducat Danaen'. The Danaë story is told correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 5.135–137 reads 'ab ipsis / ilibus', and the lines imagine Virro fawning on Trebius if Trebius came into money.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.5.12–14 is Tiresias advising Ulysses on legacy-hunting, and first fruits were offered to the Lar.

answers.accuracy_reason: Machiavelli, Istorie fiorentine IV.16, gives Giovanni di Bicci's deathbed speech to Cosimo and Lorenzo. The note rightly hedges its reading of the sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.38–40 reads 'nunc non e manibus illis… nascentur violae?', a question asked after the dead poet has been praised.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the first line of Horace, Satires 1.2, where flute-girls, quacks, beggars and mimae mourn Tigellius. Ambubaiae were Syrian flute-girls.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and explains an obscure word.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 37 says of Fortunata 'in caelum abiit' in the sense that she has risen in the world, and it has no 'recta'.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'proiecta vilior alga' is Virgil, Eclogue 7.42. Horace, Satires 2.5.8 reads 'et genus et virtus nisi cum re vilior alga est', so the link to the 'Hor.' sidenote is apt and suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and explains a puzzling sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 13.141–42 sets 'gallinae filius albae' against 'nos viles pulli nati infelicibus ovis', as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and the proverb of the white hen that the line answers.

answers.accuracy_reason: Being sent to the pistrinum is a stock threat to slaves in Plautus and Terence, and Sosia is a stock slave name. The rest of the note is a fair description of what Burton does.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Plutus (about lines 535–47), Chremylus lists what Poverty provides: lice, fleas, rags, a stone for a pillow, and so on.

answers.accuracy_reason: The full line is Juvenal 2.63, 'dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas', and the note gives its sense correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note reads the dice throws correctly, and it is properly hedged ('appears to be') on whether the jingle was proverbial.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is Georgics 4.83, 'ingentes animos angusto in pectore versant'. The note pairs the sidenote correctly with the main-text variant and identifies the augustas/angustas pun.

answers.accuracy_reason: It cites Georgics 4.83 correctly and links the line correctly to its paired sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: These verses are Porcius Licinus, quoted in Suetonius' Life of Terence.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an author that Burton leaves unnamed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.79–80 begins 'nec, si miserum Fortuna Sinonem / finxit, vanum etiam mendacemque improba finget', so dropping 'nec' does reverse the sense.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton turns the meaning of his source upside down.

answers.accuracy_reason: Theognis 175–76 addresses Cyrnus ('Κύρνε') and speaks of the monster-filled sea and steep cliffs. Reading 'Cerne' as the vocative of Cyrnus is right, though it may be a variant spelling rather than a corruption.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the locus and clears up a confusing word.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Alciato's emblem on poverty holding back great talents (one hand winged, the other holding a stone). In Alciato, 'Ut me pluma levat' comes before 'Ingenio poteram', so the note is right that Burton reverses them.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the emblem and its image, and shows how Burton reorders and cuts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Aeneid 6.625–627, the Sibyl on the punishments in Tartarus ('omnia poenarum percurrere nomina possim'). Burton does put causarum for poenarum, possum for possim, and changes the word order.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Virgilian source and shows the pointed swap of 'causes' for 'punishments'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Remedia Amoris 420, does read 'quae non prosunt singula, multa iuvant'. The note is properly hedged about Burton inverting it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points to the Ovidian line that Burton turns around.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aegeus threw himself into the sea when he saw the black sail on Theseus's ship, which he took to mean his son was dead.

answers.accuracy_reason: The locus (Ecl. 5.24–26, the mourning for Daphnis) is right. But the claim that the translation's line breaks match the Latin is only partly true: the break after 'tasted the river' does not match the Latin line, which begins 'Libavit quadrupes'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Titus 1, calls Titus 'amor ac deliciae generis humani'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and explains why Burton calls Prince Henry 'our Titus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note says Burton's wording differs from Ausonius. In fact Ausonius's epigram (after Anth. Pal. 9.44) reads 'at qui condiderat, postquam non repperit aurum, / aptavit collo quem reperit laqueum', which is essentially what Burton quotes, so the source can be named.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the story behind the couplet and where it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.667–668 describes the lament after Dido's suicide. Taking 'tecta' as the buildings or house is a fair reading.
answers.usefulness_reason: The context is helpful, but the gloss on 'tecta' is a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are Hadrian's dying verses, given in the Historia Augusta (Hadr. 25.9). Burton does leave out 'hospes comesque corporis' and the last two lines.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the poem and shows what Burton cuts.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ovid, Met. 2, Aglauros opens the chest (holding Erichthonius) that Minerva had given to Cecrops's daughters.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the myth that the allusion depends on.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Cui bono' is the question of L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla as a judge, preserved by Cicero. Burton uses it in the looser sense 'to what use?'
answers.usefulness_reason: Correct but slight background on a familiar tag.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase is associated with L. Cassius through Cicero, and here Burton uses it loosely to mean 'to what end'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Correct but slight, and it repeats the earlier note on the same phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny's letter 2.1 to Romanus is about the death and funeral of Verginius Rufus, and it contains 'Verginium cogito, Verginium video…', which Burton paraphrases.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader who Burton's 'Virginius' is and why Pliny is grieving.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'ἐγγύα, πάρα δ᾽ ἄτη' is the maxim of the Seven Sages (given to Thales or Chilon), and Erasmus renders it as 'Sponde, noxa praesto'. Prov. 11:15 does follow in Burton's text.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Greek proverb behind the Latin and links it to the scriptural parallel.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Nemesianus, Ecl. 2.43–45. His eclogues came down with those of Calpurnius and were long printed with them.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's attribution and explains how he came to make it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aen. 1.27 names the slight to Juno's beauty at the judgment of Paris as a cause of her anger. Reading it against 'cast in a suit' is a fair interpretation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and shows why it fits Burton's sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aen. 4.560 Mercury appears to the sleeping Aeneas and asks 'nate dea, potes hoc sub casu ducere somnos?' Aeneas is still at Carthage, sleeping on his ship.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the speaker and the dramatic setting that Burton's bare 'Virg.' leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ausonius's epigram on Lais's mirror (after the Greek of Anth. Pal. 6.1), 'cernere' comes in the line before, and this is the last line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Odes 3.27 is Europa's lament after the bull has carried her off to Crete.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and the situation that Burton's citation does not give.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aen. 5.21–22 Palinurus tells Aeneas that they cannot hold their course against the storm.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton turns it to a new use.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hor. Sat. 2.2.77–79 goes on 'atque adfigit humo divinae particulam aurae'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows what Burton cut from the quotation, and the cut line bears on his body–soul argument.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Per consensum' is the standard term for the sympathy between organs in Galenic medicine.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term that recurs throughout the book.

answers.accuracy_reason: φρένες does mean both the diaphragm or midriff and the mind or wits, and phrenitis comes from it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the double sense that Burton's argument depends on.

answers.accuracy_reason: The mesentery holds the intestines and is a different structure from the diaphragm, so Burton's equation of the two is a slip.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out an anatomical confusion that a reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note says 'most probably' haemorrhoides and offers haemorrhagia as an alternative, so it is properly hedged. Old medicine did count a suppressed haemorrhoidal flow as a cause of melancholy.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a garbled technical term and the medical idea behind it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Greek proverb (dis krambe thanatos) and Juvenal's 'crambe repetita' (7.154) are both correctly cited. Burton does gloss the phrase straight after it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the proverb's source and how it was used.

answers.accuracy_reason: Varro's Menippean title is correctly given and cited from Gellius 13.11. Georgics 1.461 does read 'quid vesper serus vehat'. Burton's change of wording and his English addition are described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the classical source and shows how Burton changes the wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the opening couplet of Ausonius's epigram, quoted and translated correctly, and it matches Burton's sidenote 'Ausonius'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The couplet shows the original point of the line, a warning to the newly rich, which a reader would not get from the fragment.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Ad Atticum 14.1.2, reports Caesar's remark about Brutus: 'quidquid vult valde vult'. The note correctly says Burton puts it in the plural.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a famous allusion that the text does not name.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate reference (Ps 101:7–8) and the AV reference (Ps 102:6–7) are right, and so is the reading 'in tecto'. The note is right that 'Psal. 62' is a wrong citation.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Hippocrates, Aphorisms 6.23, which Galen discusses in De locis affectis book 3. The truncation is described correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Menedemus's speech in Heautontimorumenos, Act 1 scene 1, as Burton's sidenote says.

answers.accuracy_reason: The quotation of Satires 2.7.28–29 is accurate. Burton does change the verbs to the third person and stops before "levis".

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.17–18 does read "poscis" and "recusas", addressed to an idle student. The sense given for "lallare" is right.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero does write "pudor quidam paene subrusticus" (Ad Familiares 5.12.1), and the gloss is right.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.733–734 is quoted correctly, and the note describes Burton's changes accurately. His English verse does leave out "desire".

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Cicero's verse rendering of Iliad 6.201–202, given at Tusculan Disputations 3.63, where the text reads "in campis ... Aleis".

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.728 reads "nunc omnes terrent aurae", spoken by Aeneas as he flees Troy.

answers.accuracy_reason: Unguentum populeum was made from poplar buds with narcotic herbs and was used on the temples to bring on sleep.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a pharmacological term that a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage is Horace, Satires 1.3.11–12, on Tigellius ("habebat saepe ducentos, saepe decem servos").
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies "him in the Poet" and what Horace's point was.

answers.accuracy_reason: The term is correctly glossed as a morbid, insatiable hunger.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ausonius's epigram on Echo does open "Vane, quid affectas faciem mihi ponere, pictor".

answers.accuracy_reason: In Boethian ratio theory, sesquialtera is 3:2 and sesquitertia is 4:3.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cachexia is correctly defined as a bad habit of body, with general wasting and ill condition.
answers.usefulness_reason: The definition is correct, but the word is still current in English and many readers will know it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lycanthropy is correctly glossed as wolf-madness, and Burton does treat lycanthropia with the kinds of madness (1.1.1.4).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an unfamiliar disease name and links it to Burton's own account of it elsewhere.

answers.accuracy_reason: The French 'à la mort' did give English 'alamort', meaning dejected or half dead with gloom.
answers.usefulness_reason: The note on the English borrowing is pleasant but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Galenic scale of degrees for drugs that are hot, cold and so on did stop at the fourth degree, so 'ad octo' is a joking exaggeration.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the technical scale behind the joke, which a reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Superbipartiens tertias is 5:3 and superbipartiens quintas is 7:5; both ratios are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It decodes the obscure terms of Boethian ratio that Burton uses for comic effect.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note says Burton's English renders 'only the first part', but he also renders the concurrence of stomach passions ('because oftentimes the passions of the stomach concur'). Only the clause about the organs passing the affection to each other is left out. The gloss on 'digna' and the idea of sympathy between organs are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: The point about sympathy between organs is useful, but the rest is a working note on how text and translation line up.

answers.accuracy_reason: Confessions 1.13 does read 'quid miserius misero non miserante se ipsum', and the note correctly says Burton's wording differs.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the likely Augustinian source for 'saith Austin' and points out the wordplay.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Confessions 1.13 parallel is cited correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ambubaiae were Syrian flute-girls taken to be prostitutes, and Horace, Satires 1.2.1 has 'Ambubaiarum collegia'. The glosses on spintriae and tribades are also correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the classical source and explains the whole list of obscure terms.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suffocation of the womb was the old name for hysterical fits, called 'the mother' in English.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the medical concept and ties it to Burton's 'fits of the mother'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Orestes' words in his madness in a Latin version of Euripides (Orestes 255 ff.), and Electra's reply follows in the text.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the speaker and the author correctly, but it is brief and gives neither the play nor the line numbers.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Hercules Furens 313–314, reads 'quod nimis miseri volunt / hoc facile credunt'; Burton changed 'volunt' to 'timent'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows exactly how Burton bends it to suit his subject of fear.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note says correctly that 'reminiscentia' is Plato's anamnesis, the soul recollecting knowledge it had before birth.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the philosophical doctrine Burton alludes to, which a reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: In De tranquillitate animi 17.10, Seneca gives 'nullum magnum ingenium sine mixtura dementiae fuit' and credits it to Aristotle. Burton does leave out 'fuit'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the actual source of Burton's 'Aphorism of Aristotle'.

answers.accuracy_reason: De duplici martyrio first appeared in Erasmus's 1530 edition of Cyprian. It is spurious, and scholars have suspected Erasmus of writing it.
answers.usefulness_reason: A reader would want to know that this authority is spurious.

answers.accuracy_reason: The theme is from the Elder Seneca, Controversiae 5.1 (Laqueus incisus). The note describes the rescued man's suit against his rescuer correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the declamation and explains the legal point of the case.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 4.4 reads 'alius ante ostium amicae laqueo pependit'; this opens the list, which goes on with the roof and the sword. Burton does drop the mistress and change the verb.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton altered it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 3.79–81 has 'percipit humanos odium' and 'consciscant', as the note states.
answers.usefulness_reason: The note is correct but only lists textual differences; it does not say what they mean or name the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epist. 1.2.58–59, the 'greater torment' is envy, so Burton has moved the line to melancholy.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton repurposes a well-known Horatian tag.

answers.accuracy_reason: Heauton Timorumenos 421–422 has 'dies adimere aegritudinem hominibus' as a common saying. The note describes Burton's contrastive use correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and explains the rhetorical turn, which the English after the Latin does not make clear.

answers.accuracy_reason: De providentia 6.7 reads 'cavi ne quis vos teneret invitos; patet exitus: si pugnare non vultis, licet fugere'. Burton's 'cap. 8' does not match the modern chapter numbering.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note's quotation matches De ira 3.15.4.

answers.accuracy_reason: In De ira 3.15.4, any vein in the body is a road to liberty. Reading 'these' as the steep place, river and so on fits Burton's sentence.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Nepos, Atticus 22, Agrippa, 'flens atque osculans', begs Atticus 'ne id quod natura cogeret, ipse quoque sibi acceleraret'. Burton excerpts only part of that sentence.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source, which Burton does not cite.

answers.accuracy_reason: The words are from De civitate Dei 1.11, a chapter on how long or short this life is, set among the deaths in the sack of Rome. Burton's 'cap. 29' is not the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines translate Callimachus' epigram on Cleombrotus of Ambracia (Anth. Pal. 7.471), who leapt to his death after reading the Phaedo.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Greek original behind an unattributed Latin verse.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is the last line of Martial 10.47 ('Vitam quae faciant beatiorem'), not Horace.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's misattribution.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note quotes Plautus, Trinummus 339–340 correctly. Burton's 'perit' for 'perdit' and his shortened wording are accurately described.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the 'Comical Poet' and shows how Burton changes the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Jerome's Ep. 39 Christ is imagined saying 'non recipio tales animas, quae me nolente separantur a corpore'. (The letter is in fact addressed to Paula, though the note does not touch on this.)

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Martial 2.80 on Fannius, quoted correctly, and Burton does turn the question into a statement.

answers.accuracy_reason: The usual form is Publilius Syrus' 'Cuivis potest accidere quod cuiquam potest', which Seneca quotes at De tranquillitate animi 11.8.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Aeneid line (7.312), spoken by Juno, is quoted correctly, and Burton's change of person and number is described accurately.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hercules was said to have fathered sons, the Thespiadae, on the fifty daughters of Thespius.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Somnium (published posthumously in 1634) and the Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo (1610), Kepler's reply to Galileo, are both correctly identified.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Epistles 2.1.244, on Alexander's poor judgment of poetry (he patronised Choerilus).

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase is Tacitus, Histories 5.6, on Mount Lebanon, and the note correctly says that the marked word is only the author's name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Petrus Peregrinus's Epistola de magnete (1269) even describes a magnetic perpetual-motion wheel, and the note rightly says 'probably'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an obscure name and ties it to the 'magnetical virtue' in Burton's text.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the standard definition of the limbus patrum.

answers.accuracy_reason: Revelation 14:20 in the Vulgate does read 'de lacu' and 'usque ad frenos equorum'. Burton's 200 Italian miles equals 1,600 stadia at 8 stadia to the mile.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, shows how Burton changed and cut it, and explains how Ribera got his measurement.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Job 9:6 reads 'Qui commovet terram de loco suo, et columnae eius concutiuntur'. Burton's 'ver. 4' is wrong.
answers.usefulness_reason: It confirms the verse and corrects Burton's citation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cunaeus's Sardi venales is a Menippean satire, and its disclaimer that nothing written is true plainly echoes the preface to Lucian's True History; the note says 'echoes', which is suitably cautious.
answers.usefulness_reason: The link to Lucian is a real allusion worth knowing; the remark about where the marked passage ends is only a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 5.6, has 'tantos inter ardores opacum fidumque nivibus' of Lebanon, so the omission and the change of subject are described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source wording and shows how Burton cuts it and applies it to several mountains.

answers.accuracy_reason: Marco Polo (Burton's 'Polus') describes the rukh of Madagascar this way: feathers twelve paces long, and strong enough to lift an elephant.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's main text already names the 'Rucke' and Madagascar, and the note does not say that 'Polus' is Marco Polo.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Peripatetic quinta essentia is the aether, the incorruptible matter of the heavens.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the technical term for the Peripatetic view of the heavens that Burton is setting against Tycho's.

answers.accuracy_reason: Andrea Corsali wrote to Giuliano de' Medici from Cochin in January 1516 (often dated 1516/17). The letter describes the cross and the two small clouds near the south pole, which are the Southern Cross and the Magellanic Clouds.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the observer behind Burton's question and identifies the objects in modern terms.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Species' as emanated forms is right. Dee's Propaedeumata aphoristica (1558) is built on Bacon's theory of the multiplication of species, and Bacon wrote De multiplicatione specierum. The identification is suitably hedged.

answers.accuracy_reason: The question refers to the waters above the firmament in Genesis 1:7, and Burton's English does go on to discuss the question rather than translate it.
answers.usefulness_reason: The Genesis reference is useful, but many readers will recognise it, and the second sentence is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Aeneid 10.248. There it describes Aeneas's ship after the nymph pushes it on, and Burton applies it to the speed of the heavens.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton repurposes the line, though it would be better with the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: In astronomy, motion 'in longum' and 'in latum' means motion in longitude (along the ecliptic) and in latitude.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term that a reader might misread.

answers.accuracy_reason: Galen wrote a short treatise on exercise with the small ball (De parvae pilae exercitio).
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the specific Galen work Burton is drawing on.

answers.accuracy_reason: The quotation is accurate to Virgil, Eclogue 1.6–7, and the note correctly describes Burton's change to a plural relative clause while keeping the singular 'ille'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton adapts a well-known line to his patrons, though it does not name the Eclogue.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.327 reads 'o quam te memorem, virgo?' (Aeneas to Venus). John Williams is the closest antecedent in Burton's sentence.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Virgilian echo and says who is being addressed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.34–35, goes on 'possis et magnam morbi deponere partem', as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the part of the quotation that Burton cuts off with '&c' and shows how he applies it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.3–4, reads 'planius ac melius … dicit', and its subject is Homer. Burton's 'plenius' and 'dicunt' turn the line to the philosophers.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows exactly how Burton bends the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are Heron's Pneumatica (in Latin 'Spiritalia', translated by Commandino), Belopoeica and Automata.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the works and explains 'spiritalia'.

answers.accuracy_reason: De superficierum divisionibus liber, attributed to Machometus Bagdedinus, was published at Pesaro in 1570 by Dee and Commandino.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure title and who published it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Commandino's Liber de centro gravitatis solidorum was published at Bologna in 1565.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the actual book behind Burton's bare title.

answers.accuracy_reason: Bacon's Epistola de secretis operibus does say carriages may be made 'ut sine animali moveantur'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The Bacon wording is a good touch, but the rest is a gloss plus a remark about the translation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Fulminating gold is a correct description of an explosive gold compound known to seventeenth-century chemists.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical chemical term a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The weapon-salve was a Paracelsian sympathetic ointment applied to the weapon rather than the wound, as stated.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure period remedy.

answers.accuracy_reason: Puteanus's Pietatis thaumata (1617) gave 1,022 permutations of Bauhusius's line to the Virgin.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the very feat Burton alludes to with 'Putean'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.27, reads 'fruges consumere nati'; Burton singularizes it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tempe is the Peneus valley in Thessaly, and Burton's verse renders it as 'pleasant fields'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a light gloss and does not touch the Fracastorius source.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'In fieri' is the scholastic phrase for 'in the process of being made', and Williams did found a library at Lincoln.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an unfamiliar scholastic idiom in context.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Field of the Cloth of Gold took place in June 1520, which correctly corrects the sidenote's 1519.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the event and corrects the date.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pro Archia 16 reads 'adulescentiam alunt, senectutem oblectant … delectant domi', so the reordering is described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows how Burton alters it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Odes 3.9 is indeed the amoebean dialogue with Lydia.
answers.usefulness_reason: It adds little beyond the sidenote's citation, apart from naming the ode's subject.

answers.accuracy_reason: Vulgate Psalm 118:140 reads 'ignitum eloquium tuum vehementer'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the biblical source and notes Burton's variant word.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 10, describes Cleopatra's banquet hall. The line goes on 'Tyrio quorum pars maxima fuco / cocta diu', so the coverlets are indeed dyed with Tyrian purple.

answers.accuracy_reason: Quercetanus is the Latin name of Joseph Du Chesne, who wrote the Diaeteticon polyhistoricon (1606).
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an obscure author and his work, which Burton gives only in abbreviated form.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Vulgate, Proverbs 31:13 reads 'quaesivit lanam et linum' and 31:27 reads 'panem otiosa non comedit', so the note assigns each reference correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burggravius's Biolychnium came with a tract on magnetic cure drawn from Paracelsus' Mumia. The two senses of mumia given (a drug from embalmed bodies, and the Paracelsian vital balsam) are both correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term that a modern reader would misread.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source (Velleius 2.107: an old German meets Tiberius on the Elbe) is right, and so is the point about Burton's error. But the claim that 'ullam' does not agree with a 'masculine' diem is shaky: dies is often feminine, so ullam can agree with it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and corrects how Burton misremembers it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines render Odyssey 4.71–75, and Burton's English 'Clear amber' confirms how he takes electrum.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's text already names Telemachus, Menelaus and Odyssey δ; only the remark on electrum adds a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines render Iliad 22.159–161, on the chase around Troy, and Burton does say only 'the Poet'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifying Homer helps, but the note gives no line reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: Romolo Amaseo published a Latin translation of Pausanias, and Burton's sidenote names him.
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats the sidenote, adding only that he was the translator.

answers.accuracy_reason: The quoted text of Georgics 1.139–140 is right, and 'insidias avibus moliri, incendere vepres' is Georgics 1.271.

answers.accuracy_reason: Saturn was the god of agriculture, and in 'Democritus to the Reader' Burton says Saturn was lord of his geniture (the planet ruling his birth).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a double meaning a reader might miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Juvenal 6.402–405, on the woman who gossips about everything, and the Seres are conventionally taken as the Chinese.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 5.57–58 reads 'hunc alea decoquit, ille / in Venerem putris', and 'decoquit' does mean to ruin or bankrupt.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the source Burton is adapting and explains a slang word.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note is right. Horace, Epistles 2.2.172–174, reads 'puncto mobilis horae / nunc prece, nunc pretio, nunc vi, nunc morte suprema / permutet dominos et cedat in altera iura'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton cuts and reshapes his Horace.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note implies Burton changed Augustine's verb, but Augustine himself writes 'melius enim utique tota die foderent, quam tota die saltarent' (Enarr. in Ps. 91.2). 'Arare' is only the common proverbial form, so Burton's 'fodere' may be faithful to Augustine.
answers.usefulness_reason: A variant in wording that misleads about where it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Pro Murena 13, reads 'nemo enim fere saltat sobrius, nisi forte insanit'. Leaving out 'enim' does no harm.
