answers.accuracy_reason: This is the standard definition of the fallacy ignoratio elenchi.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term from logic.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 1.22, reads 'et vetabitur semper et retinebitur'.
answers.usefulness_reason: A textual variant that changes the sense somewhat; the note is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terence, Heauton Timorumenos 342, reads 'in aurem utramvis otiose ut dormias'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the proverb and points to the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 3.234–235 reads 'nam quae meritoria somnum / admittunt?'
answers.usefulness_reason: Turning the question into a statement is a minor change; the sidenote already gives the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Terence line at Andria 309 is quoted correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the probable source of the commonplace.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 3.454 reads 'alitur vitium vivitque tegendo', and it is about scab in sheep.
answers.usefulness_reason: The original context changes how a reader understands 'vitium'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero opens De senectute 1 with Ennius: 'quae nunc te coquit et versat in pectore fixa'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a hidden allusion and explains the figurative sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Remedia Amoris 589, reads 'semper habe Pyladen aliquem, qui curet Oresten'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows Burton's change and explains the mythological pair.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passions of the mind (accidentia animi) are indeed one of the six non-naturals.
answers.usefulness_reason: It places the phrase within medical theory a reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.95: the Sibyl tells Aeneas 'tu ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names a Virgilian tag that Burton leaves unattributed.

answers.accuracy_reason: The old plague rule 'cito, longe fuge, tarde redi' is correctly described.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already says 'as in a plague' and glosses the words himself, so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Charmides 156b–157a, Socrates gives this teaching (eye, head, body, soul), which he credits to a Thracian physician of Zalmoxis. This fits the sidenote 'E graeco'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Traces the unattributed Latin back to its Platonic source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch's Consolatio ad Apollonium quotes PV 'ὀργῆς νοσούσης εἰσὶν ἰατροὶ λόγοι'. Editions number this line between 377 and 380; 378 is a common citation.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the actual line behind Burton's 'out of Aeschylus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Paeon was the healer of the gods. In Julian's letter to Maximus, the Alexander-and-Homer comparison comes before the Paeonian clause.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a learned epithet and how Burton's English and Latin fit together.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aen. 1.153 reads 'ille regit dictis animos et pectora mulcet', and Aen. 1.57 reads 'mollitque animos et temperat iras'. The note's hedge 'appears to' is appropriate.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows Burton splicing two Virgil lines together.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca Ep. 10.1 reads 'Lugentem timentemque custodire solemus, ne solitudine male utatur'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Accurate on how Burton adapts the line, but the change is minor.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aphorisms 1.1 says the patient, the attendants and externals must also do their part. Burton's Latin is a loose version of it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton and his sidenote already name Hippocrates and the first aphorism.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 394–395, says of Amphion 'saxa movere sono testudinis'. The note's explanation of testudo as the lyre is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Corrects the apparent attribution to Ovid and explains a word a reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Laws 2.666a forbids wine to the young so as not to pour fire upon fire (πῦρ ἐπὶ πῦρ).
answers.usefulness_reason: Finds the place in Plato behind Burton's claim.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tusc. 3.41 reports Epicurus on the pleasant motions the eyes take from beautiful forms. The note's 'loosely echoes' is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already cites Tusc. 3 and Epicurus, so the note only pins down the wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace Sat. 2.1.71–74 begins 'Quin ubi se a vulgo', and 'illo' there is Lucilius.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifying Lucilius gives the reader context the extract lacks.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Regimen Sanitatis Salernitanum names three 'doctors': 'mens laeta, requies, moderata diaeta'. The variant the note reports is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names the Salernitan doctors, so the note mostly adds a variant reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Machiavelli's Life of Castruccio, Castruccio does say that one held wise by day will not be held a fool by night. The note is also right that Burton's English softens the saying.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton bends it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 4.12.27 is right; the next line is 'dulce est desipere in loco'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It pins down the source that Burton's bare 'Hor.' leaves vague.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 11.104 reads 'Laida nocte volo'. The note is right that Burton has put in Thais.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the two figures and shows Burton altering his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch, Lycurgus 25, records a statue of Laughter (Gelos) set up by Lycurgus. Apuleius' festival of Risus at Hypata in Thessaly is real, and the note hedges where the sidenote belongs.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the classical sources behind the allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.6.65–66 does read 'Mimnermus uti censet'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the quotation and explains the corrupted name, which a reader could not otherwise work out.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the myth, Jupiter stretched his night with Alcmena to three nights' length, and Hercules was conceived.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a mythological allusion a reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Pergraecari' does mean to revel Greek-fashion. Plautus, Mostellaria 22–23, has 'dies noctesque bibite, pergraecamini'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses an unusual word and points to its Plautine source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Publilius Syrus' sententia does read 'Comes facundus in via pro vehiculo est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of the saying and Burton's change of a key word.

answers.accuracy_reason: The proverb is correct, and Cicero gives it in Latin at Tusculan Disputations 5.118 as 'aut bibat aut abeat'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 1 has 'mellitos verborum globulos' in its attack on the declaimers.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows Burton turning a scornful phrase into one of praise.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ad Familiares 7.22 reads 'etsi domum bene potus seroque redieram', and the suggested corruption is hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It confirms the source of 'Tully by his own confession', but is mainly a textual correction.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Simonidean epitaph on Timocreon (Anth. Pal. 7.348) runs 'having eaten much, drunk much, and spoken much ill of men, here I lie, Timocreon of Rhodes'. The Latin renders its opening.

answers.accuracy_reason: Euripides, Andromache 930: Hermione says that the visits of wicked women ruined her. The Latin version is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the original sense, which differs slightly from the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aeneid 6.743, Anchises' speech on how souls are purified, manes is traditionally read (as by Servius) as the punishment or purgation each soul undergoes. Burton's general use of it is described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a hard word and how Burton changes the context it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a medieval proverbial hexameter of uncertain authorship, and Mephistopheles quotes it in Doctor Faustus.
answers.usefulness_reason: The note places the tag and gives a familiar English parallel.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 2.458–9 reads 'O fortunatos nimium, sua si bona norint, agricolas'. The note describes Burton's reordering and his dropping of the object correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton turns a line about farmers into a saying for everyone. It would be better still if it named the Georgics.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.203 reads 'forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit'. Burton's 'atque' and his dropping of 'forsan' are reported correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Most readers will know this famous line, and dropping 'perhaps' is a small change.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Ep. 1.12, to Calestrius Tiro, laments Corellius Rufus, and Burton's 'Cornelius' is a mistake. The note also says correctly that 'or else hold thy peace' is Burton's own addition.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's name for the friend and points out his loose paraphrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.2.2 reads 'nec meus hic sermo est' (the speech is Ofellus's). The wording is cited correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, and in Horace too the speaker disclaims the speech, which fits Burton's own disclaimer.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero (Tusc. 3.56) quotes Caecilius Statius: 'saepe est etiam sub palliolo sordido sapientia'. The note's comparison is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It links the proverb to a classical saying behind it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.177, about Fama, reads 'et caput inter nubila condit'. The change to the plural is reported correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero's discussion of how the blind can be wise and happy comes near the end of Tusculan Disputations 5 (5.111–117).

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 86.4 reads 'nulla in tam magno est corpore mica salis', said of Quintia. 'Salt' means wit or charm.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, explains what 'salt' means, and shows how Burton turns a remark about one woman into a general rule.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Ep. 7.26 does read 'optimos esse nos dum infirmi sumus'; Burton gives the gist.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives Pliny's exact wording, but the sidenote already points to the letter, so it adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.9.2 reads 'sed qui bellus homo est, Cotta, pusillus homo est'; the bellus/pusillus play is described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains Martial's pun on the fop, which Burton's 'little men are pretty' depends on.

answers.accuracy_reason: Władysław Łokietek's nickname means 'Elbow-high', and a cubit is about eighteen inches; it is plausible that the couplet is spoken in his person, as an epitaph-style verse in Guagninus.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the nickname and the cubit joke behind the verse.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Ciompi speech (Istorie fiorentine 3.13) is in Italian and argues that all men have one common origin; Burton's Latin is a gist, and 'Adam's sons…born in sin' is his own gloss.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows how Burton recasts Machiavelli's secular argument in theological terms.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 8.269–71 is paraphrased correctly, and Achilles is Aeacus' grandson through Peleus.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies Achilles and gives the whole Juvenal sentence that Burton only gives in fragments.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.132: Neptune rebukes the winds with these words.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the Virgilian source and Burton's ironic reuse of it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote gives Florent. hist. lib. 3, and the Ciompi speech there does argue that the great rose by fraud and force; the Latin is a rendering of Italian (perhaps through a Latin translation).
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies 'that plebeian in Machiavel' and his speech.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace Sat. 2.5.8 and Virgil Ecl. 7.42 ('proiecta vilior alga') are both quoted and located correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows that Burton has fused a Horace line with a Virgil phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.93: Juno's sarcastic 'egregiam vero laudem' to Venus.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the source of the sarcastic aside, briefly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The claim that Burton applies the phrase to all three men is unlikely: singular 'natus' most naturally tags Horace alone, and neither Socrates nor Virgil was a freedman's son. Horace, Sat. 1.6.6/45–46 is correctly identified.
answers.usefulness_reason: The source identification is useful, but the rest of the note is grammar and a doubtful reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Met. 13.140–41: Ulysses says 'genus et proavos et quae non fecimus ipsi, vix ea nostra voco'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Supplies the context (lineage and ancestors) that makes the tag apt here.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 8.1–2 is quoted correctly, and Burton's alterations are described accurately.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the opening of Juvenal's satire on nobility and shows how Burton compresses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 4.4.31–32 reads 'neque imbellem feroces / progenerant aquilae columbam'. Burton does write 'nec enim' and leave out 'imbellem'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The note names Horace and shows what Burton changed, but it gives no locus or context, so it is mostly a textual comparison.

answers.accuracy_reason: Epodes 4.5–6 reads 'licet superbus ambules pecunia, / fortuna non mutat genus'. The note gives this correctly and corrects Burton's garbled sidenote.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the poem, shows that Burton turns Horace's direct address into the third person, and fixes the reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: Claudian, In Eutropium 1.181–182 does go on 'cuncta ferit dum cuncta timet'. Burton does finish the thought with the beggar-on-horseback proverb.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the rest of the source sentence and shows how Burton swaps an English proverb in for Claudian's line.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Secundus' is Pliny the Younger. The passage paraphrases Epistles 7.26 ('optimos esse nos dum infirmi sumus').
answers.usefulness_reason: A reader might not know who 'Secundus' is or how he differs from the 'Pliny' Burton named just before.

answers.accuracy_reason: Common law presumed a child legitimate if the husband was 'within the four seas'. The context ('married women are all honest') shows Burton is being ironic.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a legal formula and Burton's joke, which a modern reader would almost certainly miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.763–765 describes Mezentius and reads 'quam magnus Orion' and 'viam scindens'. The note gives both correctly, and Nereus does stand for the sea.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the figure in Virgil's simile, explains Nereus, and shows how Burton adapts the lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Epistles 1.16.75–77, and Horace does read 'saevo te sub custode tenebo', so the correction of the sidenote is right. The quoted Latin leaves out 'saevo' while the English keeps 'cruel', but this is minor.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects the reference and shows how Burton changes the tyrant's threat into a concession.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace reads 'simul atque volam, me solvet.' 'Opinor' begins the next sentence ('hoc sentit: moriar'), and the release meant there is death.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton turns a Stoic case for choosing one's own death into Christian trust in God's will, which is a real point of interpretation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Theocritus, Idyll 4.41–42 is Corydon comforting Battus ('tomorrow will be better; hope is for the living').
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the exact source and the speakers, and Burton's sidenote gives only 'Theocritus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Epistles 1.4.14, not Ovid.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's wrong attribution.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the Latin form of the Greek proverb (πολλὰ μεταξὺ πέλει κύλικος καὶ χείλεος ἄκρου), and Burton does use it hopefully.
answers.usefulness_reason: It links the Latin to the familiar English proverb and points out that Burton reverses its usual gloomy sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Livy 39.26.9 has Philip V say 'nondum omnium dierum solem occidisse'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader which Philip is meant and where the saying comes from, which Burton's 'Philippus' leaves unclear.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 2 prose 4 reads 'infelicissimum genus infortunii est fuisse felicem'; the locus and sense are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and gives the rest of the sentence, which Burton's next clause echoes.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Medea 176 is 'Fortuna opes auferre, non animum potest'; Burton's own sidenote quotes it, and here he gives it to Zeno in altered wording.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows where the line really comes from and how Burton reassigns it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, De officiis 1.38 quotes Ennius' Pyrrhus: 'Nec mi aurum posco nec mi pretium dederitis'; the context and variant are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a fragment that is otherwise opaque, gives its context and says how Burton truncates it.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Rebus angustis animosus atque fortis appare' is Horace, Odes 2.10.21–22, so Burton's 'Od. 11' is a miscitation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's reference and separates Horace's words from Burton's frame.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Enchiridion closes (ch. 53) with the Euripides verse saying that whoever yields well to necessity is wise; this matches Burton's sidenote to Epictetus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It ties the maxim to the source Burton cites in his margin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, De providentia 3.10 has Maecenas 'tam vigilabit in pluma quam ille [Regulus] in cruce', so Burton's wording closely condenses Seneca. The claim that it 'does not follow Seneca's text' overstates the difference.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains both figures and points to the Senecan source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pseudo-Sallust, Ad Caesarem senem 1.2, attributes 'fabrum esse suae quemque fortunae' to Appius (Claudius Caecus).
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the classical source of a familiar proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Chrysostom wrote 'Quod nemo laeditur nisi a seipso'; the following English sentence renders Seneca, Ep. 98, as Burton's sidenote shows.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and stops readers taking Burton's English for a translation of the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is a sententia of Publilius Syrus ('Fortuna nimium quem fovet, stultum facit'), who was called Publius Mimus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It decodes a garbled attribution that readers could not otherwise trace.

answers.accuracy_reason: De providentia 3.3 has Demetrius' 'nihil mihi videtur infelicius eo cui nihil umquam evenit adversi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows how Burton paraphrases it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 11.208 reads 'voluptates commendat rarior usus'; Burton adds 'quippe' and uses the singular.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an unattributed quotation and Burton's changes to it.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Dives' in Vulgate Luke 16:19 became the traditional name of the rich man.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct, but most readers will know the name already.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.16.9–12 is correct, and Burton's verse does render the lictor as 'mayors' officers'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the exact locus, explains the lictor and points out how Burton makes it English.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.10.17–18 reads 'non, si male nunc, et olim / sic erit', so Burton has added 'semper'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Naming Horace and the added word helps, but the note gives no locus and is mostly about the text's wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 5.527–529: the poet's apostrophe on the poor boatman Amyclas, whose hut Caesar visits at night.
answers.usefulness_reason: Supplies the narrative context that Burton's bare 'Lucan.' leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.466 reads 'inopem me copia fecit', spoken by Narcissus; Burton's version has 'se'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the famous Ovidian tag behind Camerarius's emblem motto.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.65 reads 'quid opus Cratero magnos promittere montis?' Craterus was a physician, and the note reads the sense correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source and explains who Craterus was, which a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 90.10 reads 'culmus liberos texit, sub marmore atque auro servitus habitat'; Burton's changes are reported accurately.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already points to Ep. 90; the note mostly compares wordings.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the end of the 'Duc me, O Jupiter, et tu Fatum' line of Cleanthes' prayer, which Epictetus quotes at the close of the Enchiridion.
answers.usefulness_reason: Ties the sidenote to the main text and identifies Cleanthes' prayer.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gildas, De excidio 20, the 'groans of the Britons' to Aetius: 'repellunt barbari ad mare, repellit mare ad barbaros'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the historical source and famous episode behind Burton's phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 1.36: asked what was easy, Thales answered 'to give advice to another'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source of the anecdote Burton attributes to Thales.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 1.49 judges Galba 'capax imperii nisi imperasset', and Burton applies the formula to several emperors.
answers.usefulness_reason: Points out the Tacitean epigram behind Burton's phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line numbers seem off by one: in standard editions 're veraque metus hominum' is 2.48, so the passage is 2.48–51, not 2.47–50. The variant readings given are correct.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Georgics 2.506 does read 'ut gemma bibat et Sarrano dormiat ostro', and Sarra is the old name for Tyre. The note's account of Burton's changes (relative clause, indicative verbs, plural 'gemmis') is accurate.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is a scholastic maxim based on Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.5 (1095b), where honour depends more on those who give it than on the one who receives it. Burton's gloss 'honours are from God' does turn it towards God as the giver.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the philosophical source of the maxim and shows how Burton turns it to his own use.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Thyestes 453 reads 'venenum in auro bibitur'. None of the nearby sidenotes credits Seneca.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.112–113 reads 'sine caede ac vulnere'. Burton has 'sanguine' instead. The glosses on Pluto and 'dry death' are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the allusions and points out how Burton changed the text.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Isaiah 5:14 is quoted correctly, and Burton's wording is a loose adaptation of it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the biblical source and shows how far Burton's wording departs from it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Georgics 2.458 reads 'sua si bona norint, agricolas'. The note describes Burton's word order and his new application of the line correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: In myth, the goat Amalthea nursed Jupiter, and her horn became the cornucopia.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epodes 2.1–3 does include 'ut prisca gens mortalium' as the middle line, and Burton leaves it out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.2.133–135 reads 'dictus, erit nulli proprius, sed cedet in usum / nunc mihi, nunc alii'. The differences in Burton's text (erat, cedit, aliis) are reported correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact place in Horace and notes Burton's changes of tense, which alter the sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.72 reads 'humana qua parte locatus es in re'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already names Persius, so the note adds only the line number and the word Burton dropped.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 2 m.5 reads 'Somnos dabat herba salubres, / potum quoque lubricus amnis'. The misprint and Burton's other changes are identified correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 5.1118–1119 continues 'neque enim est umquam penuria parvi', which matches the note.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the unmarked author and supplies the half-line Burton left out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.6.65, the country suppers with friends at his Sabine farm.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.6.4–5 reads 'nil amplius oro, / Maia nate'. Mercury is the son of Maia.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.4.17–18 has 'finxerunt animi, raro et perpauca loquentis', as the note says.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cleanthes' hymn opens 'Lead me, O Zeus, and you, Destiny', and Epictetus quotes it at the close of the Enchiridion (ch. 53).

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Thyestes 391–393, the chorus on the slippery heights of the court.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.6.1 reads 'modus agri non ita magnus', so Burton's 'parvus' reverses the sense. 'votiis' is plainly a misprint.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 10.47 is addressed to Julius Martialis. The omitted line is 'non ingratus ager, focus perennis', just before 'lis numquam'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the addressee and shows how Burton cut the poem.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.92–94 runs 'parto quod avebas, ne facias quod / Ummidius quidam', so 'utere' is not Horace's.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.108 quotes 'patria est, ubicumque est bene' from a tragedy (Pacuvius' Teucer).
answers.usefulness_reason: Traces the proverb to its classical source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Evangelus is a speaker in the Saturnalia, and the sentence does come from Seneca, Ep. 47.17 (almost word for word, not just an echo). But in Sat. 1.11 Praetextatus says these words, not Evangelus, and the note doesn't flag Burton's misattribution.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 9.108, Cornelia lamenting Pompey.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 9.475–478, Euryalus' mother. The standard text reads 'calor'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Aeneid 9.493–4, spoken by Euryalus's mother; Burton's sidenote 'Aen. 10' is wrong, as the note says.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Bravium' is the Latin form of brabeion, the prize in the games, and it appears in the Vulgate at 1 Cor 9:24.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a rare technical term and its Pauline echo.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.557–60 is Aeneas taunting Tarquitus, and the standard text reads 'patrioque' and 'aut gurgite mersum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the speaker and the context, and notes how Burton's text differs.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Greek is Iliad 19.228–9, Odysseus to Achilles; the correction of Burton's 'Il. 9' is right and suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the real source and corrects Burton's reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Annals 2.71 the dying Germanicus says 'prosequi defunctum ignavo questu'; 'quaestu' is an error for 'questu'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the right locus and context and fixes a misreading that changes the sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Calliopius recensui' is the editor's subscription in Terence manuscripts. Taking Calliopius for an actor was a common early modern misunderstanding, and Burton makes it here.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.430 reads 'quid Pandioniae restant nisi nomen Athenae?'; Pandion was a legendary king of Athens.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and explains the mythological epithet.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Homo totiens moritur quotiens amittit suos' is among the Sententiae of Publilius Syrus, although Burton's sidenote gives Seneca.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's attribution to the real source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.698–9 reads 'nondum illi flavum Proserpina vertice crinem / abstulerat', of Dido dying before her time.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the allusion and explains what it means.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epodes 5.13–14 reads 'impube corpus, quale posset impia / mollire Thracum pectora', so Burton's variants are reported correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source, which Burton's sidenote gives only as 'Hor.', and shows how his text departs from it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.696–7 reads 'nam quia nec fato merita nec morte peribat, / sed misera ante diem', of Dido; Burton's changes are reported correctly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at Matthew 17:4 reads 'bonum est nos hic esse'; Burton's sidenote gives Benzo as the source for Montezuma.
answers.usefulness_reason: The biblical echo is apt but fairly obvious.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.34 reads 'id cinerem aut manis credis curare sepultos?' (Anna to Dido); the variant '&' for 'aut' is reported correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the exact locus where Burton's sidenote says only 'Virg.' and notes how he alters it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are from Consolation 1, metrum 4, not prose 4. Boethius's next line, 'quod non sit stabilis suique iuris', is the one Burton leaves out.
answers.usefulness_reason: Corrects Burton's sidenote and shows a cut that changes the sense of the lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 68.19–20 is right, and in context 'hoc studium' is the poet's youthful pursuit of love and verse.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the locus and the context for 'studium', which Burton's 'study' obscures.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.855–856 are Mezentius's words after the death of Lausus.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the speaker and the locus, which Burton's sidenote gives only as 'Virg.'

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Terrae filii' is a standard idiom for men of no family, and Maecenas and Agrippa are proverbial for great men and patrons.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains an idiom that the literal translation leaves opaque.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.10.8 reads 'vivo et regno, simul ista reliqui'; the participle variant is reported correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: The locus helps, but the note is mostly about a textual variant.

answers.accuracy_reason: Heauton Timorumenos 210 reads 'periclum ex aliis facito tibi quod ex usu siet', matching Burton's sidenote.
answers.usefulness_reason: Mainly a note on how Burton recasts the grammar, which adds little for a reader.

answers.accuracy_reason: Erasmus, Adagia I.x.17 is 'Annosa vulpes haud capitur laqueo'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The Erasmus parallel is useful, but Burton's own text already completes the proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Phormio 241ff. is Demipho's speech, which opens 'quom secundae res sunt maxume'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the speaker and the omitted opening, which Burton echoes in his next words, 'In secundis meditare'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.103–105 are Aeneas's words to the Sibyl; the standard text has 'inopinave' and 'praecepi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the speaker and context, which the reader needs to follow Burton's 'resolute Captain'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Nathan Chytraeus (1543–1598) published the Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae in 1594.
answers.usefulness_reason: Expands an obscure abbreviated reference into a real author and book.

answers.accuracy_reason: The maxim is in the Formula vitae honestae (Martin of Braga), which circulated under Seneca's name; the note hedges this properly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains why Burton's sidenote credits it to Seneca.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Latin renders the Delphic/Seven Sages maxim ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτα (often credited to Thales).
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Greek original behind the proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 4.52 has 'tecum habita: noris quam sit tibi curta supellex', and the note gives the sense correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the rest of the line, which explains why Burton attaches it to 'Live not beyond thy means'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Occasion was pictured with a forelock in front and bald behind (the line is from the Disticha Catonis 2.26: 'fronte capillata, post est occasio calva').
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the image a modern reader may not know, though it does not name the Cato source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Horace, Epistles 1.18.37–38, and the next line Burton quotes is 1.18.39, so 'ep. 19' is indeed wrong. The standard text reads 'illius' and goes on 'et vino tortus et ira'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's reference and shows how he generalises the line from the patron to anyone.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.7 reads 'nec te quaesiveris extra', and the note gives its sense correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the locus, Burton's change of wording, and the sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Solon's law against neutrality in civil strife is reported by Aristotle (Ath. Pol. 8.5) and discussed in Gellius 2.12.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains what the law was and ties it to Burton's precept.

answers.accuracy_reason: Anteros appears in Phaedrus 255d. Anteros as a brother of Eros and son of Venus comes from later sources such as Cicero and Themistius.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses 'redamatio' and separates what is in Plato from what Burton draws from later mythography.

answers.accuracy_reason: Erasmus does collect the proverb (Adagia 1.2.29, from πρὸς Κρῆτα κρητίζειν), but I cannot confirm that his Latin heading is either form the note gives.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the proverb, the Cretan reputation behind it, and where it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: The usual form of this Publilius Syrus sententia, as I recall it, is 'veterem ferendo iniuriam invitas novam', not 'invites'; the note does not name the source.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is mostly a note on grammar and Burton's adaptation, and leaves out the author of the maxim.

answers.accuracy_reason: Adelphoe 415–416 (Demea on looking into other men's lives as into a mirror) fits the precept, and the note rightly hedges with 'probably'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It turns a bare abbreviation into a probable source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The pun on salarium and sal (salt, also wit) is right, and 'multis' is the plausible correction.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a pun that the plain translation hides.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.54–55 reads 'magna petis, Phaethon, et quae nec viribus istis / munera conveniant nec tam puerilibus annis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and completes the line that Burton breaks off.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cato lost the praetorian election for 55 BC to Vatinius, which was the classic example of an unworthy man preferred to a worthy one.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the historical allusion behind the names, which most readers will not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the opening of Ausonius's epigram on Agathocles ('Fortunam reverenter habe, quicumque repente / dives ab exili progrediere loco'), and the note gives its warning correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and the original context, which sharpens Burton's maxim.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is from Ovid, Fasti 1.419 ('fastus inest pulchris, sequiturque superbia formam'), where forma means beauty. The note names no work, so it does not repeat the mistake in Burton's sidenote ('Met.').
answers.usefulness_reason: Saying that Burton moves the line from beauty to rank is useful but slight, and the note does not give the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 2.37 tells how Socrates refused to hit Xanthippe back so that onlookers would not cheer them on; eia is a cry of encouragement.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the ancient source for the anecdote (Burton's sidenote cites Aelian).

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a proverbial jingle, and the explanation of the image is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton glosses the proverb himself, so the note adds little beyond the point about the lost rhyme.

answers.accuracy_reason: The text is Terence, Adelphoe 860–861, 're ipsa repperi / facilitate nihil esse homini melius neque clementia'; Burton reorders the words and drops 'neque'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows how Burton changes the wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: The reference to Ovid, Tristia 3.5.31–32 is correct, and in that context 'faciles motus' means being readily moved to relent.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and clears up a sense the translation's 'easily moved' leaves unclear.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aeneid 4.449 the words describe Aeneas standing firm against the pleas Anna brings him from Dido.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgilian source of the half-line and its original setting.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the prologue to Plautus's Rudens, Arcturus says that Jupiter re-judges cases won by perjury and fines the winners more heavily; the second line is translated correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the speaker, the play and the original context, and shows how Burton applies the lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate wording is quoted correctly ('per quae peccat quis, per haec et torquetur'). It is Wisdom 11:17 in the Clementine Vulgate but 11:16 in English Bibles and in Burton's sidenote, which is a small numbering difference.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the biblical source and shows that Burton paraphrases it rather than quoting it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.112–113 reads 'sine caede ac vulnere'; the notes on Pluto as Ceres' son-in-law and on 'dry death' are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the mythological allusion and points out where Burton changes Juvenal's text.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Septuagint of Genesis 4:7 ('hēmartes; hēsychason') became 'peccasti, quiesce' in the Old Latin, and Ambrose quotes it in that form.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Ambrose's phrase rests on a biblical reading that differs from the Vulgate and the English Bible.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is right: Horace, Satires 2.5.10, where Tiresias advises Ulysses on legacy-hunting. But the claim that the sidenote stands in the preceding paragraph can't be checked, because the item gives no sidenotes and the preceding text isn't shown.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source and the dramatic setting, which the bare 'Accipe… &c.' does not show.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is a proverb collected by Erasmus ('habet et musca splenem'; 'inest et formicae bilis'), and Burton's English does turn the ant into a bee with a sting.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains spleen and bile as anger and points out Burton's change in the English.

answers.accuracy_reason: Velleius 2.35 does say this of Cato Uticensis ('numquam recte fecit ut facere videretur, sed quia aliter facere non potuerat'), and Burton applies it to Censorius.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the exact source and shows Burton's slip in transferring the praise to the other Cato.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ammianus 18.1.4 gives Julian's retort as 'ecquis innocens esse poterit, si accusasse sufficiet?', and 'clam vel palam' is not in it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the context (Julian's retort) and shows how Burton expands the original.

answers.accuracy_reason: The fragment does come from the proverbial line 'felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Supplies the full proverb the reader needs to make sense of the elliptical phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a medieval rhyming proverb, the certo/certo pun is real, and 'sterco' is a non-classical form.
answers.usefulness_reason: The pun is the point of the line and is lost in translation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of 2 Corinthians 6:8 reads 'per infamiam et bonam famam'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the Pauline phrase that Jerome's wording rests on.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 64.338 reads 'nascetur vobis expers terroris Achilles', and 'armatus' is not in it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the exact locus and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca's De constantia sapientis is about exactly this theme (the wise man is untouched by insult), and Burton names Seneca but no work.
answers.usefulness_reason: Points the reader to the Seneca work that Burton is drawing on.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Persius 1.58. The stork gesture is correctly explained, and Janus, with his face behind, cannot be mocked from behind.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a gesture that is otherwise obscure.

answers.accuracy_reason: The saying is attributed to Antisthenes (in Diogenes Laertius and Marcus Aurelius) and to Alexander (in Plutarch).
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the origin of the saying and notes how Burton uses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Dio 47.49 reports that Brutus quoted these tragic verses in Greek before his death.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source and the Greek tragic origin of the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Cons. 1 pr. 4 does continue 'quotiens ostentando quis factum recipit famae pretium'. The first sentence appears to be Burton's own framing.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton cuts his source and why the clause reads oddly as a result.

answers.accuracy_reason: It correctly defines the medical and legal term 'lucida intervalla'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a correct gloss, but Burton already explains the term himself.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sense of 'ringi' is right, and Horace, Epist. 2.2.126–8 ('praetulerim scriptor delirus... quam sapere et ringi') matches the description.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Horatian context of a phrase that Burton leaves without a source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Sophocles, Ajax 554 comes from Ajax's speech to Eurysaces, as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Ajax in Sophocles; the note adds only the dramatic setting.

answers.accuracy_reason: Livy 2.48 describes the Veiens hostis as 'adsiduus magis quam gravis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton names both Livy and the Veientes, so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plautus, Captivi 255–6 has 'etiam cum cavisse ratus est, saepe is cautor captus est', and the note's hedge is apt.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source line and notes how Burton's wording differs from it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Pliny wording quoted (NH 29.18) is right, but I could not confirm the flat claim that 'animas nostras negotiantur' is not from Pliny.
answers.usefulness_reason: It compares Burton's version with Pliny's actual text.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Quid pro quo' was the apothecaries' term for substituting one drug for another.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical sense that a modern reader would miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Urina meretrix' was a proverbial phrase about urine being an unreliable diagnostic sign.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a proverbial medical phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cassius Dio 69.22 records Hadrian repeating the saying that many physicians had killed a king.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the anecdote behind Burton's allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note quotes Sallust, Jugurtha 19.2 correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and shows how Burton paraphrases it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Calling Scaliger's phrase a dismissal is uncertain. Burton's 'but as Cardan censures them' suggests the phrase marks Galen as Hippocrates' close follower or commentator, not as an object of scorn.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses the image but gives no source or context.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'In fieri' is the scholastic phrase for something still being made. The Oxford Physic Garden was founded in 1621 by Henry Danvers, Earl of Danby, and was being laid out at the time.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the idiom and connects it to the founding of the Oxford garden.

answers.accuracy_reason: Munster here is Sebastian Münster the cosmographer, and Mons Maior is Monte Maggiore (Učka) in Istria. The note's grammatical point about 'commends' carrying over is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the author and the mountain; a reader could easily take 'Munster' for a Latin word or a place.

answers.accuracy_reason: The plants are identified correctly, the sidenote 'Priest pintle' is quoted accurately, and Burton's English does soften the first clause to 'provoke lust'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the plants, links them to the sidenote, and points out how Burton tones down his own Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is Horace, Ars Poetica 139, 'parturient montes, nascetur ridiculus mus'. Burton's added 'ubi' is correctly noted.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the allusion and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The weapon-salve, attributed to Paracelsus, was put on the weapon that made the wound and was supposed to heal the wound by sympathy.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a well-known and controversial remedy that a modern reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Paracelsus' electrum magicum was an alloy of the seven planetary metals, made into rings, mirrors and bells. The note rightly hedges on the exact preparation Burton means.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains an obscure Paracelsian term.

answers.accuracy_reason: For Paracelsus, 'balsam' meant both a healing remedy and the body's own life-preserving virtue.
answers.usefulness_reason: Slight but correct background on a familiar word.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Satires 1.1.66–67, spoken by the miser, and Burton does leave out 'ipse domi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the poet behind 'as he said in the Poet' and shows Burton's cut, though it gives no line reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: Syrupus de pomis regis Sabor (King Sapor's syrup of apples) was a standard syrup in Mesue's tradition.
answers.usefulness_reason: Helpful for reading the elliptical phrase, but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diamargaritum is a pearl electuary, and 'calidum' and 'frigidum' are its humoral hot and cold forms, both listed in the passage.
answers.usefulness_reason: A brief gloss; most of it is already clear from the context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton completes the scholastic maxim 'frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora' after '(as the saying is)', and it is a form of the principle of economy.
answers.usefulness_reason: Mostly explains how the split quotation reads; it adds little beyond that, and it doesn't mention the usual link to Ockham.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note says there was a single formula attributed to both Galen and Rhazes. Period pharmacopoeias list two separate confections, an electuarium laetificans Galeni and one Rhasis, and Burton is naming both.
answers.usefulness_reason: Glossing 'laetificans' as the name of a remedy helps a little, but the note adds little else.

answers.accuracy_reason: Unguentum populeum was indeed a cooling, soporific ointment of poplar buds with poppy, mandrake, henbane and similar herbs.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a technical pharmaceutical name a modern reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.7, describes Chaos as 'rudis indigestaque moles'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the allusion and shows how Burton turns it to a new use.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diatrion pipereon was the confection of the three peppers: black, white and long.
answers.usefulness_reason: The translation already says 'three peppers'; naming the three adds only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Pharmacopoeia Londinensis was issued in 1618.
answers.usefulness_reason: The term is easy to guess, though the London example is a useful touch.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.14, reads 'quidquid delirant reges plectuntur Achivi'; Burton does leave out 'quidquid'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the source and gives the full line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 70–72, has 'cadentque quae nunc sunt in honore vocabula, si volet usus'; the note quotes it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Supplies the source and the verb Burton cuts, which explains his sentence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius, Satires 1.50–51, mocks the Iliad translation of Attius Labeo, 'ebria veratro'; Acci/Atti is a known variant spelling.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the target of the satire and explains the spelling.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Terence, Eunuchus 781, Thraso says 'ego ero post principia'; principia means the front ranks.
answers.usefulness_reason: Traces Burton's 'bragging soldier' to its comic source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.19.7–8, reads 'Ennius ipse pater numquam nisi potus ad arma / prosiluit dicenda'; the dash marks only the line break, so nothing is left out.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source and the original wording, and shows how Burton changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Theriac was the famous compound antidote, called 'treacle' in early modern English.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton himself glosses it as 'another Treacle', so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lapis Armenus was a blue copper mineral, and the note properly hedges the identification with azurite; it was used as a purge of melancholy.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains an obscure materia medica term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Simo is the old man in Plautus's Pseudolus, where Harpax says 'helleboro hisce hominibus opus est' to him and Ballio.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already cites Pseudolus, and 'nothing to translate' is a working remark, but naming the character helps a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.3.166 does read 'naviget Anticyram', and Anticyra was proverbial for hellebore.
answers.usefulness_reason: It turns the bare sidenote 'Hor.' into an exact reference and points out that Burton changed the singular to a plural.

answers.accuracy_reason: Menecrates of Syracuse, a physician, called himself Zeus and wrote to Philip as 'Menecrates Zeus'. The story is in Athenaeus and Aelian.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Greek epithet briefly but cites no source and adds little to the anecdote Burton already tells.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Pilulae sine quibus' and the 'cochiae' pills were standard compound pills in the pharmacopoeias, and myrobalans were fruits imported from the East.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses technical pharmacy names that a reader would not otherwise understand.

answers.accuracy_reason: The labour of Hercules is correct, and 'Augiae stabulum repurgare' is one of Erasmus's Adagia.
answers.usefulness_reason: The proverb is well known; the reference to Erasmus adds only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The ingredients (epithyme, lapis lazuli, agaric, scammony, cloves) match pulvis Hali. The glosses of caryophyllum, semuncia and the other terms are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the recipe and glosses its drugs and abbreviations.

answers.accuracy_reason: Francis Anthony was the best-known English promoter of aurum potabile, and Burton names him in the next sentence.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the 'Dr. Anthony' Burton names and gives the alchemical context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.11.17–18 reads 'dissipat Euhius / curas edacis'. The gloss of Euius as Bacchus and the misprint 'edates' for 'edaces' are both right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the cult name, corrects the misprint and shows how Burton reordered Horace.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Martial 10.48.14, from the dinner-menu epigram. Burton's sidenote gives only 'Mart.', so the claim that he gives no locus is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows how Burton moved a menu line into a passage about amulets.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Ebrietas est blandus daemon, dulce venenum' is commonly attributed to Augustine (probably pseudo-Augustine), and the note properly hedges on the source.
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces a phrase that Burton credits to Pliny back to its better-known proverbial source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tibullus 1.7.41–42 reads 'crura licet dura compede pulsa sonent', as the note quotes.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the author, whom Burton does not name, and shows how Burton altered the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: De tranquillitate animi 17.12 closes with 'Habes, Serene carissime, quae possint tranquillitatem tueri, quae restituere…'. The note quotes this correctly, and Serenus is the man the work is addressed to.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's 'quotation' is really a paraphrase of Seneca.

answers.accuracy_reason: Both loci are correct: Odes 3.28.2–3 and Epodes 9.33–34.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton joined two separate Horace poems into one quotation, which the bare 'Hor.' sidenote hides.

answers.accuracy_reason: Antonio Luiz (Antonius Ludovicus) was a Lisbon physician who wrote De pudore (1540). Olisipo/Olysippo is the Latin name for Lisbon.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the physician behind the sidenote and explains the Latin place-name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lac virginale was a milky cosmetic wash made from litharge (lead oxide), and Burton glosses it himself as 'strained liquor of Litharge'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader what this period cosmetic was and that it was made from lead.

answers.accuracy_reason: The officinal pilulae de cynoglosso contained opium (with henbane and other ingredients) and were given as a soporific.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains why these pills appear in a list of sleeping medicines.

answers.accuracy_reason: Requies Nicolai was an opiate electuary from the Nicolaus antidotary, and the note hedges the attribution. Burton does later quote Rulandus calling it 'ultimum refugium'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the compound and its source, and points ahead to Burton's own comment on it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Triphera magna was a standard opiate electuary of the Nicolaus antidotary and the later pharmacopoeias.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct and helpful but brief, and the opiate nature is already plain from the list it sits in.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diascordium, Fracastoro's electuary, contained scordium (water germander) and opium.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects the spelling and explains what the medicine was.

answers.accuracy_reason: Unguentum populeum was made from poplar buds together with narcotic leaves such as poppy, henbane, mandrake and nightshade, and was used as a cooling soporific.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical pharmacy term.

answers.accuracy_reason: The 1532 Strasbourg edition printed Theodorus Priscianus's works under the name Octavius Horatianus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the real author behind Burton's citation, which a reader could not otherwise trace.

answers.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus (2.45c), citing Polybius, records Ptolemy Philadelphus sending Nile water to Berenice, who married Antiochus II, the Seleucid king of Syria. The note rightly limits itself to saying that Burton credits Celsus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the better-known source of the anecdote and corrects Burton's 'King of Assyria' against the history.

answers.accuracy_reason: The salvatella is the vein on the back of the hand between the ring and little fingers, and physicians opened it in splenic and melancholic disorders.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an anatomical term, although the last sentence is only a translator's working remark.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hiera means 'holy', and hiera picra, a purgative made with aloes, was its best-known form.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical name for a purge.

answers.accuracy_reason: The os cordis cervi is the ossified cartilage in a deer's heart, which was prized as a cordial.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: The axiom is identified correctly. But the note says flatly that it is used 'jokingly', and that is not certain: Burton may simply be giving the physical reason the bellows draw out the wind.
answers.usefulness_reason: Naming the scholastic commonplace helps a little, but most readers already know it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The wording does match Cicero, De Oratore 2.21: 'discum audire quam philosophum malunt'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces an unattributed tag to its source and explains the point.

answers.accuracy_reason: The gloss on 'punctum' is right. The claim that Burton introduces the line with 'the Poet admires it' cannot be checked against the excerpt, which is cut off just before it.
answers.usefulness_reason: The voting image is worth knowing, but the note never names the source, Horace's Ars Poetica 343.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are lines 2–3 of the prologue to Terence's Andria, where the poet is spoken of in the third person.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the play and the speaking situation, which Burton only hints at with 'the Comical Poet'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase plainly reworks 'populo ut placerent' from the Terence lines just quoted.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out a link the reader could largely see without help.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Catullus 16.5–7, and the standard text does read 'nam castum' and 'ac'. The next line ('si sunt molliculi ac parum pudici') supports the gloss on 'only then'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and explains the condition Burton leaves unstated by cutting the quotation short.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Martial 11.16.9–10, and the standard text does read 'leget'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The exact reference is helpful, but the variant reading is a translator's detail.

answers.accuracy_reason: It quotes Horace, Odes 1.34.3–5 correctly and describes Burton's changes correctly: 'cogor' moved, 'nunc' dropped, 'olim' added.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already gives the ode; showing how Burton adapts it is of modest interest.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Catullus 68.45–46, and 'anus' is indeed used adjectivally there.
answers.usefulness_reason: The exact locus adds to Burton's bare 'Catullus'; the grammar point is a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.16 reads 'sunt bona … sunt mala plura', and Burton does say he inverts the verse.
answers.usefulness_reason: Quoting the original line shows the inversion, but Burton already announces it.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Sacrifice to the Graces' is a Greek proverb, best known as Plato's advice to Xenocrates.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a proverbial allusion most readers would not recognise.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the first line of Virgil's Eclogue 10, his last eclogue, addressed to Arethusa. The Third Partition is the last part of Burton's book.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how fitting the line is for Burton's last Partition.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Agathon epigram attributed to Plato is in Diogenes Laertius 3.32, and Burton's couplet is a Latin version of it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Greek original and where it is preserved, which the reader could not get from the text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caspar Barth's Latin Celestina (Pornoboscodidascalus Latinus, Frankfurt 1624) came with his notes (animadversiones).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure bibliographic reference in the sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hera's seduction of Zeus on Ida under a golden cloud is in Iliad 14.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Homeric scene, but the passage is easy to recognise and Burton's context already makes it plain.

answers.accuracy_reason: The primum mobile was the outermost moving sphere, which turned the inner spheres with it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical cosmological term and how Burton uses the image.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase comes from Alciato's emblem of the olive and the vine: the Virgin is Pallas (the olive), Bromius is Bacchus (the vine).
answers.usefulness_reason: It decodes the mythological names behind the plant antipathy, which a reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.350 reads 'carior est illis homo quam sibi', said of the gods. Burton has 'ipsis' and applies the line to God.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Symposium (202d–e) Diotima calls Eros a great daimon, between gods and mortals. Convivium is the Latin title, and 'Convivio' is its ablative.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains how 'daemon' became Burton's 'great Devil', which a reader could easily misread.

answers.accuracy_reason: The De Officiis 1.15 quotation is correct. But Burton's wording, 'ardentes amores excitaret sui', is closer to Cicero, De Finibus 2.52, which the note does not mention, so it points the reader to the less likely source.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the Ciceronian context, but it may send the reader to the wrong passage.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 3–4 has 'desinat'. Burton's 'desinit' is the indicative, and the sense of the image is given correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is mostly about the mood of the verb and does not name the work (Ars Poetica), though it does explain the image.

answers.accuracy_reason: Leone Ebreo's utile, dilettevole and onesto do go back to the three kinds of friendship in Nicomachean Ethics 8.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton himself already names Leon Hebraeus and 'Aristotle belike 8 moral.', so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Satyricon 88: 'formosior auri massa quam quicquid Apelles Phidiasque, Graeculi delirantes, fecerunt.'
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's English and sidenote already supply most of this. Only the 'little Greek madmen' detail is new.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Satires 1.1.66–67, the miser says 'populus me sibilat, at mihi plaudo / ipse domi…', and Burton quotes only the second half.
answers.usefulness_reason: It restores the miser's situation, which Burton cuts, and shows what he dropped.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.24–25 has 'rupto iecore exierit caprificus'. The wild fig's habit of splitting stone and the liver as the seat of passion are both standard. In Persius the urge is to show off one's learning, but the note's general gloss fits Burton's use.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and explains an image that is otherwise obscure.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lipsius wrote to Camden praising Britain, which he knew from Britannia and had never visited; Burton's sidenote 'Lipsius epist. Camdeno' agrees.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context the reader needs: who 'he' is and which island is meant.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.145 reads 'fratrum quoque gratia rara est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points to the classical parallel behind the proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.847–48 reads '(credo equidem), vivos ducent de marmore vultus', spoken by Anchises about other peoples' arts, so 'e marmore' is Burton's variant.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton reshapes the original context.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the correct sense of κατʼ ἐξοχήν, and it is applied correctly to 'Heroical' love.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct but goes little beyond the translation 'par excellence'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Scioppius praised Scaliger lavishly in his Suspectae lectiones, Burton's sidenote, before attacking him in Scaliger Hypobolimaeus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies who is speaking and the quarrel Burton alludes to.

answers.accuracy_reason: The ancile was said to have fallen from heaven under Numa, and the praises are Scioppius's.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a Roman allusion and the speaker.

answers.accuracy_reason: In De Senectute 7, Cicero gives 'pares cum paribus vetere proverbio facillime congregantur'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source of the proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: The image comes from Symposium 215a–b, and Erasmus's adage 'Sileni Alcibiadis' (Adagia 3.3.1) treats things that are ugly outside and precious within.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the allusion and its well-known transmission through Erasmus.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Consolation 3 prose 8, Boethius says that seen with Lynceus' eyes, Alcibiades' fair body would look most foul within; Burton moralizes this into the soul.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton bends his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Livy 3.26.7 reads 'Operae pretium est audire qui omnia prae divitiis humana spernunt', introducing Cincinnatus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It locates the source and notes how Burton cuts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The idea comes from Phaedrus 250d. Cicero gives it in Latin ('mirabiles amores… excitaret sapientiae', De Finibus 2.52 and De Officiis 1.15), and Burton's citation of the Phaedo is a misattribution.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's citation and traces how the line reached him.

answers.accuracy_reason: Parentare does mean to perform the rites and offerings at the tomb of the dead, originally of one's parents (compare the Parentalia).
answers.usefulness_reason: A correct definition of the word, but it adds little to the translation 'offer funeral rites'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gratia gratum faciens is the scholastic term for sanctifying grace, as distinct from gratia gratis data, and Burton uses it loosely for the grace that makes a person lovable.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical theological term and shows how Burton turns it to his own use.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Et serves animae dimidium meae' is Horace, Odes 1.3.8, the propempticon for Virgil's voyage.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and what kind of poem it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 5.344 reads 'gratior et pulchro veniens in corpore virtus', said of Euryalus, and the note's account of Burton's changes is accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and context, and shows how Burton altered the line to make a general maxim.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ptolemaic and medieval cosmology the primum mobile is the outermost sphere, which drives the motion of the spheres inside it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the cosmological term behind Burton's metaphor.

answers.accuracy_reason: The commonplace that the virtues of pagans are only 'splendida vitia' (traditionally credited to Augustine) is stated here correctly and without overclaiming.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the theological commonplace behind Burton's phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Angariare comes from ἀγγαρεύειν, to press someone into forced service, and from that it came to mean to harass or oppress.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an unusual word of Greek origin and how its meaning developed.

answers.accuracy_reason: The proverb (in Plautus, Terence and Ennius) means finding difficulties or faults where there are none, because a bulrush has no knots. The sidenote does sit at 'toys, trifles'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the proverb and links it to the point in the main text where the sidenote is anchored.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.367 is Dido's reproach to Aeneas, and Hyrcania lay by the Caspian Sea and was known for its wild beasts.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and explains the place-name.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase comes from Horace, Epistles 1.1.65–66: 'rem facias, rem, / si possis, recte, si non, quocumque modo rem', the cynical advice of the money-seekers.
answers.usefulness_reason: It recovers the full Horatian maxim that Burton cuts down to three words.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.314 and 317–318 read 'si bene quid de te merui' and 'miserere domus labentis', so the note correctly describes Burton's adaptation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton bent Dido's plea into a beggar's personal appeal.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.17.58–62 the trickster who really has broken his leg is not believed. 'Licet' governs the concessive clauses that include the oath, so the note's comparison is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the context of Horace's anecdote, which makes clear why the plea fails.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.17.62: 'quaere peregrinum, vicinia rauca reclamat'. The neighbours shout this at the beggar who fakes a broken leg.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Horatian scene, which explains why Burton puts the words in the rich man's mouth.

answers.accuracy_reason: In De legibus 1.1, Cicero's speaker says of the Marian oak from his poem 'Marius': 'nullius autem agricolae cultu stirps tam diuturna…'. The note reports both the context and the wording correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: The point that Cicero celebrated the oak in verse helps a little, but Burton's sidenote already names the source, and the comparison of readings is mostly a textual detail.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.414: 'inde genus durum sumus experiensque laborum'. These are the people sprung from Deucalion's stones.
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces the allusion to Ovid and explains why men are 'hard'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.150: 'ultima caelestum terras Astraea reliquit', at the iron age. Correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the myth and the source, and it shows how Burton adapts the line to fit his 'iron age wherein we live'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.24.6–8: Pudor, Iustitiae soror, incorrupta Fides, nudaque Veritas, asking when they will find Quintilius's equal. Correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the original context of lament for a dead friend, which is not otherwise obvious.

answers.accuracy_reason: Bion of Borysthenes is traditionally described as a Cynic-leaning writer of diatribe whose wit was famously caustic. The phrase comes from Horace, Epistles 2.2.60, and 'black salt' does mean malicious wit.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure name and the idiom, though it doesn't name the Horace source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Decii Mures, father and son, performed devotio by vowing themselves and the enemy to the gods below for victory. Correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a Roman religious ritual that the Latin verb refers to.

answers.accuracy_reason: Sallust, Jugurtha 10.6: 'concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia maxumae dilabuntur'. The note's claim that the reading changes is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source of a famous maxim and shows how Burton's version changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Historia Augusta, Aurelian 6.5, Vopiscus quotes a soldiers' song: 'tantum vini habet nemo quantum fudit sanguinis'. Correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It's a useful pointer that the line comes from a song, but slight; it gives no locus and doesn't mention that Burton has reworded it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Sallust, Catiline 52.13: 'credo falsa existumans ea quae de inferis memorantur'. The locus and the participle-to-second-person change are both reported accurately.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Symposium 202d, Diotima calls Eros 'daimon megas', an intermediary between gods and mortals. Correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Platonic locus and prevents a misreading of 'Daemon' as 'devil'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persa 1–5 reads 'cum leone, cum excetra, cum cervo, cum apro Aetolico, cum avibus Stymphalicis, cum Antaeo deluctari mavelim quam cum Amore'. The 'Aetolico' reading, the omitted hydra and the hedged 'slip' are all accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source context (the labours of Hercules) and shows how Burton changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are a fragment of Caecilius Statius that survives only because Cicero quotes it at Tusculan Disputations 4.68.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Caecilius and the Tusculans, so the note adds only that the lines survive through Cicero and gives the book number.

answers.accuracy_reason: Eurystheus as son of Sthenelus is right, and the couplet is Heroides 9.5–6. But the note says flatly that Ovid's text reads 'vincit'. Editions differ on this word, and on 'non' against 'Nec', so the claim needs a hedge.
answers.usefulness_reason: Naming the 'Sthenelean foe' clears up an obscure reference, though the note could also have named the poem (Heroides 9, Deianira to Hercules).

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Metamorphoses 1.523, Apollo's lament as he chases Daphne.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows why the line fits Burton's point about Apollo.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines come from Claudian's Epithalamium for Honorius and Maria, in the passage on Venus's Cyprian garden and palace. 'Felix arbor' does mean a fruitful tree.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the poem behind Burton's vague sidenote and explains a technical sense of 'felix'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Lucretius 1.12–13, from the opening hymn to Venus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It places the bare 'Lucretius' sidenote in the well-known invocation to Venus.

answers.accuracy_reason: The locus, Herodotus 1.181–2, is right. But the claim that 'lay with her' goes beyond the source is questionable: Herodotus' comparison with Thebes, where the women are said to have no dealings with men, already suggests a sexual sense.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the locus and sets Burton's wording against his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hesiod (Theogony 116–20) has Chaos, Earth and Eros come first, with Tartarus omitted here as Plato also omits it. He does not make the first two Love's parents, as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton changes Hesiod's order of first beings into a parentage.

answers.accuracy_reason: Phaedrus gives the first speech in the Symposium and argues there that Eros is the oldest of the gods (178a–c).
answers.usefulness_reason: The main text already says what Phaedrus 'contends', so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line matches Parmenides' verse quoted in Symposium 178b, where the subject is a goddess, and Phaedrus quotes it next to Hesiod.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that the line Burton sets under Hesiod is really Parmenides as quoted by Plato.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Orphic Hymn to Eros does give him the keys of aether, sea and earth, and the joke about the 'petty Pope' and Peter's keys is clear.

answers.accuracy_reason: Odes 2.14.21–22 reads 'linquenda tellus et domus et placens uxor', so the source is correctly identified.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is right: in the Amores (attributed to Lucian), Lycinus rules that all should marry and that the love of boys should be left to philosophers.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line comes from the Octavia's passage on Love ('iuventa gignitur, luxu otio / nutritur inter laeta Fortunae bona'). The note's hedged 'resembles' is acceptable, and what it says about Burton's English is accurate.

answers.accuracy_reason: Bernardino Gómez Miedes wrote a commentary on salt (De sale), and the note rightly hedges the identification with 'probably'. The sal/salax pun is real.

answers.accuracy_reason: Antigone 783–4, the ode to Eros: 'who keep vigil on the soft cheeks of a maiden'.
