answers.accuracy_reason: Aulus Gellius 19.11 preserves 'Dum semiulco savio / meum puellum savior…' as a Latin version of a Platonic epigram. The beloved there is a boy.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the true source and points out a telling change of gender in Burton's text.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Satyricon 79 the passage runs on 'valete, curae / mortales'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Completing the cut phrase is correct but adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.169–70 reads 'ille dies primus leti primusque malorum / causa fuit', which refers to the meeting in the cave. The word order really is swapped in Burton.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context in Virgil, which makes Burton's use of the line more pointed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.38 is Anna speaking to Dido. In Satyricon 112 it is the maid who quotes it to the widow, not the soldier as Burton's text implies.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Virgilian source and quietly corrects who speaks the line in Petronius.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Amores 2.4.32, and Burton's sidenote does say 'eleg. 2'. The glosses on Hippolytus and Priapus are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the two figures and corrects the citation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote cites Caspar Barth's Latin version of Aretino, the Pornodidascalus. The title belongs to the made-up Spanish count, announced by the servant whom the courtesan has disguised.
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly restates what Burton's context already makes clear, though the note about Barth helps a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terence, Andria 555 (III.iii) reads 'amantium irae amoris integratiost'. The proverb form with 'redintegratio' is the later version.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how the proverb differs from Terence's wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Juno at Aen. 7.312, 'flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo'. Burton has adapted it to the third person plural.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the speaker and shows how Burton adapts the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.610–11 reads 'hic Thessala vendit / philtra', and Thessaly was proverbial for witches.
answers.usefulness_reason: The witchcraft association helps, but the rest is only the line division and line numbers.

answers.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Sat. 116, describes Croton as a city where all either are captated or captate, meaning legacy-hunting.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton moves a remark about legacy-hunters onto bawds.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Mala insana' was the Renaissance name for the aubergine (Solanum melongena), whence Italian 'melanzana'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a botanical term a reader would not recognise.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Tibullus 1.5.48, and Burton's 'eleg. 5 lib. 1' fits Tibullus, not Catullus. The note is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's misattribution.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caspar Barth published a Latin Celestina titled Pornoboscodidascalus (1624), which matches the sidenote 'Pornobosc. Barthii'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the sidenote and the edition Burton used.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 4.465–66 reads 'secum ... decedente canebat', so Burton has made the lines first person.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton changes his source, though it does not name the Georgics.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.9.10–12, addressed to Valgius, reads 'nec tibi Vespero'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton turns consolation addressed to Valgius into a lover's own complaint.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is [Tibullus] 3.3.25–26, part of the Lygdamus poems (3.1–6).
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the authorship context for the Tibullan third book.

answers.accuracy_reason: Clitophon is the narrator and lover of Leucippe in Achilles Tatius, and Burton cites the romance in Latin translation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source of a quotation Burton leaves unattributed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aen. 4.4, 'haerent infixi pectore vultus', refers to Aeneas' looks fixed in Dido's heart.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the original context and shows how Burton applies it to lovers in general.

answers.accuracy_reason: Amores 1.9 opens 'Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido', and the poem compares love to soldiering.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of the tag and the theme of the poem.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.2 reads 'caeco carpitur igni' and is about Dido. Eclogue 3.66 reads 'at mihi sese offert ultro, meus ignis, Amyntas'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies both tags and explains 'ignis' as 'beloved'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terence, Eunuchus 85, reads 'accede ad ignem hunc, iam calesces plus satis'. Ignis is masculine, so 'hanc' is an anomaly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the source and the omitted end of the line, which gives the joke. The gender remark is minor.

answers.accuracy_reason: This renders Theocritus, Idyll 2.133–4, on Eros kindling a flame hotter than Liparaean Hephaestus. Tradition placed Vulcan's forge in the Lipari islands.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the 'Liparean' allusion and confirms the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.86–9 describes Carthage's building works stopping while Dido is in love. Reading machina as a crane or derrick is standard.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context and glosses the technical terms.

answers.accuracy_reason: Abelard's epitaph includes 'Huic soli patuit scibile quicquid erat'. Burton writes 'Cui'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own sidenote already says the line is from the epitaph.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 3 m.12, reads 'Quis legem det amantibus? / Maior lex amor est sibi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source wording and shows how Burton adapted it.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Amare et sapere vix deo conceditur' is among Publilius Syrus's sententiae, which circulated under Seneca's name. Burton's attribution is therefore explicable.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects the attribution and gives the proverbial form.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca's Phaedra 184–5 reads 'quid ratio possit? vicit ac regnat furor, / potensque tota mente dominatur deus'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton's text departs from Seneca and changes the sense, and identifies the god.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.319–21, continues 'di, precor, et pietas sacrataque iura parentum', so the summary of the omitted prayer is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It says what the '&c.' cuts off but doesn't cite the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Golden Ass, Lucius regains his human form by eating roses, and an allegorical reading as a return to reason is standard.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the roses allusion, which would be obscure to a reader without it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 1.502 reads 'si qua latent, meliora putat', said of Apollo looking at Daphne. Burton's 'puta' is an imperative.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows the ironic twist Burton gives it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 25 opens 'Cinaede Thalle, mollior cuniculi capillo', mocking the effeminate Thallus. Burton does apply the phrase to the mistress.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton turns a jibe into praise.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.789ff, Polyphemus sings 'floridior pratis', and lines are skipped before 'mollior et cycni plumis'. Burton's English does give 'withywind'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Partly useful, but most of it is about the wording and a variant, and it never names Ovid as the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cypris is Venus, and Stratonice was a Seleucid queen famed for her beauty. In his English gloss Burton puts the Spanish Infanta in her place.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure name and shows Burton bringing the comparison up to date.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are from Martial 5.37 (Erotion), which older editions numbered 38, matching Burton's sidenote. The transmitted text reads 'erat'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the poem, which is an epitaph for a dead child, and points out Burton's change of tense.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Catulus's epigram on Roscius, which Cicero preserves at De natura deorum 1.79.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the passage where the epigram survives, which Burton does not give.

answers.accuracy_reason: Margareta/margarita ('pearl') is a natural pun, and the following 'pretiosa' supports it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a nice wordplay point but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is [Tibullus] 4.2.14, one of the Sulpicia poems.
answers.usefulness_reason: It sharpens Burton's bare 'Tibullus' to an exact place, which is useful but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aristaenetus Epist. 1.1 has ἐνδέδυται… εὐπροσωποτάτη· ἐκδέδυται… ὅλη πρόσωπον. The Latin keeps the wordplay with formosa/forma.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the wordplay and gives the Greek source.

answers.accuracy_reason: At Aeneid 1.76–77 Aeolus is speaking to Juno, and the standard text reads 'quid optes'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and the situation, which Burton leaves out, so the reader can see the line is an oath of obedience.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Martial, Spectacula 25b (28 in some editions), the line reads 'mergite cum redeo'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's text already names Leander, so the note adds only a text variant.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.71 begins 'Laevia sex cyathis, septem Iustina bibatur', and that poem describes the custom of a cup per letter.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the drinking custom that makes the line make sense and corrects the name.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Odes 1.9.23–24, the girl only pretends to resist, so 'male pertinaci' means 'hardly holding on'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a phrase that is easy to misread and the playful scene behind it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 2.9–10 is identified correctly, and 'O si' does appear to be Burton's addition. But in Catullus the lines are already a wish ('possem', a subjunctive of wishing), so saying Burton added 'O si' 'to turn the lines into a wish' is misleading.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and gives the original setting of Lesbia's sparrow.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 79 reads 'Qualis nox fuit illa, di deaeque, / quam mollis torus', so Burton's 'erit' does make it future.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.429 does read 'det', so that point is right. Nothing in the text given confirms that the woman pleading is 'the Sultan's wife'; this needs checking against Burton's source.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Virgilian source and Burton's change from 'det' to 'da'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Met. 4.187–8 reads 'aliquis de dis non tristibus optat / sic fieri turpis', so the note has both the story and the verb right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and Burton's change of 'optat' to 'inquit'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace Odes 3.9 has 'pro qua non metuam mori' and 'pro quo bis patiar mori', so the note's account of the combination is accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton joins two lines of Horace into one.

answers.accuracy_reason: Met. 4.96 says 'audacem faciebat amor' of Thisbe.
answers.usefulness_reason: The change of gender is a useful but small point; the sidenote already cites Ovid.

answers.accuracy_reason: At Aeneid 4.296 Dido senses Aeneas' plan to leave ('quis fallere possit amantem?'). Burton does apply it to the cunning of love.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the original context and how Burton turns it to his own use.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line closes the Petronian poem 'Foeda est in coitu et brevis voluptas', which prefers kisses and lingering embraces to the act itself.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the poem and what it argues, which the bare sidenote does not.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is a Latin version of Mimnermus fr. 1 ('What is life, what delight, without golden Aphrodite? May I die…'). Burton's English gives only the second sentence, and loosely.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Greek original and how Burton's English treats it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The epigram is Martial 8.73, not book 9 as the sidenote has it. The Pelignian land is Ovid's homeland and Mantua Virgil's; Corinna and Alexis are their beloveds.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects the sidenote's reference and explains the allusions.

answers.accuracy_reason: Verrines 2.3.76 describes the Persian and Syrian kings giving cities to their wives in this way.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context of Cicero's passage, which the sidenote only cites.

answers.accuracy_reason: Socrates talks in the Piraeus (Republic) and the Lyceum (Euthydemus), and under the plane tree in the Phaedrus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains places a reader may not recognise, including the Phaedrus setting.

answers.accuracy_reason: The full line is right (Terence, Heauton Timorumenos 77), and the note describes Burton's use of it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Giving the full line helps, but the note doesn't name Terence, so the allusion is left without its source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid does call himself 'praeceptor Amoris' (Ars Amatoria 1.17). The note rightly hedges the exact wording.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out an Ovidian allusion that Burton turns around.

answers.accuracy_reason: Apuleius, Met. 10.2 goes on 'lassa genua, quies turbida, et suspiritus...'. Burton's 'restless thoughts, short wind' do render items past where his Latin stops.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's English draws on more of the source than his Latin quotes.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the correct scholastic sense of anima informans: the soul as substantial form.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term that a modern reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Catullus 5.7–9 readings are given correctly. Burton's own sidenote supports the statement that the English is Jonson's imitation.
answers.usefulness_reason: The textual variants are mostly a working point; the remark about Jonson's freedom is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is an Erasmus adage, and it goes back to Euripides (Stheneboea fr., quoted in Plato's Symposium 196e).
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces the saying back to its Greek origin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Josephus, Ant. 18.66–80: Decius Mundus, of equestrian rank, offered Paulina 200,000 drachmae.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the person and the story behind a bare name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 4.1079–81 has 'premunt arte... dentes inlidunt saepe labellis / osculaque adfigunt'. The note hedges suitably on both the slip and the compression.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton's version differs from it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Heroides 15.79 (Sappho to Phaon), and the note quotes it correctly. It is not from Theocritus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects a misattribution in Burton's sidenote and gives the real source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Alphitomancy is correctly derived from alphiton and defined as divination by barley-meal. The note fairly observes that Burton's gloss about beans in a cake describes a folk custom.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure term and notes how far Burton's gloss is from it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Anacreon fr. 360 PMG calls the beloved the one who 'holds the reins of my soul' (charioteer). The note paraphrases it fairly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Greek source of Burton's phrase; it could have added that Anacreon was addressing a boy.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Martial 9.59.3, from the epigram about Mamurra.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the exact locus that Burton leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are from Seneca's Phaedra (379–380). Phaedra is the daughter of Pasiphae, who was the daughter of the Sun, so the note's line of descent is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the allusion in 'Phoebeae facis' and 'gentile', which a reader would otherwise miss, though it does not name Seneca.

answers.accuracy_reason: The note quotes Plautus, Cistellaria 69–70, correctly and shows how Burton shortens it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton altered it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Terence (Eunuchus 59–61) and the Plautus (Mercator, from Charinus' opening speech) are rightly identified. Plautus does read 'incogitantia', and 'aviditas' is the correct form.
answers.usefulness_reason: It sorts out the two joined sources and Burton's changes to them.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Hesiod's Theogony (933–936), Phobos and Deimos are the children of Ares and Aphrodite. The note's description is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Hesiod, and the note does not cite the Theogony or mention that Hesiod makes them sons, not daughters.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are indeed the last two lines of Catullus 107.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already names Catullus on Lesbia; the note only adds the poem number.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ptolemaic astronomy the primum mobile was the outermost sphere, which carried the spheres below it round.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term that Burton's image depends on.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.523, spoken by Apollo while he pursues Daphne.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and its setting, and points out what Burton's English leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 6.428 wine is drunk before the meal 'rabidam facturus orexim', and 'orexis' is Greek for appetite.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Greek word and the context in Juvenal.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Theocritus' Idyll 14 the lovesick speaker is Aeschinas, a man, while Burton introduces the lines with 'she'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out how Burton bends his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are a Latin version of Theocritus, Idyll 13 (around line 71), on Hercules searching for Hylas. The liver was the traditional seat of love.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context and explains the liver, though it does not name the idyll.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aeneid 4.660 the standard text reads 'sub umbras'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the speaker and moment and notes Burton's variant reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage is Metamorphoses 4.149–150, which reads 'est et mihi fortis in unum / hoc manus'. Burton's sidenote '3 Met.' is wrong, and the note rightly corrects it. The English verse that follows does not translate these lines.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects the reference, shows what Burton cut, and explains the mismatched English verse.

answers.accuracy_reason: Parthenius of Nicaea wrote the Erotika Pathemata, a prose collection of unhappy love stories. The accusative after 'Read' is correctly explained.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an obscure author and work that Burton gives only in abbreviated Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe story (Met. 4.166) ends 'una requiescit in urna', and Burton's subjunctive turns the statement into a wish.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and shows how Burton adapts the line to Gismunda's request.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Lugentes campi' is Aeneid 6.441, the region for those consumed by love, and the sidenote is glossed correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Virgilian source and explains what the Mourning Fields are.

answers.accuracy_reason: Sallust, Catiline 15, says Orestilla hesitated to marry Catiline for fear of his adult son (her prospective stepson). Burton's Latin is indeed a paraphrase, possibly by way of Valerius Maximus, whom his sidenote also cites.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the historical source and context for the anecdote.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Met. 1.524 (Apollo chasing Daphne), reads 'nec prosunt domino'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Apollo; the note adds only the Ovidian source and a small variant, and does not name the work.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Sat. 1.2.116–119 is quoted correctly, and Burton's omissions are described accurately.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton cuts the source, notably removing the 'puer' and the clause about assaulting him.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caspar Barth published a Latin version of Celestina (Pornoboscodidascalus, 1624), as Burton's sidenote indicates.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already gives the source, and the remark about the sentence's grammar is a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terence, Eunuchus 732, reads 'sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus', and Liber is Bacchus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the allegory and identifies the classical source of the proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Vitex agnus-castus, the chaste-tree, was traditionally held to be anaphrodisiac.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton himself supplies 'Agnus castus' and its virtue; the note adds only the modern common name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Remedia Amoris 139, reads 'periere Cupidinis arcus'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is mainly a variant reading and does not name the work, though 'arts' for 'bows' is a small point of interest.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.126–129 reads 'Averno' (with 'Averni' as a variant) and 'hoc opus, hic labor est'. Avernus is the lake near Cumae.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains Avernus and notes how Burton changes the famous line.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Principiis obsta' is Ovid, Remedia Amoris 91, and the infinitive form is Burton's general precept.
answers.usefulness_reason: It links the maxim to its well-known Ovidian source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Psalm 118:37 in the Vulgate reads 'Averte oculos meos ne videant vanitatem'. Burton quotes only the opening words.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the verse behind Burton's bare 'saith David'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Jerome's letter 52 to Nepotian tells him to treat the girls and virgins of Christ equally: love them all alike or ignore them all alike. Burton's English gloss does turn 'love' into 'see'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context of the letter and shows how Burton shifts its meaning in his gloss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 7.79–81 is the simile for Medea's quieted love flaring up again when she sees Jason in the temple of Hecate.
answers.usefulness_reason: The narrative context makes the simile fit Burton's point about love reviving at sight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 3.44 reads 'fuge litus avarum' (Polydorus' warning), and Burton has replaced 'avarum' with 'amatum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows a pointed adaptation that a reader would probably miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.23 has Dido's 'agnosco veteris vestigia flammae'. Burton puts it in the third person and applies it to Hermotimus from Aristaenetus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a famous allusion and how Burton has changed it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Possidius, Life of Augustine 26, says that not even Augustine's own sister lived in his house. The note's 'usually' is fair, since Gregory the Great also passes on the story.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the usual source of the anecdote behind Burton's attribution.

answers.accuracy_reason: Remedia Amoris 79–81: 'Dum licet…' begins line 79, the pentameter 'si piget, in primo limine siste pedem' is line 80, and 'Opprime…' is line 81. Burton has joined them.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton puts the quotation together from separate lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Aeneid 6.468, Aeneas 'lenibat dictis animum' when he tries to soothe Dido in the underworld. Here it is the woman who soothes, so the roles are reversed.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and the ironic reversal.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.472 reads 'tandem corripuit sese atque inimica refugit'. Burton writes 'proripuit' and changes the word order.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Dido and Aeneas, and his sidenote gives Aeneid 6. The note adds only the original wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Plautus, Curculio 147ff., Phaedromus begs the door-bolts to spring back and let Planesium out. Burton turns the lines to mean removing the woman, and 'gurcu.' is plausibly a garbled Curculio.
answers.usefulness_reason: It restores the original comic context, which Burton turns around.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.27 lists 'iudicium Paridis spretaeque iniuria formae' among the causes of Juno's anger.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an unattributed Virgil allusion and what it refers to.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terence, Eunuchus 49, is Phaedria's 'redeam? non si me obsecret'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already gives 'Ter.', so the note adds only the play and the speaker.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gordonius is Bernard of Gordon, and part 2, chapter 20 of the Lilium medicinae is his chapter on amor hereos. The object 'pannum menstrualem' does follow at once in Burton's text.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies Burton's medical authority and the chapter on lovesickness, which a reader would want to know.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Suda's story (from Damascius), Hypatia cures an admirer by producing her menstrual rags. 'Shows' is a little softer than the source's 'threw', which matches Burton's 'conjectis', but it is not wrong.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses the euphemism, but the Gordonius remedy just before the sidenote already makes the sense clear.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Historia Augusta's Life of Aelius (5.11), Aelius Verus tells his wife, when she complains of his affairs, that 'uxor' is a name of dignity, not of pleasure.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the speaker and the context of the saying, which Burton's 'as he said' leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase comes from Horace, Satires 1.2.35 ('alienas permolere uxores'), where 'permolere' is a crude sexual metaphor.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the obscene sense of a word a reader might take literally.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of John 6:60 reads 'Durus est hic sermo', the disciples' complaint.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out a biblical echo that adds irony to the use of the marriage vows.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the standard Aristotelian and scholastic idea of prime matter: formless potentiality that 'desires' form.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the philosophical term behind Burton's comparison.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Conjurgium' is the well-known pun that puts 'jurgium' (quarrel) inside 'conjugium' (marriage).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains wordplay that the translation 'a quarrelling' loses.

answers.accuracy_reason: Semonides fr. 7, lines 99–100, says that a man who lives with a woman never passes a whole day cheerful. Burton's sidenote names Semonides.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Greek source of the Latin line and its context in the poem on women.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Suetonius, Augustus 65, Augustus quotes in Greek an adaptation of Iliad 3.40, Hector's rebuke to Paris, wishing he had lived unwed and died childless.
answers.usefulness_reason: It locates the source and shows that Burton is giving his own Latin version of a Greek line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Augustus 65, has Augustus call the two Julias and Agrippa Postumus his 'three boils and three cancers' (tris vomicas ac tria carcinomata).
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader which children Augustus meant and what he actually said.

answers.accuracy_reason: The remark is in the Historia Augusta, Life of Severus 20, attributed to Spartianus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a correct but bare source identification, and Burton already names Spartian.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 6.167–8 ('malo, malo Venustinam quam te, Cornelia, mater Gracchorum'), the speaker prefers a simple girl to the haughty, virtuous Cornelia. Burton's use of it for the over-accomplished wife fits the passage that follows.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes the line that was cut off and explains the point of the contrast.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.460 reads 'intolerabilius nihil est quam femina dives', and the note shows Burton's recasting correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source, which Burton doesn't, and shows how he reworks the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 1.26 tells how Thales, urged by his mother to marry, said it was not yet time and later that the time had passed. This fits Burton's lines just before the phrase.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies 'that Philosopher' and the anecdote behind the phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.288–289 reads 'Mnesthea Sergestumque vocat fortemque Serestum, / classem aptent taciti sociosque ad litora cogant'. The note reports Burton's changes correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact place and shows that Burton has changed the names.

answers.accuracy_reason: The full line is 'cum castum amisit polluto corpore florem', so Burton breaks off before 'polluto corpore florem', not 'just before florem'. Burton also drops 'est' after 'suis', which the note doesn't mention. The rest is right: Catullus 62, and the readings convulsus and quem.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the wedding song and supplies the sense Burton leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 12.34 ends 'nulli te facias nimis sodalem: / gaudebis minus et minus dolebis', which is second person as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the original context and shows how Burton turns the line to his own use.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.438–439 reads 'nullis ille movetur / fletibus aut voces ullas tractabilis audit', on Aeneas unmoved by Dido.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the Dido context behind Burton's application.

answers.accuracy_reason: The word is clearly formed from Xanthippe, and Burton glosses it as 'a shrew to my wife'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own gloss already gives the sense, so the note adds only the origin of the word.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius (Iul. 52.3) does not present the law as a rumour. He says the tribune Helvius Cinna told many people he had the bill drafted and ready to propose on Caesar's orders. Burton's 'others suspect it' refers to commentators such as Torrentius.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Suetonius locus behind Burton's allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius has 'uti uxores liberorum quaerendorum causa quas et quot vellet ducere liceret', which the note's hedged 'roughly' fairly covers. The point that Burton generalises the law to great men is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton cuts and extends his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Andria 254–255 reads 'uxor tibi ducendast, Pamphile, hodie… abi domum. id mihi visust dicere "abi cito ac suspende te"', as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton abridges and reframes Terence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plautus, Asinaria 87, reads 'argentum accepi, dote imperium vendidi', and Burton does attach the line to his Seneca citation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the real comic source of the tag, which Burton credits to Seneca.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Nubere' is used of the bride, and the joke works as the note describes. The line is Martial 8.12, though the note doesn't name it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the joke but leaves out the source, Martial 8.12, which a reader would want.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Idiota' is the accepted pen name of Raymundus Jordanus, who wrote the Contemplationes de amore divino.
answers.usefulness_reason: Tells the reader who the obscure 'Idiota' of Burton's citation is.

answers.accuracy_reason: The 'Tom. 2 in votis' citation points to Lucian's Navigium (Vota), where Lycinus and Timolaus are speakers. 'Simus' means snub-nosed, and Burton's English does say 'crook-nosed'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the dialogue and shows a reader where Burton's English departs from the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Joseph Hall published Mundus alter et idem under the name Mercurius Britannicus, and Viraginia is its land of women.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a pseudonym and a book that a reader would not otherwise recognise.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Parmeno's in Terence's Eunuchus, 1.1 (lines 57–58).
answers.usefulness_reason: Expands a bare abbreviation into the play and the scene.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.3.19–20, has the crow (cornicula) 'furtivis nudata coloribus'. Burton changes it to the accusative.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies an unmarked Horatian allusion that fits Burton's next words, 'Aesop's Jay'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 3.89.2 reads 'nam faciem durum, Phoebe, cacantis habes'. Burton leaves out 'durum' and turns the line on a woman.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows how Burton cuts the source and reapplies it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, In Catilinam 1.10, reads 'Patent portae; proficiscere', and 'profiscere' is a corrupt spelling of it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already gives the source, so the note adds only the exact wording and the spelling.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is from the chorus on the transience of beauty in Seneca's Phaedra (around line 773).
answers.usefulness_reason: Narrows Burton's bare 'Seneca' to the play and its context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 2.113, reads 'forma bonum fragile est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies an unmarked allusion to Ovid.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Phaedra 761–762, in the same chorus, and Hippolytus is the play's other title.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already names the source, so the note mainly explains the 'Hipp.' abbreviation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.297–298 reads 'rara est adeo concordia formae / atque pudicitiae'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies an unmarked quotation and how Burton trims it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Rufinus, Greek Anthology 5.94, gives Melite Hera's eyes, Athena's hands, Aphrodite's breasts and Thetis' ankles. Saying that 'Idem' points to the preceding note's author is the normal meaning.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the 'mistress of the sea' and the Greek epigram behind the lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: Thucydides 2.45: Pericles says a woman's greatest glory is to be least talked of among men, whether for praise or blame.
answers.usefulness_reason: Places the citation in the funeral oration, which the reader would not otherwise know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Anteros is correctly described as the god of returned love, or the avenger of slighted love.
answers.usefulness_reason: Knowing what Anteros means explains Burton's point that no one could light the lamp, since no one's love was returned.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Satires 1.2.54 the words are not Horace's own boast of restraint. They are the self-praise of a profligate (Sallustius), whom Horace mocks for ruining himself on freedwomen. The rest of the note is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the source and how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.69–70, is correctly quoted and glossed.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies a well-known allusion and shows how Burton applies it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus (13.559) quotes this Menander fragment on marriage as a sea of troubles.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own text already names Menander and Athenaeus, so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines come from Seneca's Hercules Oetaeus, in the speech about Deianira's jealous rage.
answers.usefulness_reason: Narrows the vague sidenote to a play and a dramatic context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Semonides fr. 7 calls women the greatest evil Zeus made. The note rightly calls the Latin a paraphrase, not a quotation.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the Greek source and says how loosely Burton renders it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tyrotarichum (a dish of cheese and salt fish) appears in Cicero's letters to Atticus as a cheap, simple meal.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a rare word that a reader needs, though the grammar remark is only a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus book 13 preserves this comic fragment, which the sidenote attributes to Eubulus.
answers.usefulness_reason: Repeats what the sidenote already says and does not name Eubulus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.43 does read 'stulta maritali iam porrigit ora capistro', and Burton's change from 'iam' to 'qui' is described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the exact locus and shows how Burton adapts the line to his sentence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pausanias 7.23 does say the Selemnus' water is worth more than great wealth, and the note properly hedges the identification.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the unnamed 'he' and the source of the claim.

answers.accuracy_reason: Menander's Leukadia fragment, preserved by Strabo, describes Sappho leaping 'with stinging desire' (oistrônti pothôi). Burton's Latin renders it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the source and the figurative sense of 'oestrus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Capitolinus (Life of Marcus Aurelius 19), the Chaldaeans told Faustina to wash in the blood of the gladiator after he was killed. So the note is right that the cure uses the gladiator's blood, not a mistress's.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's general recipe doesn't fit the example he gives from his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 100.7 reads 'cum vesana meas torreret flamma medullas'. In the surrounding text the line is applied to Venus, whom Apollo sends to the Leucadian rock.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and Burton's change of pronoun to fit the new subject.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage is Heroides 15.167–9, and the standard text reads 'Hinc', 'misit' and 'nec mora, versus amor'. One caveat: Ovid's line continues 'fugit', so Burton reordered the words rather than substituting one.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and explains Burton's old numbering of the epistle.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Publilius Syrus A31, 'Amoris vulnus idem sanat qui facit'. His sententiae did circulate in the pseudo-Senecan proverb collections.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects the attribution in Burton's sidenote and explains how the error arose.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ausonius's poem is usually titled 'Cupido cruciatus'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the poem and shows that Burton's title differs from the usual one.

answers.accuracy_reason: In medieval medical writers such as Guainerius, 'heros' means the sufferer from amor hereos/heroicus, that is, the lover.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term that a reader would probably misread as 'hero'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.129 reads 'hoc opus, hic labor est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives a correct locus for a well-known tag, but the point is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Papinian was the Roman jurist and Paul the apostle. The sentence is Jerome's Letter 77.
answers.usefulness_reason: Most readers won't know who Papinian was, and the contrast depends on it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Dio 56.1–10 records Augustus speaking separately to the unmarried and married equites (AD 9), and Burton's sidenote cites the same book. 'Rome' is indeed English.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects how the passage was marked and points the reader to the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is a correct description of the Roman ius trium liberorum.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct but adds little that the translation and Burton's own gloss don't already give.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.28 has 'sponsi Penelopae'. 'Penelopes' is a Greek genitive.
answers.usefulness_reason: It hints at the Horatian echo but spends most of its length on spelling and doesn't spell the allusion out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Phaedra 461, comes from the Nurse's speech to Hippolytus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the speaker but leaves out the exact line and Burton's change of 'coles' to 'colunt'.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Hippolytus' outburst against women in Seneca's Phaedra (about line 566).
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct, but it mostly repeats Burton's sidenote and his own 'with Hippolytus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Philippus Beroaldus the elder married Camilla, daughter of the jurist Vincenzo Paleotti, and the gloss of 'ex animi sententia' is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: Naming the speaker helps, but the second sentence is a translator's gloss.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Latin renders Odysseus' words to Nausicaa (Odyssey 6.182–4) about husband and wife living of one mind, so 'Latin Homer' as Homer in a Latin version is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the puzzling phrase 'our Latin Homer' and gives the Homeric source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.284 reads 'quae prima exordia sumat?', of Aeneas wondering how to approach Dido.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Seneca's Phaedra the Nurse urges Hippolytus with these lines to give up his chaste, solitary life.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and the dramatic situation, which Burton's bare 'Seneca' leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.9.17, has 'donec virenti canities abest morosa', and Burton's 'viventi' departs from it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, which Burton does not name, and points out the altered reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: Moschus' Idyll 6 is the chain Pan–Echo–Satyr–Lyde and closes on this thought of mutual hatred.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a source Burton does not name here and explains the context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Valerius Maximus (7.2 ext. 1) records Socrates' answer that a man will repent whether he marries or not.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the sidenote's reference and the anecdote behind the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 9, Iphis, a girl raised as a boy, is turned into a man (by Isis) so she can marry Ianthe.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the myth behind the allusion, which a reader is unlikely to know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The refrain 'Hymen o Hymenaee, Hymen ades o Hymenaee' is that of Catullus 62.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already gives Catullus; the note adds only the poem number and an obvious gloss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 5.56: Aeneas says this on landing again in Sicily at Anchises' tomb.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Virgilian context and shows how Burton repurposes the line, and the sidenote 'Catullus' could otherwise mislead a reader here.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines come from Catullus 61 (about lines 204–5), near the end of the epithalamium for Manlius and Junia (or Vinia), and Burton's English adds the details the note mentions.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the poem and points out how Burton's verse expands the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Historia Augusta (Gallieni duo 11.8) preserves Gallienus' epithalamium with these lines. Burton's 'O juvenes' differs from the text's 'o pueri', but the note doesn't claim otherwise. Burton's English does say 'oyster kissings'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names an obscure source a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Theocritus, Idyll 18 (the Epithalamium of Helen) has Ζεὺς Κρονίδας granting lasting wealth. The note rightly hedges the Saturnus explanation with 'probably'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and explains the odd 'Saturnus'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid Met. 8.708–710 is Philemon's first-person prayer, quoted correctly, and Burton does recast it in the third person.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton adapts his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are Aen. 9.446–447 on Nisus and Euryalus, and the sidenote Ovid Met. 8 does refer to the preceding lines.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an unmarked allusion and its new use here.

answers.accuracy_reason: Genius as natural appetite or inclination ('indulgere genio') is the right sense here.
answers.usefulness_reason: It stops a misreading of the word as 'talent', but the point is slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Heauton Timorumenos 213–216 is Clitipho's complaint about 'iniqui patres … a pueris ilico nasci senes', which Burton quotes.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and speaker behind a bare abbreviation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Ecl. 2.19 is Corydon addressing Alexis.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an unmarked allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 3.284 reads 'fugit inreparabile tempus', so the phrase is an echo, as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: The echo is useful, but the remark about quotation status is a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Theocritus, Idyll 12.15–16 has the golden men of old, when the one loved loved back.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source of a Latinized Greek line.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Sat. 1.1.68, 'Tantalus a labris sitiens fugientia captat flumina'. The note doesn't give the locus, but what it says is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes the image that Burton breaks off.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Cons. 3 pr. 7 cites Euripides (Andromache) saying the childless man is 'infortunio felix'. Burton's gloss does reverse the paradox.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows the source chain and Burton's twist.

answers.accuracy_reason: Met. 1.478–480 reads 'aversata' and has line 479 ('inpatiens expersque viri…') between the two lines Burton quotes.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton alters and cuts his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 2.56 reads 'Rusticus es, Corydon; nec munera curat Alexis', with Corydon addressing himself; Burton's 'est' makes it third person.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the Virgilian original and shows how Burton changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.426 is said of Narcissus and his reflection; Burton's 'he dotes, is doted on again' applies it to a pair of lovers.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows the ironic shift from self-love to mutual love.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Native' (natus) is indeed the astrological term for the subject of a nativity.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a technical term that a modern reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The palinode is Stesichorus' recantation about Helen. Burton is quoting Philippus Beroaldus, who married Camilla Paleotti, as the sidenote shows.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the allusion and says whose words these are.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Resolutions upon a question' are horary judgements, and whether one will win a mistress is a standard horary question.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the branch of astrology Burton means.

answers.accuracy_reason: The seventh house is the house of marriage, the second governs wealth, and the twelfth governs servitude, imprisonment and secret enemies. That is standard astrological doctrine.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the technical system that makes the aphorism make sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.438–39 reads 'sed nullis ille movetur / fletibus…' and is about Aeneas; Burton's 'illa' makes it feminine, and his English couplet is indeed a free generalization.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows Burton changing the gender of a Virgilian line to suit his point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.353–55 reads 'cupiere', 'dura' and 'tetigere'. The note's account of Burton's variants and their effect is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Mostly a comparison of readings, though it points out a real change in sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton plays on phlebotomy (opening a vein, here for a pleurisy) and Hymen, the god of marriage.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the medical joke.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.7.27: 'nil desperandum Teucro duce et auspice Teucro'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Correctly identifies a familiar tag, but a reader loses little without it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 1.669–70 continues 'si non et cetera sumpsit, / haec quoque quae data sunt perdere dignus erit', as the note paraphrases.
answers.usefulness_reason: Supplies the part Burton leaves unsaid, which carries the point, though it should name the Ars Amatoria.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 12.937 reads 'tua est Lavinia coniunx', spoken by the defeated Turnus; Burton's subjunctive 'sit' changes the force.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source and shows how Burton recasts the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: Heauton Timorumenos 213 (Clitipho) does read 'quam iniqui sunt patres in omnis adulescentis iudices', and Burton's sidenote 'Ter.' matches.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the exact line Terence's phrase comes from, in the same play Burton quotes next.

answers.accuracy_reason: At the end of the Heauton Timorumenos, Clitipho turns down the red-haired girl his father offers and asks for Archonides' daughter instead. The note describes this and Burton's use of it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a phrase that makes no sense without the scene in Terence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 9.32–33 reads 'fatum est et partibus illis / quas sinus abscondit', and it does refer to the private parts. The note reports Burton's change of 'et' to 'in' correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader what the euphemism means and how Burton's wording differs from Juvenal's.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are the closing lines of the Ausonian 'De rosis nascentibus' (Idyll 14), where a rose blooms at dawn and has faded by evening. Eous is the Morning Star.
answers.usefulness_reason: Knowing the subject is a rose shows how Burton has turned the lines toward a woman.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Ars Amatoria 2.669, and it continues 'tolerate labores' as the note says. But in Ovid the 'labores' are already the work of love, in praise of older mistresses. So 'Burton applies it to love' wrongly suggests he changed its sense. The note also doesn't name the work.
answers.usefulness_reason: Giving the rest of the line is of some use, but without the work named or the context, the reader learns little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Catullus 5.4–6, and the standard text reads 'perpetua'. The English is from Jonson's song 'Come, my Celia' in Volpone, as Burton's sidenote says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and the textual variant, and it confirms where the English verse comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Megadorus' speech in the Aulularia (about lines 478–482). The quotation does start partway through his sentence.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and the play behind Burton's 'Comical old man'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the usual story (Callimachus, Ovid Heroides 20–21), Cydippe reads the oath aloud and so binds herself to marry Acontius. The masculine forms in Burton's Latin do turn it into Acontius' own promise.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out a real change Burton made to the story, which a reader would not spot alone.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aelian, Varia Historia 13.33, does tell the story of Rhodopis' shoe and the eagle.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own sidenote already gives 'Aelian. lib. 13 cap. 33', so the note mostly repeats it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The proverb appears in Terence, Phormio 506, and in Erasmus, Adagia I.v.25, and it means what the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the classical source and the Erasmus adage that Burton's readers would have known.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Cornutum' (the horned argument, or dilemma) is a standard term in logic.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term from logic and the image of the two horns behind it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Arabic 'parts' (lots) of marriage and lust, and the triplicities, are described correctly. Calling 'triplicates' a probable corruption is properly hedged. 'Ruled by a planet' is a loose simplification but acceptable.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains astrological jargon that most readers will not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Nepos, Atticus 11.6 has 'sui cuique mores fingunt fortunam'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the classical source of the maxim, which Burton leaves unsourced.

answers.accuracy_reason: The standard text of Phaedra 339–343 reads 'Venere instincti' and 'mugitu'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is mainly a textual-variant note, though it does narrow Burton's bare 'Seneca' to the Phaedra.

answers.accuracy_reason: Macrobius, Sat. 2.5.10 gives the saying to Julia, the daughter of Augustus, in the first person.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the ribald joke and corrects Burton's attribution of the saying to Livia.

answers.accuracy_reason: It renders Mimnermus fr. 1 ('hateful to boys, despised by women') about old age.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already names Mimnermus; the note adds only the old-age context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Panegyricus 83 reads 'ita foris claros domestica destruebat infamia', in a passage about wives.
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly records Burton's small verbal changes to the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Florida 3 has Marsyas mocking Apollo as 'genis gratum, corpore glabellum, arte multiscium, fortuna opulentum'; the attribution is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It locates the Apuleius allusion and its ironic context.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Institutes 1.1.3 give the three precepts, and Q. Mucius Scaevola and Trebatius were Roman jurists; the remark on 'eam' is offered as interpretation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the legal joke a modern reader would miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Heroides 16.288 (Paris to Helen).
answers.usefulness_reason: It turns Burton's bare 'Ovid' into a specific source with its telling context, Paris's seduction letter.

answers.accuracy_reason: Thyestes 217–218 reads 'sanctitas pietas fides / privata bona sunt'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It locates the tyrant's maxim and shows how Burton altered the list.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Divus Julius 51 records the soldiers' verse at the Gallic triumph.

answers.accuracy_reason: Divus Julius 52 has the elder Curio's 'omnium mulierum virum et omnium virorum mulierem'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton cut the second half of the gibe.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Amatoria 2.373ff. reads 'nec lea' and builds up to the woman who catches a rival in her bed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aen. 3.490: Andromache, looking at Ascanius, says Astyanax had such eyes, hands and face. The words do describe her dead son.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aen. 4.11, Dido to Anna about Aeneas; reading armis as armus 'shoulders' is the usual reading, going back to Servius.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the source and speaker and sorts out a real ambiguity in the word.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.652–4: wives watch Alcestis die in her husband's place, and the standard text reads cupiant.
answers.usefulness_reason: The Alcestis context sharpens the joke, which Burton's paraphrase loses.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Lycoris elegies printed under Cornelius Gallus's name (Gauricus, 1501) are by Maximianus, and imbellis in an erotic sense is well attested.
answers.usefulness_reason: Corrects Burton's attribution and explains the sexual sense of the word.

answers.accuracy_reason: Euripides, Andromache 944–6: Hermione blames the women who visited her.
answers.usefulness_reason: Pins the bare sidenote 'Euripides' to the play and speaker.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.62: Laevina, chaste as a Sabine, goes to Baiae, falls for a young man and leaves her husband.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the epigram's story, which differs from Burton's framing of women feigning illness.

answers.accuracy_reason: In La Celestina (Tragicomedia de Calisto y Melibea), Pármeno says more than five thousand maidenheads were made and unmade on her authority. The note's 'thousands' is safe.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the allusion and the work, which most readers will not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The syrinx test of virginity and Leucippe's ordeal are in Achilles Tatius book 8 (8.6, 8.13–14), not book 6.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the episode and corrects Burton's reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Qur'an 2:223 (al-Baqara) as quoted in Riccoldo da Monte di Croce's Confutatio, which the sidenote cites.
answers.usefulness_reason: Mostly repeats the sidenote ('cap. Bovis'); it would be more useful if it gave the verse number and named Riccoldo.

answers.accuracy_reason: The wording (fons cladium, seminarium delictorum) is from Cyprian's De zelo et livore, where zelus is envy. The note is properly hedged, and its point about 'murders' is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows that Burton applies Cyprian's words about envy to sexual jealousy, and notes his free rendering.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, De officiis 2.25: Alexander of Pherae was killed by his wife Thebe propter pelicatus suspicionem.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the legal term and names the wife from the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Adulterare is used of debasing coin, and it is related to adulterium.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the pun, but slightly, and does not give the Philo locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Machaon was the Greek physician at Troy. The English stanza is Harington's version of Orlando Furioso 31.5, as the sidenote shows. The note leaves out that the couplet is Ovid, Remedia Amoris 545–6, but it says nothing wrong.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses Machaon and makes clear that the stanza is a separate quotation, but it misses the Ovid source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Epistulae 6.4 does read 'nullius boni sine socio iucunda possessio est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact place for an attribution Burton makes without a locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Modern texts of Amores 3.4 read 'ni velit' and 'nec corpus servare potes, licet omnia claudas'. But 'mentem' and 'si velit' may be readings in older editions, so saying Burton himself changed the line claims more than the evidence allows.
answers.usefulness_reason: Setting the passage against Ovid's text shows how it differs and makes the sense clearer.

answers.accuracy_reason: Amores 3.4.19–20 does read 'et hos unus saepe fefellit Amor', with 'hos' referring to Argus's eyes. The sidenote does point to the Ariosto lines quoted next.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the real source, which is Ovid even though Burton says 'as in Ariosto', and points out his change to the line.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the opening line of Ausonius' epigram. In it the wife adds quicksilver, and the two poisons cancel each other out.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the joke behind Burton's allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Valerius Maximus 6.7.1, Tertia Aemilia, wife of Scipio Africanus and mother of Cornelia, ignores her husband's affair with a slave girl. Burton's 'Tertius Aemilius' wife' is a garbled version of her name.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects and identifies the story behind Burton's muddled reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Proverbs 19:14 reads 'a Domino autem proprie uxor prudens'.
answers.usefulness_reason: A comparison of wording for a verse Burton already cites; a reader loses little without it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Herodotus describes the Babylonian custom at 1.199 (Clio), not in Erato, and 'Baylonicae' is a misprint.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's wrong locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 129 reads 'funerata est illa pars corporis, qua quondam Achilles eram'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, shows how Burton reshapes it, and explains the allusion to Achilles.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horologium principum is the Latin version of Guevara's Reloj de príncipes, which was presented as the work of Marcus Aurelius.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains why Burton names M. Aurelius for a work by Guevara.

answers.accuracy_reason: Alessio Piemontese wrote the Secreti and Giambattista della Porta wrote Magia naturalis; both identifications are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies two authorities that readers would not know from the bare names.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 3.26.1–2 reads 'Vixi puellis nuper idoneus / et militavi non sine gloria'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's switch to the third person is a small point, and the misprint is a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Sophocles' saying about escaping desire as from a raging, savage master is in Plato, Republic 329c, and Cicero repeats it in De Senectute. Burton's Latin echoes it, and the note's 'recalls' is properly hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: Tells the reader where the image comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: Silicernium was a funeral feast, and Terence's Adelphoe uses the word as an insult for a decrepit old man, as Festus also explains.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a rare word and its comic use as an insult. Only the last sentence is a translator's working remark.

answers.accuracy_reason: Blefken did write on Iceland. In Herodotus 6.61–62 Ariston gets the wife of his friend Agetus by a trick over an exchange of gifts, so calling Burton's version loose is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the author and the Herodotean story, and shows how Burton bends it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The poem is Martial 3.93, addressed to Vetustilla.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the modern number in place of Burton's '3. 62' and the right name in place of his 'Vetustina'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pyrgopolinices says 'nimiast miseria nimis pulchrum esse hominem' in Miles Gloriosus 68.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the comedy's speaker and Plautus's exact wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gellius 5.11 preserves the line from Ennius' Melanippa, with 'stata forma' meaning middling beauty.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the source through which the Ennius line survives and explains the term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Birdlime was made from mistletoe, which thrushes spread. Erasmus' Adagia gives the proverb as 'Turdus ipse sibi malum cacat'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains an obscure proverb and gives its source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Anima does mean both breath and soul, and the Asinaria jokes about a wife's foul breath. Burton's 'deformed souls' does use the other sense. The quotation is close to Plautus' wording, not exact.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows the pun and how Burton turns Plautus's joke.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.463 reads 'hinc miseri viscantur labra mariti', and the note explains the face-paint correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the image and records Burton's change of wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch, Cato the Elder 21, says Cato let his slaves go with the female slaves for a set fee and forbade them other women.
answers.usefulness_reason: Confirms Burton's source and glosses the key phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch (Conjugal Precepts) explains that the gall was left out of wedding sacrifices so that bitterness would be kept out of marriage.
answers.usefulness_reason: Correct, but the symbolism is fairly plain from Burton's context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Commanding and obeying signs are equidistant from the equinoctial axis, and antiscia are symmetrical about the solstitial axis. This matches Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos 1.14–15.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains astrological terms a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Convivium is the standard Latin title of Plato's Symposium, as in Ficino's translation.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the work by its English title, but it leaves out what the 'two furies' are.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the correct description of the lictor's office.
answers.usefulness_reason: A brief gloss of a fairly familiar term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terra Australis Incognita was the hypothetical southern continent shown on early modern maps.
answers.usefulness_reason: Brief context; the name mostly explains itself.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote's 'Lib. 4 Tit. 4 de Instit. reipub.' confirms this is Francesco Patrizi of Siena's De institutione reipublicae.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the author and work and distinguishes him from the other Francesco Patrizi.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Pliny, NH 30.4 (modern 30.13), 'eam' does refer to magic, and '&c.' does close Burton's English list.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton turns Pliny's remark about magic into one about superstition.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Matthew 11:30 reads 'iugum enim meum suave est et onus meum leve'; it is the burden that is light.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the biblical source and shows how Burton merges its two halves.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 3.3.7–8, reads 'impavidum ferient ruinae'; Burton's 'impavidos' makes it plural.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and shows how Burton applies it to all believers.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Romans 8:31 reads 'si Deus pro nobis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and notes Burton's change of wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: In scholastic usage, totum compositum means the whole composite of body and soul.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term a modern reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny says Britain practises magic so devoutly that she might seem to have taught it to the Persians, its supposed inventors.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's English gloss bends Pliny's sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: The distich 'Nocte pluit tota... divisum imperium cum Iove Caesar habet' is quoted as Virgil's in Donatus's Life of Virgil.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the line Burton parodies and the word he substitutes.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Brocard (Burchard of Mount Sion), set against the Greek Church, 'Latini' means the Western Church; Burton's English renders it as 'our Church'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Correct, but it largely restates the shift that is already visible in Burton's English.

answers.accuracy_reason: New Spain was indeed the Spanish viceroyalty centred on Mexico, covering North and Central America.
answers.usefulness_reason: A correct but brief gloss on a fairly familiar place-name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Castilla del Oro was the Spanish name for the territory on the Isthmus of Panama and the neighbouring coast (now Panama and northern Colombia).
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a colonial name most readers will not recognise.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 5.13, calls the Jews 'gens superstitioni obnoxia, religionibus adversa', and Burton's English renders that phrase.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton turns Tacitus's remark about the Jews against the Scandinavians, which a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is Juvenal 14.109: 'fallit enim vitium specie virtutis et umbra'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the classical source behind Burton's tag.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at 1 Corinthians 9:27 reads 'castigo corpus meum et in servitutem redigo'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It turns Burton's bare 'Paul' into an exact biblical reference.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate uses 'pythonissa' or 'habens pythonem' for the witch of Endor (1 Samuel 28; 1 Chronicles 10:13), and the term comes from the Pythia at Delphi.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the standard Catholic definition of the limbus patrum.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses a theological term that many modern readers will not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Plutarch (Lucullus 10) the south wind smashed Mithridates' siege engines, above all the great tower, rather than wrecking a fleet. The note also says nothing of Plutarch's 'Pontic trumpeter'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Critias 109b–c describes the gods dividing up regions and tending men like a shepherd's flock. The note rightly calls Burton's Latin a paraphrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: The preamble to Zaleucus's laws survives in Greek in Stobaeus and opens by requiring that inhabitants be persuaded the gods exist. The note's remark about the main text is accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the real source and the original language of Burton's Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caesar, Gallic War 6.14 reads 'hoc maxime ad virtutem excitari putant, metu mortis neglecto'. Burton's 'ut … incitarent' does recast this as a statement of purpose.

answers.accuracy_reason: The prayer is traditionally given as Aristotle's dying words and is generally held to be apocryphal; the note hedges this properly.

answers.accuracy_reason: The half-line is Petronius fr. 27 and also appears in Statius, Thebaid 3.661. Burton's English does apply it to obedience.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Lucian's Necyomantia 7, Menippus describes the fruit-and-water diet and sleeping in the open that Mithrobarzanes prescribed. Burton quotes a Latin version.

answers.accuracy_reason: The closest wording is Curtius 4.10.7, not Tacitus, and the note correctly leaves the Tacitus attribution as Burton's own.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's source attribution is shaky and points to the real parallel.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote cites Cardano's commentary on Ptolemy's Quadripartitum (the Tetrabiblos), where Cardano does discuss the character of the different religions ('leges').
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats the sidenote's citation, and its remark on the syntax is a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at Isaiah 14:14 reads 'similis ero Altissimo'; Burton changes it to the third person.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a biblical allusion and how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The words come from Gallic War 6.14. Burton's 'go from one to another' renders 'ab aliis post mortem transire ad alios', the rest of the sentence.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifying the source helps, but it repeats the earlier note on the same Caesar passage (f175).

answers.accuracy_reason: Marco Polo's account of the Old Man of the Mountain (Aloadin) and his garden is about the Nizari Ismaili leader, and the identification is standard.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader who Burton's 'Tartar Prince' really was.

answers.accuracy_reason: Curtius 4.10.7 reads 'alioquin impotens, saeva, mutabilis, ubi vana religione capta est, melius vatibus quam ducibus suis paret'. There 'impotens' describes the multitude, so Burton's 'feeble women' is his own change; the note hedges this properly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It sets Burton against his source and shows how he alters it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The term comes from 'python', a spirit of divination named after Pytho (Delphi). The Vulgate uses 'pythonissam' for the witch of Endor at 1 Chronicles 10:13.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term and its biblical use.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are Seneca, Troades 405–406, from the chorus beginning 'Post mortem nihil est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and its context, which suits Burton's point about priests who disbelieve.

answers.accuracy_reason: Augustine, De civ. Dei 4.31, reports Varro saying that many true things are not useful for the people to know, and that it suits the people to believe some false things otherwise. That is Varro's view of the civil religion. Burton's English gloss does loosely recast it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context of the source and shows how Burton turns it to his own use.

answers.accuracy_reason: Justin, 1 Apology 26, reports the inscription. The 1574 find of 'Semoni Sanco Deo Fidio' makes the Semo Sancus explanation the standard one, and the note rightly hedges it with 'probably'. Burton does break off with '&c.'
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader about the famous misreading behind Justin's story.

answers.accuracy_reason: Eudo (Éon) de l'Étoile was a Breton heretic of the 1140s, condemned at Reims in 1148.
answers.usefulness_reason: The identification is correct but slight, since Burton already describes him and names William of Newburgh as his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Ptolemaic system the primum mobile is the outermost sphere, and it drives the daily motion of the spheres inside it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the cosmological term behind Burton's metaphor.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Laws 644d and 803c Plato calls man a puppet or plaything of the gods. The note says 'echoes', which is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points to the Platonic source of the phrase, which fits Burton's mention of the Platonists.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.76, addresses the Roman people as 'belua multorum es capitum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the classical source of the phrase, though without giving the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, De vita beata 1.3, reads 'pergentes non quo eundum est, sed quo itur', said of people who follow the herd like cattle.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source, and Seneca's herd image matches Burton's sheep.

answers.accuracy_reason: Implicit faith (fides implicita) means belief taken on authority without examining it. That is a correct gloss.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a theological term that Protestant polemic used against Rome.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.59–60, has 'at pueri ludentes "rex eris" aiunt "si recte facies"'. It is a children's game rhyme.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and the children's game behind it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of 1 Corinthians 8:1 reads 'scientia inflat'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out the scriptural echo.

answers.accuracy_reason: Both scholastic terms are glossed correctly, and 'codigno' is clearly an error for 'condigno'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains technical theological terms that Burton is attacking.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.14, has 'nullius addictus', said of himself. Burton's plural fits his 'they' who follow only their own spirit.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tertullian, De praescriptione haereticorum 38 reads 'ad materiam suam caedem scripturarum confecit' about Marcion's sword rather than pen. The note quotes it correctly, and Burton's change to the plural is described accurately.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus, the original target (Marcion) and how Burton widens the line to heretics in general.

answers.accuracy_reason: Eon de l'Étoile (Eudo de Stella) was a twelfth-century Breton heretic. William of Newburgh, cited in Burton's sidenote, reports that he claimed divine status.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an obscure figure a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Lucilius fragment is preserved in Lactantius, Divine Institutes 1.22, and Book 1 is titled De falsa religione. The note is right that the sidenote's locus is Lactantius'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the misleading sidenote and the indirect transmission of the lines.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Persius, Prologue 8–11: 'quis expedivit psittaco suum χαῖρε … magister artis ingenique largitor venter'. Reading the belly as gain fits how Burton applies the line.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes the quotation, names the source and gives the punchline Burton leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: Machiavelli argues in Discourses II.2 that Christianity has made men weak. The claim about where the Latin wording comes from is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the work behind Burton's vague 'political disputations' and points to the argument there.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Imaginatio laesa' is the standard term in Renaissance medicine for the damaged faculty that produces melancholy delusions.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical medical term that links this passage to Burton's theory of melancholy.

answers.accuracy_reason: Febris was a Roman goddess of fever with several temples in Rome (Valerius Maximus 2.5.6). Most Roman fevers were malarial, so 'malaria' is acceptable.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a correct gloss on one name in a long list, but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.8 opens 'Olim truncus eram ficulnus, inutile lignum', spoken by a statue of Priapus that the carpenter chose to make a god.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the joke behind Burton's '&c.'

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 15.34–38 does have 'ardet adhuc, Ombos et Tentyra. summus utrimque' between these lines, and the standard text reads 'credat' and 'colit'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton cut the source and why the Latin has no verb, though the variant readings are a lesser point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 1.101 closes the Iphigenia passage, and 'religio' there means superstition or fear of the gods.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context and the special sense of 'religio' a reader needs.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 1.6–7 is part of the opening lines on civil war.
answers.usefulness_reason: Knowing the context of civil war explains why Burton applies the lines to Christians fighting Christians.

answers.accuracy_reason: The definition of the limbus patrum is the standard theological one.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a useful but brief gloss on a fairly familiar theological term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Burton's 'propitius' echoes the people's prayer to the deified Romulus in Livy 1.16.3 ('volens propitius'), not Proculus's announcement (1.16.5–7). Calling the line a summary of Proculus's speech is too confident. That it is not Livy's exact wording is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: The gloss on Quirites and the warning that this is not a verbatim quotation help a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Herodotus 1.50 is right about the 3,000 of each kind of beast and the burned couches and cups. But those were destroyed. What went to Delphi was gold ingots cast afterwards plus other offerings, so 'the gifts were then sent on' is loose. Sardis as the place of the pyre is implied in Herodotus, not stated.
