answers.usefulness_reason: Shows how Burton's summary moves the sacrifice to Delphi.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ammianus 25.4.17 gives the white oxen's greeting to Marcus Caesar with 'si iterum viceris, perimus'. Burton does drop 'iterum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the joke, identifies the source and notes Burton's change to the text.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Herodotus 1.47–48 the oracle names the tortoise and lamb that Croesus was boiling in a bronze cauldron.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains an allusion a reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: The limbus infantum was the limbo assigned to infants who died unbaptised.
answers.usefulness_reason: A useful but brief gloss on a theological term.

answers.accuracy_reason: De carne Christi 5 reads 'credibile est, quia ineptum est'. Burton's version is the familiar paraphrase.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the real wording and locus behind a famous misquotation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of 2 Cor 10:5 reads 'in captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the biblical source and how the wording was changed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ipse dixit (autos epha) was the formula by which Pythagoreans appealed to their master's authority.
answers.usefulness_reason: The background is well known and the note is slight; part of it is a working note about which words are Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels, reads 'nec fides habet meritum, cui humana ratio praebet experimentum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Finds the source and shows how Burton's wording differs.

answers.accuracy_reason: The saying 'Domine, si error est, a te ipso decepti sumus' is in Richard of St Victor, De Trinitate 1.2, which matches the sidenote.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own sidenote already gives the work, so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The jibe is traditionally attributed to Averroes, and the note hedges that attribution properly.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the traditional attribution for an anonymous quotation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The pyx and 'idem corpus numero' (numerical identity) are glossed correctly, and the framing matches what Burton says about Muslim and Jewish objections.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a liturgical object and a scholastic term.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 15.10–11 reads 'quibus haec nascuntur in hortis / numina', and the satire mocks Egypt's worship of leeks and onions.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names leeks and onions, so the note adds only the context and a minor textual variant.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Dii maiorum/minorum gentium' does come from the ranking of patrician houses as patres maiorum and minorum gentium, and it was applied to the greater and lesser gods.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an idiom that a reader would not otherwise understand.

answers.accuracy_reason: The episode is from Geoffrey of Monmouth, which is right. But the Merlin commentary printed under the name of Alanus de Insulis is of disputed authorship, probably not Alan of Lille's, and the note states it as his without a hedge.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source of the allusion and explains Burton's sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lactantius (Div. Inst. 2.2) quotes Seneca on worshipping images while despising the craftsmen who made them.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader how Seneca's lost words have come down to us.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ammianus (22.12) records that Julian was mocked as 'victimarius' for his many sacrifices, and the glosses of the two nicknames are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the nicknames and gives their historical source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Branchidae is Didyma near Miletus, the site of Apollo's oracle and temple.
answers.usefulness_reason: The place is identified correctly, but Burton's 'Apollo Didymeus' already makes most of the point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Livy (8.9) has the Decii devoting themselves to the Di Manes and Tellus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a brief gloss that adds little to the translation.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Laethi' is a spelling of 'leti', and Propertius (3.13 in modern numbering) describes Eastern widows competing to die on their husband's pyre.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context of the quotation and explains an odd spelling.

answers.accuracy_reason: The gloss of 'ad vitam corrigi' as reform of their way of life is questionable. Set against burning, it more likely means to be corrected and so keep their lives.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Eudo de Stella, and the rest is a gloss of wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 6.525–527 the woman crawls on bleeding knees, and 'si candida iusserit Io' begins the next clause about going to Egypt, so Burton does join the two.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton reshapes his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: De beneficiis 4.5.1 reads 'non necessitatibus tantum nostris provisum est: usque in delicias amamur'. The doubt about which quotation the sidenote belongs to is properly hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the true locus and shows how Burton altered the wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pro Flacco 69 reads 'Sua cuique civitati religio, Laeli, est, nostra nobis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and points out how Burton's change of mood serves his argument.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Titus 3:10 does read 'haereticum hominem post unam et secundam correptionem devita'. The note's description of how Burton's wording differs is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the verse Burton quotes without citing it, and shows how he changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 1.190–91 reads 'immedicabile corpus / ense recidendum', and the 'vulnus' form did circulate as a proverb.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Ovidian source and the change Burton makes to it.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the last aphorism of Hippocrates (Aph. 7.87), on drugs, knife and cautery. The note glosses 'iron' and 'fire' correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source, explains the medical terms, and shows how Burton turns the saying against heretics.

answers.accuracy_reason: The words are Caecilius's in Octavius 10. Burton abridges and reorders them, and 'scilicet' is ironic there.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Caecilius in Minucius; the notes on the abridgement and the sarcasm add only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 2.152 the bath fee is the quadrans, and small children went in free.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a piece of Roman custom without which the last line is obscure.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Nero 38, reports the Greek line 'emou thanontos…' and Nero's reply 'emou zontos'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the anecdote and source behind Burton's allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.61 ('nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa') praises a clear conscience; Burton uses it of men who feel no guilt at all.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows the source and how Burton bends it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Amores 3.9.35–36, the elegy on Tibullus, begins 'Cum rapiunt mala fata bonos'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It turns Burton's bare 'Ovid' into a precise source and context.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Contra Celsum 3.34 and following, Celsus sets Zalmoxis, Mopsus, Amphiaraus, Trophonius and others beside Christ.
answers.usefulness_reason: It mostly repeats the names Burton gives in the main text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Giordano Bruno was burned in Rome in February 1600, and 'infelix' does carry the sense 'ill-fated'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The identification is fairly obvious; the date of the burning adds some useful context.

answers.accuracy_reason: The couplet 'Nocte pluit tota…' is attributed to Virgil in the Donatus Life of Virgil.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the famous couplet and its traditional attribution.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 1 prose 4 has 'Si quidem deus est, unde mala? bona vero unde, si non est?', and Cotta argues the point in De natura deorum book 3.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives a close parallel and points to the source of Burton's next allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Germania 46 on the Fenni is quoted correctly. Burton does reverse the order of the clauses and shorten the wording.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and shows how Burton reworks it.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Aeneid 6.471, on Dido's shade unmoved by Aeneas. Marpessos is indeed the marble mountain on Paros.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion, explains an obscure epithet and shows how Burton turns the line to his own use.

answers.accuracy_reason: The proverb appears in Terence, Phormio 186 ('laterem lavem'), and in Erasmus's Adagia ('Laterem lavas').
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the proverb and where it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source is Tacitus, Annals 16.19. Tacitus's text has no 'amicos' and reads 'sapientium', so both claims about Burton's changes are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names Tacitus, and the rest of the note is mostly about textual variants.

answers.accuracy_reason: These are Peter's words in Matthew 17:4, and the Vulgate does read 'bonum est nos hic esse'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a biblical allusion and shows how Burton twists it ironically.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caecilius says this in Octavius 12, and Burton's wording is indeed loose.
answers.usefulness_reason: The main text and the sidenote already point to Caecilius in Minucius Felix, so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Euripides' Cyclops (lines 334–335), Polyphemus sacrifices only to himself and to his belly, 'greatest of the gods'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a Greek source a reader would be unlikely to recognise.

answers.accuracy_reason: Modern editions number this Martial 4.21 and name the man Segius. Burton's sidenote cites it as 1.21.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's citation and the name he gives.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Octavius 12.2 the passage is longer ('ut dicitis, egetis, algetis, operibus et fame laboratis…'), so Burton has abridged it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own note already names Caecilius in Minucius, so the only addition is that the passage is abridged.

answers.accuracy_reason: The English gloss does echo Acts 26:24, and the Vulgate of Romans 11:20 does read 'noli altum sapere'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out a biblical echo and the gap between Burton's Latin and his English.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Semper paret, semel iussit' is from De Providentia 5.8. The note links the rest to Naturales Quaestiones 2.35 with a hedge ('echoes'); Burton's sidenote cites chapters 33 and 36 of the same book.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton has combined two Senecan sources and gives the exact locus of each.

answers.accuracy_reason: Peregrinus 13 calls Christ 'that crucified sophist' (τὸν ἀνεσκολοπισμένον ἐκεῖνον σοφιστήν). In ch. 11 he is 'the man crucified in Palestine', so Lucian never calls him a god.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's 'crucified god' is not what Lucian wrote, which a reader could not tell from the translation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 1.62–65 praises Epicurus, and 'religio' there means fear of the gods, or superstition.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context of the lines and the special sense of 'religio', which matters for Burton's argument.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Natural History 7.188 (book 7, chapter 55 in older editions) reads 'omnibus a supremo die eadem quae ante primum'. The sidenote paraphrases this.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the passage in Pliny and shows that the sidenote is a summary, not a quotation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Letters 54.4 reads 'hoc erit post me quod ante me fuit'. The note rightly records that Burton has 'Idem' for 'hoc' and cites an older numbering.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the exact passage, notes Burton's change of wording, and squares his reference with the modern one.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Letters 54.5 compares a lamp after it is put out with the lamp before it was lit. The note rightly calls Burton's sentence a paraphrase.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of an unattributed sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: The three-rings parable is Decameron 1.3. The claim about where the Latin wording comes from is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the story Burton points to, which many readers will not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: De tribus impostoribus was a legendary book that was rumoured more than seen, and the Cymbalum mundi is by Bonaventure des Périers. 'Inquit' most plausibly refers to Mersenne, whom Burton names just before.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains two notorious books and the obscure 'Peresius', and says who is speaking.

answers.accuracy_reason: Erasmus does collect 'Omnium horarum homo' in the Adagia (1.3.86), for a man suited to every occasion and company.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the proverbial source and sense of the phrase, which Burton turns into an insult.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 2.17–18 reads 'heus age, responde (minimum est quod scire laboro) / de Iove quid sentis?'. The note describes Burton's changes correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names Persius but gives no line number, and is mostly about Burton's wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.21–22 is about an unbaked pot: 'sonat vitium percussa, maligne / respondet'. The account of Burton's changes is correct, and the biblical echo is fairly hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the cracked-pot image behind a hard line and how Burton reshaped it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.16.45 reads 'introrsum turpem, speciosum pelle decora', in the singular.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names Horace but no exact passage, and is mostly about Burton's change to the plural.

answers.accuracy_reason: Romans 2:5 in the Vulgate reads 'thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the scripture Burton is echoing.

answers.accuracy_reason: Genius was a person's guardian spirit, and 'genio indulgere' is a standard Latin idiom for indulging oneself.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a Roman idea that sits behind Burton's English phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero (Tusculan Disputations 4.18) defines desperatio as 'aegritudo sine ulla rerum expectatione meliore'. The note hedges properly on who added 'animi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names Burton's source and shows how the quotation was changed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 13.198 reads 'gestare', which depends on 'poena' in the line before. Burton's 'gestant' makes the line stand on its own.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton adapts his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 13.2–4 reads 'prima est haec ultio' and 'gratia fallaci praetoris vicerit urna', as the note says. The explanation of the urn is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the locus, explains the voting urn, and points out Burton's changes.

answers.accuracy_reason: The phrase is Seneca's, from Hercules Furens 385 ('sequitur superbos ultor a tergo deus'). Psalm 44:16 does speak of 'the avenger'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the classical source hidden under Burton's biblical attribution, though naming the play would make it stronger.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Taxa was the published papal schedule of fees for absolutions and dispensations.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct but adds little to what Burton himself says about the book.

answers.accuracy_reason: Complexio is the standard term for temperament, the mixture of humours.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses a technical term that a modern reader could misread.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Lucian's Cataplus (The Downward Journey), the bed and the lamp are called as witnesses against the tyrant Megapenthes.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an allusion that Burton only half names.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Nodum in scirpo quaerere' is a well-known proverb for finding difficulties where there are none.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the proverb, but Burton's own English already gives the sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Antilytron' is the Greek word used in 1 Timothy 2:6, meaning a ransom given in exchange.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that the word is Greek and links it to the verse Burton cites.

answers.accuracy_reason: The pun on mundus ('world' and 'clean') against immundus ('unclean') is real. Burton's 'fair world' does pick up the 'world' sense.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a wordplay that is lost in translation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Revelation 21:6 reads 'ego sitienti dabo de fonte aquae vitae gratis', and Burton recasts it in the passive.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already gives the verse; quoting the Vulgate wording adds only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Ecclesiastes 9:1 reads 'nescit homo utrum amore an odio dignus sit'. The added 'ira' is Burton's own.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the scriptural source behind 'saith Solomon' and shows what Burton changed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hypericum perforatum is named for the translucent oil glands in its leaves, which look like tiny holes.
answers.usefulness_reason: A pleasant explanation of the name, but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: The epigram is usually ascribed to Varro Atacinus. Licinus is traditionally the rich ex-barber, and the standard text reads 'Pompeius nullo'. The claim that Burton erred is properly hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the epigram and its targets and flags the variant reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.1.60–61, the brazen wall is 'nil conscire sibi', a clear conscience. Burton applies it to the certainty of faith.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows how Burton bends the source to a new purpose.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caecilius is the pagan speaker in the Octavius, and in ch. 10 he mocks the Christians' single, solitary God. The note correctly says Burton cuts the phrase off.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies who Caecilius is and where the words come from.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'In puris naturalibus' is the scholastic term for human nature without added grace, and the note applies it correctly to the Pelagian position.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a technical term, but the translation already conveys most of it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Zwingli's Fidei expositio (1531) was addressed to Francis I, and it famously places Socrates, Aristides, Cato and others in heaven.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the work's content that Burton is alluding to.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.116ff., Pythagoras asks 'quid meruistis, oves, placidum pecus'. The note's account of how Burton applies it is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the allusion and how Burton re-uses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Ars Poetica 410–411, on nature and art working together, and the omitted words 'res et coniurat amice' are correctly given.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the source and its original sense, which fits Burton's call for physic and counsel together.

answers.accuracy_reason: The definition of preterition (the reprobate are passed over rather than actively condemned) is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a technical theological term a reader is unlikely to know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Holding that fallen man is the object of reprobation is the infralapsarian position.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the doctrinal position behind the phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch (Themistocles 29) attributes the saying 'we should have perished had we not perished' to Themistocles in exile. The note's attribution is suitably cautious.
answers.usefulness_reason: Traces the saying to a classical source the reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 6.3–4: 'Cynthius aurem / vellit et admonuit'. Apollo tugs the poet's ear as a warning, and Burton uses the phrase of God.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgilian allusion and shows how Burton changes it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Wisdom 11:21 in the Vulgate reads 'omnia in mensura et numero et pondere disposuisti'. Burton does put the three words in a different order.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the biblical source and points out Burton's change of order.

answers.accuracy_reason: Vulgate Psalm 39:2 (English Psalm 40:1) reads 'Expectans expectavi Dominum'. The doubled form is a Hebraism, and Burton puts it in the third person.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, the idiom and Burton's change to it.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Thus' (tus) is the Latin word for frankincense.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a note on a single word, and the translation already gives 'frankincense'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pythonissa means a woman with a pythonic spirit of divination. The Vulgate uses the term for the witch of Endor, and it is linked to the Delphic Pythia.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an unusual term and the context a reader needs for it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Galatians 5:6 reads 'fides quae per caritatem operatur', not 'per dilectionem'. 'Dilectionem' is the wording Augustine and the Old Latin use.
answers.usefulness_reason: Pointing out the Pauline echo and how the syntax runs on is helpful but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Vulgate Psalm 67:2 (English Psalm 68:1) reads 'Exsurgat Deus et dissipentur inimici eius'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already names the psalm; the note only adds the English numbering and the rest of the verse.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage is from Sermo 393, De poenitentibus, which has come down among Augustine's works. The note's hedged wording fits the doubts about its authorship.
answers.usefulness_reason: It places the closing quotation and explains its point about repenting before the deathbed.

answers.accuracy_reason: The 'Ludus de morte Claudii' is the Apocolocyntosis. The quotation 'quis coacturus est?' comes from its first chapter.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the work under the title modern readers know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Terence, Eunuchus prologue, line 41: 'nullumst iam dictum quod non dictum sit prius'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It traces Wecker's tag back to its source in Terence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 11: 'scimus, et hanc veniam petimusque damusque vicissim'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes the line but gives no exact place in Horace.

answers.accuracy_reason: The ancient Vita Persi is attributed to Valerius Probus and contains 'editum librum continuo mirari homines et diripere coeperunt'. The note correctly describes the missing verb.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies Probus and the Life of Persius that Burton quotes.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 88 does have 'monstras mihi qui sint modi flebiles; monstra potius quomodo inter adversa non emittam flebilem vocem', and Burton's English paraphrases it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the exact source and shows how Burton's English reworks it.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Virgil, Eclogue 3.8, the shepherds' exchange 'novimus et qui te transversa tuentibus hircis', which is an obscene taunt.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes the half-quoted allusion and explains its bawdy point and how Burton uses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cyprian's Ad Donatum (ch. 6) attacks war; 'Madet orbis mutuo sanguine', quoted just after, comes from it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It turns a cryptic abbreviation into a named work and says what that work is about.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.23–24 reads 'prima fere vota et cunctis notissima templis / divitiae'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the missing word, riches, that gives the fragment its point after Burton's 'Queen money'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Genius as a person's guardian spirit and appetite for enjoyment, and genium defraudare (Terence) meaning to stint oneself, are both correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a Latin idiom that a modern reader would misread as 'talent'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Martial 13.2 the sentence ends at 'ipse ego quam dixi.', and 'quid dentem dente iuvabit rodere?' begins a new one. So Burton breaks off mid-line, not 'in mid-sentence'. The omitted lines on Atlas and Latinus are correctly described.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains nasutus and shows exactly what Burton cut from Martial.

answers.accuracy_reason: Intellectus agens is the scholastic-Aristotelian active intellect, and Burton uses it loosely as a gloss on 'soul'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical philosophical term and its playful use here.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Lucian's Navigium (Ploion or Euchai), Timolaus wishes for magic rings, as Burton's text says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It decodes an abbreviated sidenote into a specific dialogue and episode.

answers.accuracy_reason: Morbus Neapolitanus was a standard early-modern name for syphilis.
answers.usefulness_reason: A reader would not otherwise know which disease is meant.

answers.accuracy_reason: Mar del Sur is Spanish, Balboa's name for the Pacific, and Burton's spelling is a variant.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a helpful identification, but the translation 'South Sea' already does most of the work.

answers.accuracy_reason: Proverbial (Gellius, praef.; Erasmus), and Lucretius 6 does say swine shun marjoram.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure proverb and its classical basis.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 12.61.10 has the singular 'scribit', of a drunken poet scrawling verses in charcoal and chalk on a dark archway that people use as a privy, so 'privy walls' is loosely right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source context and notes Burton's change from singular to plural.

answers.accuracy_reason: The saying is proverbial (it is in Erasmus' Adagia). It goes back to Ennius' line 'qui ipse sibi sapiens prodesse non quit, nequiquam sapit', which Cicero quotes in Ad Familiares 7.6.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader where the proverb comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.18.29, a rich patron tells his poorer client 'meae stultitiam patiuntur opes': his wealth can afford his folly. Burton does twist this into 'wealth and folly go together'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton bends his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plagiarius first meant a kidnapper, and Martial (1.52) uses it for a literary thief. Burton's 'a trifler, a trivant' does not translate the word.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the history of the word and how Burton's gloss relates to it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Caligula 53, reports that Caligula called Seneca's writing 'harenam sine calce' (sand without lime).
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the anecdote and what the image means, which a reader would not know from Burton's bare sidenote.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Letters 115.1, reads 'quaere quid scribas, non quemadmodum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact place in Seneca and lets the reader see Burton's adaptation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Romans 14:5 reads 'unusquisque in suo sensu abundet'. Burton's version changes the mood and the word order.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a biblical echo that a reader could easily miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the closing sentence of the Phaedo, where Phaedo is speaking to Echecrates.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and corrects Burton's 'Eucrates'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Symposium (221c–d) Alcibiades says Socrates is like no one 'of the ancients or of those now living', and draws the comparisons with Achilles and Brasidas and with Nestor, Antenor and Pericles.
answers.usefulness_reason: It places the phrase in the speech Burton is paraphrasing.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ammianus 23.6 says this of the Persians ('iudicatur is beatus... qui in proelio profuderit animam'). Burton's sidenote heads it 'de Parthis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It fixes a small slip in Burton's attribution but adds little else.

answers.accuracy_reason: Georgics 4.441, on Proteus, reads 'omnia transformat sese in miracula rerum'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names Virgil as the source but not the work. The rest is a point about grammar.

answers.accuracy_reason: The translation of Adam of Bremen's Latin is accurate, and Burton's English is indeed loose.
answers.usefulness_reason: Most of the note translates the sidenote, which helps a little but gives little new context.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Satires 2.3.300–302, Horace asks the Stoic Damasippus 'qua me stultitia, quoniam non est genus unum, insanire putas?'. Burton rearranges the lines.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the speaker and the setting in Horace's dialogue.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suisset is Richard Swineshead, the fourteenth-century Oxford author of the Liber calculationum, known as 'the Calculator'. Pene is the late spelling of paene.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an obscure figure that most readers would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Timaeus 22b an Egyptian priest tells Solon that the Greeks are always children.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader who the unnamed 'he' is and where the story comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: Timaeus 22b has only 'you Greeks are always children'; the list of modern nations is Burton's own addition.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton stretches his source to cover his own age.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Germania 2 does read 'informem terris, asperam caelo, tristem cultu aspectuque', and Sabellicus clearly reverses it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the classical text behind the passage and shows how Sabellicus turns it round.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Erasmus's colloquy Diversoria the German innkeeper tells a guest who complains to look for another inn. This matches the sidenote 'Erasm. dial.'
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the literary source of the anecdote.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Historia Augusta, Spartianus (Hadrian 18) says Hadrian had bankrupts flogged on the back in the amphitheatre ('catomidiari in amphitheatro').
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Roman precedent behind Burton's harsh law against bankrupts.

answers.accuracy_reason: Claude de Seyssel wrote La Grand'Monarchie de France; Sleidan's Latin translation was published as De republica Galliae.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies an author who is hidden behind an obscure Latinised name.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucian (Against the Ignorant Book-Collector 13) does tell of Epictetus' lamp being sold for 3,000 drachmas. The word 'earthenware' is a detail I can't confirm: Lucian calls it only a clay or iron lamp in some versions, and the note states it as fact.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the anecdote and its source in Lucian.

answers.accuracy_reason: The saying 'vox et praeterea nihil', said of a plucked nightingale, is well known (Plutarch's Spartan sayings), and Lipsius' phrase echoes it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It links the sidenote to the nightingale in the main text, but gives no source for the saying.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is Horace, Satires 2.3.78–80, and Horace does read 'tristive'. Calling the missing words the sentence's 'main verb' is loose, since 'calet' belongs to the relative clause, but nothing in the note is false.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus, what Burton leaves out, and the reading Burton changes.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Satires 2.3.165–166 the words 'ambitiosus et audax; / naviget Anticyram' do occur. Burton's line is close to a direct quotation, so 'echoes' undersells it, but the note is not wrong.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Anticyra and hellebore allusion and gives the Horace locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 3.76 is addressed to Bassus, who lusts after old women and scorns girls. The standard text does read 'non haec est mentula demens'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the context of the epigram, warns that the word is obscene, and shows where Burton's wording differs.

answers.accuracy_reason: Quintilian 10.1.128 does have 'multa rerum cognitio' in the nominative, but 'omnem fere studiorum materiam' is accusative there as well. The 'multa probanda, multa etiam admiranda' comes later, at 10.1.131, so this is not one original sentence.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source as Quintilian's verdict on Seneca and shows how Burton stitches it together.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juno Moneta's temple on the Capitol held the Roman mint. That is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Roman background that Burton is playing on.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plica polonica, a matting of the hair thought endemic in Poland, is correctly described.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a medical term that a modern reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The words come from Cyprian, Ad Donatum, which asks the reader to look down on the world from a lofty watchtower ('in illa sublimi specula constitutus').
answers.usefulness_reason: The main text already names Cyprian, so naming the work adds only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 13.16–17, does contain both 'semper incipit vivere' and 'foeda hominum levitas cotidie nova vitae fundamenta ponentium, novas spes etiam in exitu inchoantium'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton condenses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Quintilian 10.1.129 reads 'in eloquendo corrupta pleraque, atque eo perniciosissima quod abundant dulcibus vitiis'. The note quotes it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton's cut sharpens a criticism that was originally about Seneca's style.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 9.36 reports the saying, and Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.104, quotes it as Democritus' own words.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the ancient sources of the saying.

answers.accuracy_reason: Gellius 19.3 has 'turpius esse... exigue atque frigide laudari quam insectanter et graviter vituperari'. The note quotes it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points out a real change that Burton makes to his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ex Ponto 1.5.15–16 reads 'me quoque, qui feci, iudice digna lini'. The note is right that Burton's sidenote gives the wrong elegy number.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects both the wording and the citation.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Epistles 1.1.4, from the passage where he gives up verse after the Odes. Reading it as giving up lyric poetry is the usual view.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes Burton's bare 'Hor.' and shows that the line fits his own retraction.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.4.9–10, says Lucilius dictated two hundred verses an hour 'stans pede in uno'. The note is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and explains who 'he' is in Burton's sentence.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.19.2–3 does say that poems written by water-drinkers cannot please or live long, and the note rightly hedges the allusion with 'probably'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows the literary joke behind Burton's claim that he drinks no wine.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 9.2 reads 'antistans mihi milibus trecentis', said of Veranius, the friend he prefers above 300,000 others; the change from participle to verb is described correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton turns it to a new use.

answers.accuracy_reason: The plucked-nightingale saying is in Plutarch's Sayings of Spartans (Moralia 233A), and the Latin form is a version of the Greek.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the anecdote behind 'as he said of a nightingale'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Epistles 108.29 has the ox, the dog and the stork in one meadow; it is not about Pontus and has no maiden. The note's judgement is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It finds the real source and points out what Burton added and got wrong.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Topiarius' means an ornamental gardener, and the dogs lapping the Nile on the run for fear of crocodiles is a well-known proverb (Pliny, Phaedrus, Macrobius).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical term and a proverbial allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage is from Apocolocyntosis 1, and Seneca's next words, 'ego scio me liberum factum', are echoed in Burton's 'I am a free man born'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the locus and shows how Burton reworks the sentence that follows.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Virgil, Eclogues 7.4–5, said of Corydon and Thyrsis.
answers.usefulness_reason: The exact locus and the context add a little to the sidenote 'Virg.', but a reader loses little without it.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Cicero, Brutus 187, Antigenidas tells his pupil 'mihi cane et Musis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and gives the meaning: a private life, not seeking applause.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 2.1.115–16 has the indicative 'promittunt medici'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is mostly a grammar point and does not give the exact locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is the usual explanation of the proverb (Horace, Epistles 1.18.15), and Burton does gloss it as 'moonshine in the water'.
answers.usefulness_reason: The gloss is correct but slight, and it gives no source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The proverb comes from the story of Apelles and the cobbler (Pliny, Natural History 35.85).
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the anecdote behind the proverb.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 410–11 has this wording and says it of natural talent and training.
answers.usefulness_reason: It completes the quotation and shows how Burton changes its use.

answers.accuracy_reason: In the Tablet of Cebes, Deceit (Apatē) gives everyone entering life a drink of error and ignorance. The note's 'cup of Error and Ignorance' is a fair summary of that.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the allegory Burton names but does not describe.

answers.accuracy_reason: The sidenote 'Praefat. hist.' points to the preface of Giovio's Histories, where he speaks of his long years at the papal court. Burton's own text sets his 30 years at Christ Church against this.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the speaker and shows how Burton adapts the boast to himself.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Ars Poetica 140, 'quanto rectius hic qui nil molitur inepte', and it is said of Homer. Burton does turn it into a question.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton changes the line, though it could have named the Ars Poetica.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the standard account of the andabatae: gladiators who fought blind in closed helmets.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure term and the image of blind Fortune that goes with it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Proverbs 26:4 in the Vulgate reads 'Ne respondeas stulto iuxta stultitiam suam'. The note quotes it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the biblical source and gives the Vulgate wording, but this famous proverb is easy to recognise, so a reader loses little without it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Letters 10.96, does read 'Fuerunt alii similis amentiae'. Older editions numbered this letter 97, which matches Burton's sidenote.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the famous letter about the Christians and explains Burton's reference number.

answers.accuracy_reason: The lines are Lucretius 3.1043–44 on Epicurus, where 'omnis' is the object of 'restinxit'. The note's remark on Burton's punctuation is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and its subject, plus a point about how Burton's punctuation shifts the sense.

answers.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch both record that Anaxagoras was nicknamed Nous ('Mind') because of his doctrine.
answers.usefulness_reason: It briefly explains the nickname; this is slight but helpful.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lowering the fasces (fasces submittere) was the Roman gesture of deference, as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the Roman image but does not identify the source of the couplet.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.34.2–3 reads 'insanientis dum sapientiae / consultus erro', and it refers to Epicurean philosophy. Burton's own sidenote agrees.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the full Horace line and its sense, which the fragment Burton quotes hides.

answers.accuracy_reason: The allusion to Lucius, turned into an ass in Apuleius' Golden Ass, is right. The reading of 'inverted' is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an allusion the reader needs in order to follow the image.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Sileni of Alcibiades come from Plato's Symposium 215 and Erasmus' adage 'Sileni Alcibiadis'. That adage itself describes inverted Sileni.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of the image and explains why the Sileni are 'inverted'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.3.50–51 reads 'ille sinistrorsum, hic dextrorsum abit, unus utrique / error, sed variis illudit partibus'. Burton does leave out 'abit' and add 'omnes'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names Horace as the source, but it is mostly about Burton's wording and gives no locus or context (the Damasippus satire).

answers.accuracy_reason: The story of Hippocrates' visit to Democritus does come from the pseudo-Hippocratic letter to Damagetus, and Democritus is the speaker ('inquit').
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of the anecdote and says who is speaking.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.848 has 'de marmore' and comes in Anchises' speech about the arts of other nations. Burton applies it to lifelike statues.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the allusion, its original context and how Burton redirects it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 5.117 has 'servas'. Erasmus' Adagia collects 'Cretizare cum Cretensi' (lie to a Cretan, since Cretans were proverbial liars). 'Vulpinarier' means to play the fox.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies Persius and the Erasmian proverb and explains the Cretan allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: This is the opening of Horace, Satires 1.1, and the standard text reads 'seu fors obiecerit'. The line continues with 'laudet diversa sequentis', as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the locus and the cut-off clause that fits Burton's point.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.2.42–43, the rustic waits for the river to run dry while it glides on for ever.
answers.usefulness_reason: The context in Horace sharpens Burton's river image.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.6 mocks an interminable 'Orestes' that has filled the margins and the back of the roll and is still unfinished.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the joke Burton borrows and how he applies it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan 1.6–7 ('infestisque obvia signis / signa') describes civil war.
answers.usefulness_reason: Knowing it is civil war gives point to Burton's use of it for warring sects.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca's lost De superstitione survives in fragments quoted in Augustine, City of God 6.10, including this passage.
answers.usefulness_reason: It tells the reader where a lost work's words are preserved.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.3.38 reads 'caelum ipsum petimus stultitia'. Burton makes the verb passive.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the ode and how Burton alters it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, In Catilinam 1.30 has 'haec tam adulta rei publicae pestis', and the note hedges the identification appropriately.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points to a likely Ciceronian echo that a reader would miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 9.641 has 'sic itur ad astra'. Burton's 'hac' and the irony are correctly described.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is a correct identification of a familiar tag, but it gives little context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Insulsus does literally mean 'unsalted', hence 'witless'. 'Vos estis sal terrae' is Matthew 5:13.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the pun on salt, which a reader without Latin would miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.15 reads 'quo me cumque rapit tempestas, deferor hospes'. Burton does change me to se.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton changed it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.41 reads 'unius ob noxam et furias Aiacis Oilei'. Burton cuts the line off before the name.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton is echoing the epic, where many suffer for one man's crime.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Sic itur ad astra' is Aeneid 9.641. Burton writes hac, and he means it ironically of the conquerors' fame.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion and points out the irony.

answers.accuracy_reason: Pro Milone 4.11 reads 'silent enim leges inter arma'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's sidenote already says 'Tully', so the note adds only the exact place and wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan 10.407 reads 'nulla fides pietasque viris qui castra sequuntur'. Burton does change nulla to rara and pietas to probitas.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton softened his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.12 reads 'quamquam animus meminisse horret', where Aeneas begins his account of Troy's fall.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion, which carries the fall of Troy into Burton's list of sacked cities.

answers.accuracy_reason: In De anima 30, Tertullian calls plague, famine and wars a 'tonsura insolescentis generis humani'. Burton does answer 'sed ruina'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives Tertullian's context and explains Burton's retort.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucan 1.8 reads 'quis furor, o cives, quae tanta licentia ferri?' This comes in the poem's opening lament over civil war.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion, which fits the civil-war context.

answers.accuracy_reason: The source and the 'quare' point are right: Aeneid 7.340, Juno to Allecto. The last clause is confused, though. Juventus is singular in Virgil too; what Burton changed is the verbs, which he made plural (volunt, poscunt, rapiunt).
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgilian source and its context in Juno's speech.

answers.accuracy_reason: Agricola 30 reads 'auferre trucidare rapere falsis nominibus imperium'. Burton puts 'virtutem vocant' where Tacitus has imperium.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton changed Calgacus' words.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.12 reads 'sed sum petulanti splene cachinno'. It was a common ancient belief that the spleen was the seat of laughter.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the physiology behind the phrase and gives its source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.9.66 reads 'meum iecur urere bilis', and the liver was the seat of anger. The comment on Burton's following clause is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Horatian source and explains the bile-and-liver idea.

answers.accuracy_reason: Nicolaus of Damascus, the 'Damascen' of Burton's text, does report that the Celts thought it shameful to flee a falling wall or house.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the obscure 'Damascen' and the story behind the phrase.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 7.461 reads 'saevit amor ferri et scelerata insania belli', and Burton's genitive 'scelerati' does attach the curse to the war.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the Virgilian source and points out how Burton altered it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 8.96 reads 'cum Pansa eripiat quidquid tibi Natta reliquit', in a passage on provincial governors, and the note rightly hedges that Burton gives it loosely.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the names and points to the Juvenal source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The pirate's retort to Alexander appears in Augustine, City of God 4.4, and in Cicero, De re publica 3 (a fragment).
answers.usefulness_reason: It sends the reader to the better-known versions of the story Burton credits to Curtius.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 4.13–14 the thought 'nam quod turpe bonis… decebat Crispinum' is complete at Crispinum, and 'quid agas…' begins a new clause, so saying the quotation breaks off mid-sentence is questionable. The rest of the note is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the stock names and who Crispinus was.

answers.accuracy_reason: It reads the cry correctly as egging on both quarrelling parties, and Xanthippe was proverbially a shrew.
answers.usefulness_reason: It clarifies the joke but names no source, so it is fairly slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Satyricon 116, gives 'aut captantur aut captant' (legacy-hunting at Croton) and the 'cadavera… corvi' comparison as separate sentences.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the technical sense of captare and shows how Burton joined two sentences.

answers.accuracy_reason: A succenturiator was a soldier added to fill up a century, a reserve or substitute, so the gloss is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses a rare military term that shapes Burton's self-presentation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Annals 4.18, on Silius and Tiberius, has 'dum videntur exsolvi posse'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It pins down the source behind the bare 'Tac.' and links it to Silius in the main text.

answers.accuracy_reason: Manius Curius Dentatus was the byword for old Roman frugality, and the Bacchanalia were riotous revels. (The line is Juvenal 2.3.)
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the antithesis a modern reader may miss, though it omits the Juvenal source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.73 has the 'turba Remi', which 'sequitur fortunam… et odit damnatos', in the passage on Sejanus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the subject but adds little beyond the translation and Burton's own context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.56: the complaisant husband who stares at the ceiling while his wife's lover is with her. The note identifies him correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the allusion and the scene behind 'wittol', which a reader would not otherwise get.

answers.accuracy_reason: Utopia book 1 has the sheep that 'homines devorent ipsos... oppida vastent'. Burton paraphrases it, as the note says.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the enclosure context and that Burton paraphrases rather than quotes.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.65–66: Aeneas tells Dido about Sinon's treachery, 'crimine ab uno disce omnis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgilian source and its original application.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Cat. 1.32 Cicero wishes that what each man thinks of the republic were written on his forehead. The locus is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the exact locus, which Burton omits.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.188 is 'multos da, Iuppiter, annos', and Seneca Ep. 10.5 reads 'quod scire hominem nolunt'. Both claims are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It separates the two sources Burton has blended and notes his altered reading.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 334 ('aut simul et iucunda et idonea dicere vitae') and 344 ('lectorem delectando pariterque monendo') are correctly identified, and the substitution is correctly reported.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton splices two lines and changes one of them.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.118 reads 'non sani esse hominis non sanus iuret Orestes'. The note quotes it and glosses it correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton turns Persius's statement into a question.

answers.accuracy_reason: Harpaste in Seneca Ep. 50 is correctly identified, and the note hedges suitably on the phrase itself.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names 'Seneca's blind woman', whom Burton leaves unexplained.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace Epist. 1.2.38–39 is a question beginning 'nam cur'. 'est' does come from edo.
answers.usefulness_reason: The gloss on 'est' prevents a likely misreading, and the locus is given.

answers.accuracy_reason: Clodius was notorious for the Bona Dea sacrilege and for adultery. The tag is Juvenal 2.27.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the irony that makes the tag work, though it could have cited Juvenal.

answers.accuracy_reason: I recall the saying from Pliny's Natural History (book 18, on Cato), where the point seems to be practical gain from another's extravagance, such as buying a farm someone else has built up. The gloss 'learning by their mistakes' does not obviously fit that context, and the note does not say which Pliny work it means.
answers.usefulness_reason: The contrast in sense is worth having, but the source is vague and the gloss is uncertain.

answers.accuracy_reason: Catullus 22.21 reads 'sed non videmus manticae quod in tergo est', and the fable of the two wallets is Aesop's (Phaedrus 4.10).
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the fable behind the image and identifies the verbal source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 3: Agamemnon says teachers must 'cum insanientibus furere' or be left alone in their schools ('soli in scholis relinquentur').
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the original context, which changes the quotation's point.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'amabilis insania' is Odes 3.4.5–6 and 'mentis gratissimus error' is Epistles 2.2.140; both loci are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies two sources Burton has joined together.

answers.accuracy_reason: Epistles 2.2.128–140 tells of the man of Argos who sat in an empty theatre imagining he heard tragedies; once cured, he says 'pol me occidistis, amici'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Supplies the anecdote behind the quotation, which fits Burton's point about pleasing delusions.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.283–284 reads 'clames licet et mare caelo / confundas'; 'surdo narrare' is proverbial and appears in Terence (Heaut. 222).
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows a stitched quotation and where each part comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: De Senectute 85 reads 'libenter erro; nec mihi hunc errorem... extorqueri volo', said of belief in the soul's immortality.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows how Burton turns Cicero's hopeful belief into a picture of stubbornness.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 2 says those reared in the rhetoric schools can no more 'sapere' than kitchen-dwellers can smell sweet; the double sense of sapere is real.
answers.usefulness_reason: The pun and the source context both help the reader.

answers.accuracy_reason: Amphitryo prologue, line 35, spoken by Mercury: 'nam iuste ab iniustis petere insipientia est'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains Burton's otherwise puzzling phrase 'our comical Mercury'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Tusculans 3.59 Cicero gives his own Latin version of lines from Euripides (Hypsipyle).
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the 'old Poem' Burton mentions.

answers.accuracy_reason: Satires 2.7.83–88; the Stoic sage as a smooth sphere is the standard reading of 'teres atque rotundus'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains a well-known image a reader may not grasp.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 13.26–27 continues: 'numera, vix sunt totidem quot / Thebarum portae vel divitis ostia Nili'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Restores the part Burton leaves off and shows the joke in it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The meanings of the names (forethought and afterthought) are correct, and the phrase reads as proverbial.
answers.usefulness_reason: A helpful gloss on the names, but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: Asclepius 6 has 'magnum miraculum est homo'; Burton's 'homo sapiens' version is an elaboration of it.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies the Hermetic source and Burton's change to it.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is a Greek proverb, quoted by Plato in the Phaedo (69c): 'many are the thyrsus-bearers, but few the Bacchoi'. The note's explanation is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names where the saying comes from and explains the thyrsus emblem, which a reader may not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suisset is Richard Swineshead, 'the Calculator'. Vives mocks his kind of logical subtlety in De causis corruptarum artium, the work in Burton's sidenote.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies 'Suisset' as Swineshead and says what is being mocked, which a reader needs.

answers.accuracy_reason: Theriac (Venice treacle) did contain viper's flesh.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the medical term and why the antidote comes from the poison.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 3.36, reads 'insanire libet quoniam tibi'. 'Lubet' is the older form of 'libet'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton changes its sense by cutting the words from their context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Phaedrus, prologue to book 5, reads 'novo si marmori adscripserunt Praxitelen suo'. The note's account of the change and of the forgery is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, shows how Burton changes it, and explains the point about forgery.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.374: Aeneas speaks to his mother Venus, disguised as a huntress, about his troubles.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the dramatic context and shows how Burton applies it to himself, though the line reference would help.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Salus populi suprema lex esto' is from Cicero, De legibus 3.8. Plato's Republic 4 (420b) holds that the aim is the happiness of the whole city, not of one class.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source of a famous maxim Burton leaves uncited and notes his change of wording.

answers.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 9.28, reads 'miserae'. Mantua's lands were taken because they bordered Cremona's, which had been confiscated.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the historical point of the line and how it fits Burton's 'bad neighbours'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.630 reads 'Non ignara mali', spoken by Dido to Aeneas.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already names Dido and Virgil, so the note adds mainly a textual variant.

answers.accuracy_reason: De oratore 1.200 reads 'est enim sine dubio domus iuris consulti totius oraculum civitatis'. The quotation and locus are correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It adds the exact locus and an omitted word to a source Burton already names; this is useful but slight.

answers.accuracy_reason: It is proverbial, and Juvenal 7.154 has 'crambe repetita'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the proverb and points to the classical parallel.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plutarch, Cato Major 23: Cato mocked Isocrates' pupils as growing old in his school, as if to plead their cases before Minos in Hades.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source of Burton's anecdote and explains his joke about pleading in hell.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.53.12 reads 'stat contra dicitque tibi tua pagina "fur es"', addressed to the plagiarist Fidentinus. Burton does change the pronouns to 'mihi mea'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton turns Martial's charge against himself, which is the point of the allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Livy 36.32 Quinctius compares the Achaeans in the Peloponnese to a tortoise drawn into its shell. Burton condenses this into a Latin tag.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact locus and shows that Burton is adapting the image, not quoting it.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Virgil reference (Aen. 2.6–8) and the omitted middle line are right. But calling the second question 'unfinished in Burton's text' is misleading: Burton finishes it in English ('who is he that can sufficiently condole...'). The claim that it is Gerbelius's own wording also rests only on Burton's 'so he prosecutes it'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Virgil, the line Burton leaves out, and the route through Gerbelius.

answers.accuracy_reason: Grotius's Mare Liberum (1609) argued for the freedom of the seas in the Dutch interest. The phrase was central to the Anglo-Dutch fishing disputes, so calling it a catchword is fair.
answers.usefulness_reason: A reader may not know the topical point: Burton is borrowing the title of a contemporary political pamphlet.

answers.accuracy_reason: Herodotus 2.177 records Amasis's law that every Egyptian must declare his means of living each year. The Latin here is not Herodotus's wording.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the ancient source and says plainly that Burton's Latin is not a quotation of it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Annals 13.53 has these words and credits the Arar–Moselle canal plan to L. Antistius Vetus under Nero. Burton's 'Domitian' is therefore an error.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and corrects Burton's mistake about the emperor.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Sus Minervam (docet)' is in Erasmus's Adagia (1.1.40). The note's account of its sense and of how Burton applies it is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: The translation already gives the sense; the reference to the Adagia adds only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line is Terence, Andria 68: 'obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit'. The verjuice saying is a separate English proverb.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source of 'as he said' and the half of the line that Burton leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Augeae' is the correct genitive, and cleansing the Augean stables was proverbial for reforming deep-rooted abuses (it is in Erasmus).
answers.usefulness_reason: The translation already makes the allusion clear; the note on the spelling is mostly a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 2.1.117 reads 'scribimus indocti doctique poemata passim'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It supplies the missing words, but it does not name the work, so a reader gets only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.63 reads 'iubeas miserum esse libenter', so Burton's 'stultos' does replace 'miserum'. The note is suitably hedged.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies a hidden adaptation of Horace and says what Burton changed.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 9–10 reads 'pictoribus atque poetis / quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas'. The note quotes it correctly, though it does not name the work.
answers.usefulness_reason: The missing words carry the point Burton relies on in 'You know what liberty Poets ever had'.

answers.accuracy_reason: In More's prefatory letter to Peter Giles, a theologian wants to be made bishop of Utopia and counts it 'sanctum ambitum'. The sense 'canvassing for office' is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the allusion behind Burton's 'Archbishopric of Utopia', which a reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, De Officiis 1.22, gives the maxim as Plato's (Letter 9) and goes on to say that country and friends each claim a share in us.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source of the tag and the rest of the saying, which Burton cuts off with '&c'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The line comes from Cicero's De consulatu suo, and Cicero quotes it himself in De Officiis 1.77 and In Pisonem.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the symbolic sense of the toga, which bears on the 'scholars before soldiers' context.

answers.accuracy_reason: The passage matches Plutarch, Lycurgus 26, on elections to the gerousia ('not the swiftest among the swift…'). The note rightly hedges the identification.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the likely source, the Spartan election of elders, for a passage Burton leaves without a citation.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Indulge genio' is in Persius 5.151, and the note explains genius correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the idiom and gives a classical parallel.

answers.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus 14 (639c, citing Berosus) describes the Sacaea as a Babylonian feast in which servants rule their masters. The note's description is accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It is correct, but Burton's own sidenote and his Saturnalia comparison already give most of this.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Historia Augusta, Hadrian 18.9, Hadrian orders that spendthrift bankrupts be 'catomidiari in amphitheatro'. The etymology and the explanation of the punishment are standard.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the meaning of a rare technical term that Burton only glosses loosely.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 2.31 to 2.33 speaks of laws 'ipsis Veneri Martique timendas', in the passage on Domitian reviving the adultery law. The note is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Juvenal allusion and its ironic context.

answers.accuracy_reason: Politics 7.16 (1335a) recommends marriage at about 37 for men and 18 for women, so Burton's figures misreport Aristotle.
answers.usefulness_reason: It corrects Burton's misstatement of his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boece's Scotorum Historia, book 1, describes the customs of the ancient Scots. Burton's main text does soften the rule to a ban on marriage.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton tones down his source.

answers.accuracy_reason: The monte di pietà was a charitable pawn-lending institution that charged low interest.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton already glosses the term ('bank of charity… lend money upon easy pawns'), so the note adds little.

answers.accuracy_reason: The primum mobile was the outermost sphere in the Ptolemaic system, and its daily turning carried all the heavens. That fits Burton's use of it as a standard of measure.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a technical cosmological term, which matters here because the translation 'Prime Mover' is misleading.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Philippics 5.5, has 'nervos belli, pecuniam infinitam'; the phrase is a common proverb for money.
answers.usefulness_reason: Burton's own text already says money is the sinew of war; the Cicero parallel adds only a little.

answers.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.85–86 ends with 'farrago libelli est'; Burton leaves out 'est', and the gloss on farrago is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives the exact source, Burton's change to it and the sense of farrago.

answers.accuracy_reason: Plautus, Aulularia 325, has 'homo trium litterarum' for 'fur' (thief).
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the riddle and gives its classical source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Cicero (Ad Fam. 7.25) has 'manum de tabula'. In Pliny (NH 35.80), Apelles says he knew when to take his hand from a picture and Protogenes did not, so the note's short version is acceptable.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the proverb and where it comes from.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ennius's line as Cicero quotes it (Pro Murena 30) reads 'pellitur e medio sapientia'. The proverb appears in Apocolocyntosis 1, a work traditionally attributed to Seneca.
answers.usefulness_reason: Identifies both sources and shows how Burton changed the first.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.8, describes the Iliad; the gloss on aestus is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Points to the Horatian context, which suits Burton's 'Iliads, Aeneids'.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.14, reads 'quidquid delirant reges plectuntur Achivi'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Names the author and gives the full line, but no locus; the note about the omitted word is a minor point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 2.1.270, reads 'et piper et quidquid chartis amicitur ineptis'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Restores the pepper that Burton's 'lap spice in' echoes and explains the joke about bad poets' paper.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, De tranquillitate animi 17.10, attributes the saying to Aristotle.
answers.usefulness_reason: Shows the route by which the 'Aristotle' saying reached Burton.

answers.accuracy_reason: 'Doctor Irrefragabilis' was Alexander of Hales's title. Occam was called 'Venerabilis Inceptor' and 'Doctor Invincibilis'. Scotus was the 'Subtle Doctor'.
answers.usefulness_reason: Points out that Burton gives Occam a title that belonged to another man, which a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: The description of the tmesis is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: Explains the wordplay, though the translation already shows most of it; the last sentence is a translator's working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Anticyra was famous for hellebore, the classical remedy for madness.
answers.usefulness_reason: Gives useful background but does not identify the line as Horace's (Ars Poetica 300).

answers.accuracy_reason: The definition 'vir bonus dicendi peritus' (Cato, quoted by Quintilian) is the classical one, and the phrase does invert it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It points to the definition behind Burton's jab, which gives it its point.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.640 describes the phantom of Aeneas that Juno makes. Burton's syntax allows the line to be read as said of the nightingale and then applied to the orator.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and shows how Burton turns it to a new use.

answers.accuracy_reason: Epiphyllides are the small gleaning grapes. At Frogs 92 Aristophanes uses the word of feeble young poets, which matches Burton's sidenote.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains an obscure Greek word and the Aristophanic allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate wording of Job 28:13 is quoted correctly, and verse 12 asks 'Sapientia vero ubi invenitur?'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton adapts the verse, but the sidenote already gives Job 28.

answers.accuracy_reason: Livy 21.4.9 reads 'has tantas viri virtutes ingentia vitia aequabant', said of Hannibal.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and shows how Burton compresses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 4.16 is correct, and Anticyra was famous for its hellebore.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source and explains the allusion to the madness cure.

answers.accuracy_reason: In NH 36.75 Pliny calls the pyramids 'regum pecuniae otiosa ac stulta ostentatio'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It locates the source of Burton's phrase, which the sidenote gives only as a book number.

answers.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 1.414 reads 'inde genus durum sumus'. The remark about the gloss is accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the Ovidian line behind the Deucalion allusion.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ulrich von Hutten's 'Nemo' does play on proverbs about 'no one' as praise of 'Nobody'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains Hutten's joke, without which the passage is hard to follow.

answers.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.110 reads 'per me equidem sint omnia protinus alba', and the sense given for 'white' is right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source and explains the sense of 'white'.

answers.accuracy_reason: The hellebore association and the reading of dolabra as boring the skull, matching Burton's gloss, are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains both halves of the remedy and what Burton's gloss leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: At D.L. 7.127 Chrysippus says virtue can be lost through drunkenness and melancholy.
answers.usefulness_reason: It glosses the medical term and gives the ancient source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.106–108 is quoted correctly. The changes Burton makes (ad summum, no est) are described accurately, and pituita does mean phlegm or catarrh.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source, shows how Burton compresses it and supplies the missing predicate.

answers.accuracy_reason: Neuhaus's 1618 tract on the Rosicrucians has the subtitle 'An sint? Quales sint? Unde nomen illud sibi asciverint?'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the tract Burton's sidenote is quoting.

answers.accuracy_reason: The Homer source is right: Odyssey 10.495, on Tiresias among the dead. But in Burton the line is the 'parasitical testimony of Dousa' about Lipsius, so it is Dousa who applies it; Burton quotes it ironically. The note credits the application to Burton.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the Homeric original and points out the irony.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 3.11–12 does continue 'omnia nos itidem depascimur aurea dicta', addressed to Epicurus.
answers.usefulness_reason: The sidenote already names Lucretius; the note adds the continuation but neither the locus nor the addressee.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.2.27, 'nos numerus sumus' means mere ciphers who make up the count, and Burton does turn it on himself.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the sense of the tag and how Burton uses it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.4.103–105 is quoted correctly, and the omissions and change of word order are described accurately.
answers.usefulness_reason: This is mostly a textual comparison with the source, of modest interest to a reader.

answers.accuracy_reason: Martial 10.33.10 is 'parcere personis, dicere de vitiis'; 'licuit semperque licebit' is Ars Poetica 58.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton has joined two separate sources into one quotation.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace's line reads 'quamquam ridentem dicere verum / quid vetat?'. So 'quamvis' is Burton's substitute for 'quamquam', not something he added.
answers.usefulness_reason: Giving the locus is useful; the rest is a textual detail, and it is wrong.

answers.accuracy_reason: Eunuchus prologue 4–6 does continue 'responsum, non dictum esse, quia laesit prior', and the change of sense when Burton breaks off is correctly described.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton's cut changes the meaning of the source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Annals 15.68 has 'asperis facetiis… quae ubi multum ex vero traxere, acrem sui memoriam relinquunt'. The changes are described accurately, and so is Burton's English, which leaves out the clause about truth.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows how Burton adapts Tacitus and what his own English leaves out.

answers.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Odes 4.1.15, 'centum puer artium' describes Paullus Fabius Maximus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the allusion, but briefly and without giving the locus.

answers.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Epistles 84.8 reads 'etiam si apparuerit unde sumptum sit, aliud tamen esse quam unde sumptum est appareat', in a passage on digesting what one reads.
answers.usefulness_reason: It shows that Burton has split one sentence of Seneca and explains the image of digestion.

answers.accuracy_reason: The citations check out: Persius 1.12 ('sum petulanti splene cachinno'), Martial 10.25.4, Apuleius's festival of Risus (Met. 2–3) and the pseudo-Hippocratic letter to Damagetus. 'Ne tu Democrite sapis' is Burton's paraphrase of those letters rather than a quotation, but the note's 'comes from' is close enough.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies several allusions (Persius, Martial, Apuleius, the Hippocratic letters) and explains terms a reader would not know.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.1.44–46 is quoted correctly, and the note is right that Burton changes 'qui' to 'Si' and drops 'flebit'.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and shows how Burton adapts it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Veratrum is indeed hellebore, the classical remedy for madness, and the summary of the pseudo-Hippocratic letter to Damagetus is accurate.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the medical term and gives the story the sidenote paraphrases.

answers.accuracy_reason: A tradux is a vine layer, and 'ex traduce' is the standard term for traducianism. Reading 'as some hold' as Burton's own comment is correct.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains a theological technical term a reader would likely not know; the last sentence is only a working note.

answers.accuracy_reason: Horace Epist. 1.4.10-11 reads 'et cui / gratia, fama, valetudo contingat abunde', so both the 'et cui' continuation and the fama/forma variant are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: Mostly a textual-variant and syntax note that a general reader barely needs, and it names no source.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hosea 13:9 (Vulgate) reads 'Perditio tua, Israel', which is a plausible source, but the claim of a 'proverbial form' with 'ex te' is unconfirmed.
answers.usefulness_reason: Pointing to the Hosea verse is helpful, but the link is loose.

answers.accuracy_reason: Entelechy is Aristotle's term (De anima 2.1) for actuality or completion, and Burton does follow it with the Latin gloss and then the English.
answers.usefulness_reason: Correct and mildly helpful gloss of a technical term, though Burton's own glosses already explain it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Caninus appetitus, fames canina and bulimia are the standard terms for ravenous, insatiable hunger.
answers.usefulness_reason: A correct but slight gloss of a term that is fairly clear from the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Augustine, Conf. 11.29 has 'tumultuosis varietatibus dilaniantur cogitationes meae', so 'multuosis' is probably a corruption, and the note hedges it properly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It identifies the source, explains the garbled word, and shows how Burton altered the Latin.

answers.accuracy_reason: Lucida intervalla is the standard medical and legal term for periods of sanity between bouts of madness.
answers.usefulness_reason: A correct gloss of a term that is fairly transparent.

answers.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Cons. 3 pr. 7 reads 'Tristes vero voluptatum exitus esse, quisquis reminisci libidinum suarum volet, intelliget', so the source and the libidinum/voluptatum change are right.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the exact source and shows how Burton's quotation differs from it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Aurum potabile was an alchemical and medical cordial of 'drinkable gold', and Burton's pun on drinking away one's estate is correctly described.
answers.usefulness_reason: It explains the technical term and the joke, which a modern reader would otherwise miss.

answers.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Domitian 13 gives 'Dominus et deus noster hoc fieri iubet', and the note lists Burton's changes correctly.
answers.usefulness_reason: It gives the source and the context of Domitian's formula, and shows how Burton adapted it.

answers.accuracy_reason: Hippocrates, Aphorisms 6.23 says only that prolonged fear or despondency is melancholic, so Burton's 'causes and offspring… in a circle' expands on it.
answers.usefulness_reason: It warns the reader that Burton's attribution overstates what Hippocrates says.

answers.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Met. 3.353 reads 'multi illum iuvenes, multae cupiere puellae', and the passage is about Narcissus.
answers.usefulness_reason: It names the source, but most of the note is a minor textual variant.
